A room is a chat of the owner with several agents, each an ordinary session of its own with its
own model and system prompt; what an agent writes at the end of its turn goes to the room by
itself, so the agent needs no tool for it (user decision, 2026-11-15). The room is a session with
no workspace, no worker and no agent (`agent.runtime: none`, `room_mode`, §3 Session): no
process starts for it, it takes no `model`, `permission_mode`, `browser` or pause (`409 room`, §6), and
it is no target of `hqc_rename` with `session` or an agent's schedule (`not_found`, as a service
session), nor of `hqc_ask` (`invalid_args`: a room answers no ask, §7). Since 0.172 it is a target of `hqc_send` from a session that is not one of
its agents (user decision, 2026-11-17): the message goes into the room as `hqc_room`'s first message does (§7) — a
`peer.message` from the sender in the room, its chain moved on as a send's, its files with it —
and the room hands it to its agents as the owner's message (in a `conversation` the speaker, else
the first agent; in a `council` every agent); the posts limit counts from it, and the room tells
the sender when the round ends (a room's notice, below). An archived room is
`not_found` to a send, as an archived session is. An agent of the room sends nothing to its own room (`invalid_args`: its final
message is posted there). An agent of a room sends nothing to another agent of the
same room with `hqc_send` or `hqc_ask`, nor schedules it one with `hqc_schedule` (its own session
it may): `invalid_args` "<target's address> is another agent of
your room: your final message is posted to the room, and the other agents read it there; answer
there, not in a message to them" (an agent told to discuss with the others asked one of them
with `hqc_ask`, and the answer went past the room). `POST /api/projects/{id}/rooms` (§6) makes it with its
agents' sessions, whose `room_id` and `spawned_by` are the room, each with its `name`, `model`
or `provider_id` (§3 Provider) and `system_prompt`, in the order of the request: the room's
order of its agents (`created_at`, then `id`). An agent's session title is its name in the
room: `hqc_rename` without `session` from an agent's session is `invalid_args` ("this session's
title is its name in its room: it is not renamed"), since the requirement of §7.2 has every agent
rename its own session. `POST /archive` archives the room alone, and `POST /unarchive` takes it
back although it has no workspace (§6). `DELETE /api/sessions/{id}` of a room deletes its agents'
sessions first, archived ones too, each as a session is deleted (§17.4: its agent killed, its
files on the worker cleaned up), then the room: no agent is left behind as a session of its own.

- The owner's message in the room (`POST /input`) is a `user.message` there without
  `delivery`. An agent of the room that is not archived gets it in its input queue as a
  `peer.message` from the room: `from_session_id` the room, `from` its address, the message's
  `text` and `artifact_ids` (linked to the agent's session, so its worker downloads them),
  `mode: send`, `room {session_id, seq}` (the room and the message's `seq` there), its
  `event_id` derived from the agent and the message. Its `artifact_ids` are the files of the
  event it carries, then those of the messages that go in front of it (below), each once; all
  of them are linked to the agent's session. An agent whose process is stopped starts
  with it. In a `council` it wakes every agent at once. In a `conversation` it wakes one: the
  speaker (below) when there is one, else the first agent in the room's order; the speaker's
  turn that is running takes it in (below; user decision, 2026-11-16). A repeat of the owner's
  message (the same `client_op_id`, §6) hands it again to the same agents, so one the first
  request did not reach gets it and the others store nothing twice: in a `conversation` the
  speaker is taken as of the message (the events before its `seq`).
- Such an input goes to the agent without `session.input.peer`: the send's header would tell
  the agent to do what another session asks as if its owner asked. The hub writes the text it
  goes with, as for a fork's note (§6), and the feed keeps the text as sent; an input whose room
  the hub does not find goes with the header of a send instead, so that no agent's text reaches
  another as the owner's. When other agents posted in the room after this agent's previous
  input from the room and before the event this one carries (by `seq` in the room, so an input
  sent again carries the same), or in a `conversation` the owner wrote there, the line `[hqc
  room <room address> | since your last turn]`; oldest first, per post the line `[hqc room
  <room address> | post from "<agent's name>" (<agent's address>)]`, per owner's message (in a
  `conversation` only: in a `council` every agent gets each of them) the line `[hqc room <room
  address> | message from your owner]`, per message of a session that is not one of the room's
  agents (the one that made the room with `hqc_room`, or one that sent with `hqc_send`, §7; in a
  `conversation` only, as the owner's) the line `[hqc room <room address> | message from
  "<its title>" (<its address>)]`, its text and an empty line, as the worker's block of buffered
  sends (§7.1); and `---`; then the line `[hqc room <room address> | from <your owner | "the
  sending session's title" (its address)> | your final message is posted to the room, where the
  other agents read it: do not message them | reply exactly NO_REPLY to post nothing | your name
  in the room is "<the agent's own name>": do not rename your session]`, an empty line and the
  text. The agents see each other by their names in the room (user decision, 2026-11-17), each
  next to the address the hub stored with the post or the input (`from`). A name is the
  session's title when the hub sends the input, which any session of the owner may change
  (`hqc_rename` with `session`, `PATCH`), so in a hub's line it loses every invisible character
  (zero-width, bidi, variation selectors; since 0.175), and every
  `|`, `[`, `]`, `"`, every character that folds to one of them by NFKC (fullwidth `［］｜＂`,
  since 0.175), every Hangul filler (shown as a blank, since 0.175) and every control character
  becomes a space (runs of spaces one, trimmed), and
  it stands in double
  quotes, which the hub's own words (`your owner`) never take: a title cannot close the line or
  pass for another sender or the owner, and the address next to it names the sender. A title
  that comes out empty leaves the address alone, unquoted.
  In every text the hub puts there, the posts', the owner's messages' and the input's own, what
  reads as `[hqc room` (any case; since 0.175 fullwidth and other compatibility forms, any run of
  Unicode whitespace between the words, invisible characters inside) becomes `[hqc-room-text`, as the
  worker escapes `[hqc peer` (§7.1, one function for both): every line of the
  hub's own that opens the block, a post or the input starts with `[hqc room`, so no text makes
  one, and a line in a post written as
  another agent's post, or a `---`, stays under the line that names the post's author; the
  feed keeps the text as sent.
- The final `agent.message` from the worker of a turn that took such an input, whose message is
  from after the room's last "Stopped" (`POST /stop`, below), is the agent's post in the room:
  the input that opened the turn (`in_reply_to`), or one acknowledged as `joined` (§17.2) and
  stored between it and the final message, so the answer of a turn on the owner's message in the
  agent's own session that a room's input joined is a post too; when that input's `joined` ack
  reaches the hub only after the final message (§5.2), the answer is no post, and the turn's end
  is decided as one without a post (below). The post is a `peer.message`
  authored by the agent (`from_session_id`, `from` its address, `mode: send`, the text, and as
  `artifact_ids` the files of the turn, as the reply to an ask has them, §7.1: the agent's
  artifacts of the `attachment` events between the turn's input, or the agent's final message
  before this one when that came later (a second post on one input, below, or an input that
  waited while an earlier turn ran), and this final message, oldest first, each once, at most 32,
  the owner's only, linked to the room), without `delivery`, written by the hub without the
  checks and limits of `hqc_send`. A text that is exactly `NO_REPLY` once trimmed posts nothing:
  it is the agent's pass, `system room_passed` in the room, "<agent's title> passed",
  `from_session_id` the agent, in both modes; the client shows it as a quiet line (user
  decision, 2026-11-16). A reply the runtime wrote itself (`runtime: true`, §4: an API error,
  "Credit balance is too low") posts nothing: in a `council`, and from the speaker in a
  `conversation` (below), it is `system room_stopped` "<agent's title>: <the reply>", the reply
  cut to 200 characters. An answer cut off by an interruption (`interrupted`, §8.1) posts nothing
  and counts as a turn without a post. Any other turn posts nothing: a turn without a final
  message, a turn
  on an input the agent got otherwise (the owner's message in the agent's own session, another
  session's send) that no room's input joined, and a turn on a message from before the room's
  last "Stopped" that no later one joined; its final message, the part of a turn the stop cut
  included, stays in the agent's session. A turn the CLI starts by itself after a background
  task carries the `in_reply_to` of the turn before it (§8.1, §17.2), so its final message is a
  post too; its input already had a final message before it, and such a post is an aside,
  `aside: true` in its payload: the circle of a `conversation` goes on as if it were not there
  (below). Such a turn's `NO_REPLY` or reply the runtime wrote itself writes nothing: a pass
  would count on the room's last message, and the runtime's reply would stop the room. A post
  wakes nobody by itself.
- `council`: nobody is woken but by the owner's message or a non-member's; each agent sees the other agents' posts
  with its next input from the room (above).
- `conversation`: the agents speak one at a time, in the room's order, the first after the
  last (user decision, 2026-11-16). The speaker is the agent the room woke last (its latest
  input from the room, by `room.seq`; of two woken by one event the one woken later) while the
  room has, after that `seq`, no `system room_stopped`, and not every agent but the author of
  the room's last post that is no aside, or owner's message, passed after it; the hub derives it
  from the stored events. Its posts and its pass end nothing by themselves: the end of the speaker's turn
  (`status idle` or `error`, its turn lost: the agent's process stopped, its worker restarted
  or `/restart`, or the watchdog, §17.3) moves the circle on, when none of the speaker's inputs
  from the room is still `pending` (not taken by its worker); with one still pending (the
  owner's message that came while the speaker's answer was written, which the CLI runs as its
  next turn, §17.2) the turn that takes it decides at its end. An `ack` for the speaker's input
  that opens no turn, with no turn open, decides then: `joined: true` that comes after the turn
  already ended, or a plain one after the turn that answers the input ended (an `ack` lost with
  the worker's link and sent again after its outbox, §5.2). What the speaker said since it became
  the speaker (its first input from the room since another agent was woken, the room stopped or
  the owner wrote last) decides: its latest post that is no aside goes to the next agent after
  it as the owner's message does, from the posting
  agent (`room.seq` the post's) with the post's files, while at most as many posts as the `hops`
  limit of a chain (20, `HQC_PEER_HOPS_PER_CHAIN`; above and §20) follow the owner's last
  message before it (or a non-member's, §7), else the room gets `system room_stopped` instead;
  without a post, its pass goes on with the room's last post that
  is no aside, or owner's message, to the next agent after the passer that is not that message's author, from
  its author (the room for the owner's message), and once every agent but that author passed
  nobody is woken and no other line is written; with neither, `system room_stopped` "<agent's
  title>'s turn ended without a post; the agents go on when you write", or for a lost turn
  "<agent's title>'s turn was lost (<its agent process stopped | no events for N s>); the agents
  go on when you write". A post of an agent that is not the speaker (an aside, the answer of a
  turn on an input that waited) is stored and wakes nobody, and an aside does not open again a
  round that every agent passed (a background task's report after the last pass used to wake
  the next agent). After any
  `room_stopped` there is no speaker, and the owner's next message wakes the first agent. While
  the room is archived its agents' posts are stored and wake nobody, in both modes.
- `POST /stop` of the room (§6), in both modes, writes `system room_stopped` "Stopped" and
  stops every agent as the agent's own Stop does (§8.1: its background subagents spared;
  §10.1: the runtime's open requests left to a connected worker); the agents' inputs are not failed
  (since 0.231 the worker of an agent whose turn runs at the Stop writes the inputs it holds into
  the agent's history without a turn, each acked `quiet`, §8.1, §17.2; the others wait and run).
  A turn on a message from
  before "Stopped" posts nothing unless a later one joined it (above), and with no speaker no
  turn's end wakes an agent.
- The hub decides and stores all of this under one lock per room, in the hub's memory (the hub
  is one process, §2): the owner's message stored and handed on, an agent's final message and
  what it posts, an input's ack that opens no turn, a turn's end or loss, a failed input and `POST /stop`
  take turns, each seeing what the one before stored.
- An input from the room that fails delivery, with its agent's failed start or rejected by the
  worker (§5.2), writes `system room_stopped` "<agent's title> did not get the message:
  <reason>" in the room, in both modes. Since 0.241 not when the room's message it carries is
  older than the room's last "Stopped" (`POST /stop`): that Stop wrote its line and ended the
  round already. An input the agent's worker drops at that Stop, its cap below `allow_all`
  (§17.2), fails so.
- An input from the room that reaches an agent while its turn runs joins that turn, as a
  person's message does (`joined`, §17.2): the turn's final message answers both and is one
  post.
- Notifications (§16): an agent's final message pushes nothing; its post in the room does, under
  the room's title with the body "<agent's title>: <text>", and the click opens the room; so does
  a non-member's message there, with its sender's title. The agent's approval requests and
  questions push as in any session.
- The client lists only the room: an agent's session (`room_id`) is in no list or count; the
  room's state there is its agents' (one needs the owner — needs you, else one runs —
  running), its row has the room's icon (two speech bubbles) in place of the state dot, in the
  dot's colors, and the
  room's header names its agents with their state, each a link to its session, has Stop (`POST
  /stop` of the room) and the room's cost, the sum of its agents' (each as its own header counts
  it, one with a provider left out), "$X this room"; since 0.229 with its agents' tokens summed
  the same way ("$X · N tokens this room"; an agent on a provider counts its tokens). A room has no
  Restart, no Pause and no Move, in its menu or by dragging its row. The room's feed
  shows its agents' open approval requests and questions, an agent's post under its agent's
  title in place of "Message from", a pass as a quiet line, and (since 0.189 in the live block above the input, before 0.189 at
  the bottom of the feed) a row per agent at work, as a session shows its own agent's work (§6,
  §17.1); on the project bar the rate and the
  count of agents at work of a room are those of its running agents (§6). "New room…" in the
  session column head's "⋯" opens a window like a new session's (`#/p/<id>/new-room`): chips over the input — one per agent, which
  opens its name (`name`, §6), model and prompt, "+ Agent", then the mode, the workspace, the
  folder and the permissions — and the first message creates the room (`POST
  /api/projects/{id}/rooms` without a title: "Room N") and goes in as its first message. Search (§15) leaves out an agent's inputs from the room, which the room has: the
  owner's message in a room is found once, in the room, and the rest of an agent's session (its
  commands, their output, its messages) is found there, by its address.
- Only a person's message starts a chain in a room (§7.1): each input made from the owner's
  message starts a chain of its own, as a person's input does. An input made from a non-member's
  message (`hqc_room`'s first message, an `hqc_send` into the room) continues the chain stored
  with it, its sender's moved on; an agent's post is stored with the chain its agent's `hqc_send`
  would carry from that turn (the turn's chain moved on), and an input made from a post continues
  it. So a loop through a room with no person in it — an outside session writing in, an agent of
  the room answering it with `hqc_send`, and so on, or a post waking the next agent, which writes
  to that session — ends at the chain's limits (§7.1, §20) as any loop of sends does. The owner's
  message that joins an agent's running turn (§17.2) gives that turn's post the chain of the input
  made from it, moved on, not the chain of the input that opened the turn. A post is stored and
  wakes the next agent whatever its `hops`: only the posts limit stops a conversation, and the
  chain's limits refuse the agents' own sends, spawns and schedules. A post or a message into a
  room counts once in its chain's messages (§20): the inputs the room makes from it for its agents
  are not counted. The owner's
  message carries no cap (T39); a non-member's message carries its sender's cap to the inputs
  made from it, as a post does. A post keeps in its chain the cap that its agent's `hqc_send`
  would carry (above: the lower of its mode and the cap of its turn, `capped_by` as there),
  decided when the post is stored. An input made from an agent's post carries that cap, but only to an
  agent whose own mode, when the post is stored, is above it (the mode the user asked for, else
  the one its worker reported, `allow_all` while neither is known): a capped input never joins a
  running turn (§17.2), and agents in the same mode keep joining. In both modes the posts that
  go in front of an agent's input (above) cap it as well (T40): when the input is stored, its
  chain takes the lowest cap kept with them (`capped_by` that post's, else its author's address)
  where that is below the agent's own mode, so agents in the same mode keep joining here too. A
  mode the owner raises after the input is stored is not held down by it: the cap is left out so
  that agents in the same mode join (a known limitation).
  Kept in the input's chain, the cap holds the turn on it, and what that turn sends and posts
  carries it on, so an agent's text does not reach a higher mode one post later.
- A room's notice: when a round of the room ends, the room tells every session that wrote in it and
  is none of its agents (`hqc_room`'s first message, an `hqc_send` into the room) how it ended
  (user decision, 2026-11-17: before it, the session that made the room polled it until it was
  quiet). A round ends in a `conversation` when every agent but the last message's author passed
  ("every agent but <name> passed"), at the posts limit ("the agents posted 20 times", the
  number the limit's), on any other `room_stopped` (its text) and on the room's Stop ("stopped by
  the owner", after the agents
  are stopped); in a `council` when no agent has a turn open or an input from the room pending
  ("every agent answered"). The reason is cleaned as a name is (§7.1.1 above), its agents' titles
  in it too, and names them unquoted (an empty one by its address). The notice is a `peer.message`
  into that session from the room (`from_session_id` the room, `from` its address, author the room,
  `delivery: pending`, so it starts a turn there as a send does, with the send's header), with
  `notice_seq`, the room's last `seq` when the round ended, and no `room`: the line `[hqc room
  <room> | the discussion ended: <reason>]`, then, oldest first, the last two entries of the room
  after the session's previous notice from it, or, never told, after its first message there (user
  decision, 2026-11-18: the whole discussion is not worth carrying, the session reads the rest
  itself if it needs it): a post under `[hqc room <room> | post from "<name>" (<address>)]`, the
  owner's message under `[hqc room <room> | message from your owner]`, another session's under
  `[hqc room <room> | message from "<title>" (<address>)]`, its own under `[hqc room <room> |
  message from you]`, as in an agent's input. When more came, the first line ends `| N earlier
  entries left out, read them with hqc_read`; over 64 KiB (`MAX_ARGS`) the older of the two is left
  out too, and the newest alone over it is cut. A session never told is told at the first round end
  after its message, with the reason alone when nothing came after it; one with nothing in the room
  since its previous notice is not told again; it is told of every later round with something in
  it, the owner's too; neither is the owner told, who reads the feed, nor an archived or deleted
  session. The notice continues the chain of the last post since that boundary, else of the
  session's message, moved on, whatever the chain's limits (as a post is stored), so a loop of
  notices and sends ends at the limits on the session's own sends; its cap is the lowest kept with
  the posts and other sessions' messages since that boundary, shown or left out (the turn can read
  the left-out ones), and with its own messages capped by another session, where below the
  session's mode (T40). It is stored under the room's lock with the end that caused it, once per
  session and end (its `event_id` derived from the room and `notice_seq`).

### 7.2 Requirements for the hqc MCP server
- A stdio process `hqc-worker mcp [--socket <path>]` that the runtime starts itself: Claude
  Code via `--mcp-config` as a JSON string, ACP agents via `mcpServers` in `session/new` (§7).
  JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per line; it implements `initialize` (it answers the runtime's
  `protocolVersion` if it knows it — `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, `2024-11-05` —
  else the newest; Claude Code 2.1.308 asks for `2025-11-25`), `ping`, `tools/list`,
  `tools/call`, `notifications/cancelled`; another method gets `-32601`, an unlisted tool
  `-32602`. Hand-written (no MCP SDK crate) since 0.33, T30.
- `initialize` gives `instructions` (since 0.66): that the tools act with the owner's rights,
  that the user reads the session in the hqc chat, two requirements (since 0.126), a third
  (since 0.176) and a fourth (since 0.197), and every
  other tool by its use (`hqc_proto::mcp::INSTRUCTIONS`, a test checks each tool is named). The
  requirements: in every session the agent calls `hqc_rename` without `session` (its own
  session) with a short title the moment it understands what the work is, usually on the first
  message and before it answers, and again whenever the work turns to something substantially
  different, always without `session`, also when it thinks it knows its address (since 0.133;
  the description of `hqc_rename` says the same): a fork (§6) carries the history of its
  source, and an agent in a fork passed the source's address it saw there and renamed the
  source; and
  every file it makes for the user to look at (images, charts, reports, diffs)
  goes into the chat with `hqc_attach` in the same answer, also unasked, with a file made
  outside the workspace (a scratchpad in `/tmp`) copied first into `.hqc/out/` of the
  workspace, since `hqc_attach` takes only workspace files and the worker adds `.hqc/` to
  `info/exclude` (§8.1), so the copy does not end up in a commit. Said softly the agent skips them: with
  Claude Code 2.1.312 and Opus 5.5, a one-line question from another session got no rename when
  the rule ended the tool list or opened with "Name this session" (one session each), and an
  agent gave paths of images in its scratchpad until asked to attach them; worded as in 0.126, the
  agent renamed on the first message and again on a different second task, and an agent asked
  only to make a chart wrote it into `.hqc/out/` and attached it (checked on 2026-11-12).
  The third: when the user's latest message asks for a task that is not part of the session's
  work (not a question, a quick check or one small edit), the agent asks the user first with its
  question tool (Claude Code's `AskUserQuestion`, a question card in the chat, §10.1) "Start this
  in its own session?" with the options "New session" and "Do it here"; on "New session" it
  starts the task with `hqc_spawn`, whose description says how (§7), and does not do it here; a
  message from another session or a room (an `[hqc peer` or `[hqc room` header, §7.1, §7.1.1)
  gets no question: that session or room gave the task and chose where it runs. A scheduled run
  (§16) reaches the agent as the owner's own message and is not told apart. As in the Claude
  app's Code tab, the agent decides what is unrelated; hqc has no tool, card or setting of its own
  for it, and the new session may report back with `hqc_send`, as the app's side session does.
  With Claude Code 2.1.312 (checked on 2026-11-18, each a fresh session that had done one task
  before), Opus 5.5 asked on 5 of 5 unrelated tasks (two scripts, a shell script, a word count,
  a letter) and not on a quick question, a follow-up of its own task or a task in another
  session's `hqc_send`; on "New session" it called `hqc_spawn` with its own project and a brief,
  answered with one line and the address and ended its turn; on "Do it here" haiku did the task
  there. Haiku asked on 2 of 5, taking a small script or a letter for "one small edit".
  The fourth: when the user asks how a subagent the agent started is doing, what it has done or
  what it is thinking, and when the agent reports its progress itself, the agent reads the
  subagent with `hqc_read` (`subagent` is the `agentId` from the result of its Agent call,
  `thinking: true` adds its thinking, §7) and does not judge it by the files it changed. The
  requirement also says why the agent may: the result of a background Agent call (Claude Code
  2.1.312) calls the `agentId` an internal ID not to mention and says "If the user asks for
  progress, say the agent is still running", since the subagent's output file would overflow the
  context. Named only in the tool list, `hqc_read` was not used for it: asked "?" about its
  coder, Opus 5.5 reported which files had changed, said it had not read the coder's thinking,
  and read it only when told it had a tool for it. With Claude Code 2.1.312 and Sonnet 5.5, a
  background subagent of six 10 s steps and "how is the subagent doing?" 45 s later (checked on
  2026-11-21): without the requirement 0 of 3 read it, each answering that it was still running;
  with it 3 of 3 read it and told the step it was on; asked "did you read its thinking?", 2 of 2
  called `hqc_read` with `thinking: true`. With Sonnet 5.5 a turn that read a subagent's
  thinking ended in a refusal ("Sonnet 5.5's safeguards flagged this message") in 3 of 3 runs,
  with and without the requirement; Opus 5.5 read and used it (2026-11-20).
  Claude Code keeps
  server instructions in the system prompt while the tools wait behind `ToolSearch` (§8.1), so
  the agent knows them from the first turn; without them it did not attach files unasked
  (checked on 2026-11-04 with Claude Code 2.1.310: haiku quoted them with only the tool names
  visible). Since 0.209 they also say to publish a page or a file at a public link anyone can
  open (`hqc_publish`) only when the user asks, that the user allows it in the chat first, and
  to give the link in the answer.
- Gets `session_token` only from `HQC_SESSION_TOKEN`; does not write it to tool
  results, runtime logs or files (§7).
- Forwards every call to the worker daemon over a Unix socket `$HQC_HOME/mcp.sock` (mode
  0600, one per daemon: a second daemon with the same `HQC_HOME` does not start; a peer of
  another OS user is refused) with this token; the daemon sends it to the hub in an
  `mcp.call` frame (§5.2). Keeps no state of its own except its open calls (since 0.35 not
  the `chain` either: the hub sets it, §7.1).
- The daemon accepts on the socket only the token a running agent of one of its sessions was
  started with, and since 0.39 (T36) only from a process that descends from that session's
  agent process: the peer's pid comes from the kernel (`LOCAL_PEEREPID` on macOS,
  `SO_PEERCRED` on Linux) when the connection is accepted, and its parents are walked
  (`proc_pidinfo` / `/proc/<pid>/stat`, at most 32 levels) up to the pid the adapter started
  (`Adapter::pid`; a hello waits up to 10 s for it while the agent starts; an adapter that
  reports no process gets no MCP server). The token is on the agent's command line, which every
  process of the OS user can read; another session's agent that uses it is refused (T30
  question 2). Claude Code starts its stdio MCP servers inside its own process tree
  (checked on 2.1.308 on 2026-10-25: `live_mcp` and `live_peers` pass with the check on). It checks the token again on every call (the agent may have stopped since), and sends
  `mcp.call` with the session's latest token from the hub (§5.2): an agent that keeps running
  across a reconnect's `session.start` keeps its MCP process and its token. When the agent
  stops, its open calls fail with `unavailable`.
- The server name in the runtime config is `hqc`, the tools are `hqc_*`; in Claude Code they
  are allowed up front via `--allowedTools mcp__hqc` (§8.1).
- While a call waits for a reply (`hqc_ask`), sends `notifications/progress` with the
  `progressToken` from the call's `params._meta` at least once a minute. Without it Claude Code
  cuts the call off after 30 minutes of idleness (§7.1); the server gets no
  `notifications/cancelled` in that case. Since 0.35 (T32): every 30 s for every open call
  that has a `progressToken`, with `progress` 1, 2, … and the message "waiting for the hub",
  until the answer or the cancel.
- If the runtime cancelled the call (`notifications/cancelled`, e.g. on `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT`)
  or the MCP process exited with an open call (EOF on stdio: the process exits and the daemon
  sees its socket close), the worker daemon closes
  the corresponding ask `PendingRequest` with an `mcp.cancel {request_id, reason}` frame (§5.4);
  it sends `mcp.cancel` for every call open at that moment, fast ones included, and the
  cancelled call gets no response (MCP);
  the idle cutoff without a notification is prevented by the progress notifications, so
  there is no separate detection for it.

## 8. Runtime adapters

Two adapters on the worker: a native one for Claude Code (§8.1) and a generic ACP one (§8.2)
for Hermes and any agent from the ACP registry. The third, the bare model, lives in the hub
(§8.3). All implement one interface: `start`, `input`, `stop`, `steer?`, `kill`, `resume`,
`answer_approval`, `answer_clarify`, plus the event stream of §4. The input queue is the
worker's responsibility, not the adapter's (§17.2).

### 8.1 Claude Code
The process `claude -p --output-format stream-json --input-format stream-json
--include-partial-messages --replay-user-messages --permission-prompts host
--permission-prompt-tool stdio --thinking-display summarized [--strict-mcp-config] --mcp-config '<json>'
--allowedTools mcp__hqc [--disallowedTools <rules…>] [--settings '<json: the environment's rules, crossSessionInbound?, skillOverrides?>']
[--plugin-dir <the hub's skills>]
(--setting-sources user,local | --setting-sources user,project,local | --restricted)
--permission-mode <"ask" mode | auto>
[--append-system-prompt <text>] --session-id <uuid>` for a new session
(the hub assigns the uuid and puts it in `runtime_session_id`) and `--resume <uuid>` to
continue. The choice between them depends on whether the transcript
`<config>/projects/<encoded cwd>/<uuid>.jsonl` exists (§9), not on `mode` from `session.start`:
both `start` and `resume` of the adapter use `--resume` when the file exists, otherwise
`--session-id`. Since 0.100 a session with `has_history` that gets `--session-id` (its
transcript is gone: the CLI deletes those older than `cleanupPeriodDays` at its start, 30 days
by default; RUNBOOK sets it high) has `system transcript_missing` in its feed once the process
started: the agent goes on without the conversation, and the owner knows. A session that moved (§5.3, §6) finds no file there: since 0.75, before every
start, when the transcript is not at the place of the working directory, the worker looks for
`<uuid>.jsonl` in every folder of `<config>/projects`, by uuid rather than by the old folder, so
a move also survives a worker restart between the hub's `session.start` and the agent's start,
and moves it there with its `<uuid>/` folder (subagents): only when exactly one file has that
uuid, only one written in another folder (the `cwd` of its mirror row, which a move sets, else
the folder its records give, §9; symlinks resolved, through its deepest existing ancestor when
the folder is gone, as a worktree deleted after the move) inside `allowed_roots`, never over an
existing file or folder (a hard link, then the old name is removed), and not while a live Claude
Code process
outside the worker holds it: such a process would go on appending to the moved file while the
agent appends too. The worker reads Claude Code's registry of live sessions (§9.3) at that
moment, its own agent processes left out as the mirror leaves them out, and does not rely on the
hub's `held_by`, which may lag; without the registry folder there is no such check. Otherwise the
start fails (`agent_start_failed`, §5.2; for a holder the message names its `entrypoint` and
pid) and the file stays where it was. A transcript written in the
working directory itself, under another name of it (a path through a symlink), is not moved. The mirror's row for
the new path is written first (§9.2) and removed again when the file does not get there. This is
the one place where hqc moves a Claude Code transcript; elsewhere it never modifies or deletes
one **[decision]**. That `--resume` in the new folder keeps the conversation is
what the live test `live_move_resumes_in_the_new_folder` checks **[verify]**.
`--permission-prompt-tool stdio` is required: without it the CLI asks the host
nothing and rejects outright everything that needs confirmation
(`system/permission_denied`, `permission_decision.source: config`), and `AskUserQuestion`
is not in the tool list (checked on 2.1.307). `--allowedTools mcp__hqc`
allows all tools of the hqc MCP server so their calls do not go through `can_use_tool`
(§7); on 2.1.307 the forms `mcp__hqc` and `mcp__hqc__*` work the same; without the flag an
MCP tool call arrives as `can_use_tool`. `--thinking-display summarized` (since 0.69) is what the
VS Code extension passes: without it the `thinking` blocks of opus 5.5 come with empty text on
2.1.312, so there was no `agent.thinking`; with it they carry the summarized thinking, in
stream-json and in the transcript under the same `uuid` (checked live on 2.1.312 with haiku).
The flag is not in `--help` (`choices: summarized, omitted, highlights`); the binaries of
2.1.233, 2.1.277 and 2.1.312 have it. The worker passes it without a version check, and the CLI
refuses an option it does not know (`error: unknown option`, 2.1.312), so a CLI that drops the
flag fails every session start. Checked on 2.1.300: `--resume` continues the same uuid and appends to the same
jsonl file. `--strict-mcp-config` disables MCP servers from `~/.claude.json`
and the project's `.mcp.json`; they can be allowed only through the environment (§14,
`allow_local_mcp`: since 0.56 such a session runs without the flag, the hqc server still comes
in `--mcp-config`; checked on 2.1.328: without the flag the agent gets every server the
machine's CLI knows, the account's `claude.ai` connectors included). Since 0.262 (iteration 9)
an environment's `mcp_servers` (§14) come in `--mcp-config` next to `hqc` and the hub's relays,
each under its own name as the launcher `<worker binary> mcp --socket <socket> --local <name>`
with the session token in its `env`, and `--strict-mcp-config` stays: the launcher gets the
server's resolved command, environment or headers from the daemon (§7.2), so none of their
values is on the CLI's command line. Since 0.245 the skills of the hub (§5.3 `session.start.skills`, §14
`hub_skills`) come as a plugin folder the worker builds, `--plugin-dir
$HQC_HOME/hub-skills/sets/<hash of the set>`: `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` `{"name": "hqc"}`
written by the worker and `skills/<name>/` unpacked from each archive, nothing of the hub's
elsewhere in it. The CLI lists such a skill as `hqc:<name>` in `system/init`, and `/<name>` and
`Skill("<name>")` find it without the prefix when the name is unique (checked on 2.1.312 and
2.1.328); `--settings` gets `"skillOverrides": {"<name>": "off"}` for each, which hides a
same-named skill of `~/.claude/skills` (or of the repository with `project_settings`): the hub's
copy wins, `/<name>` typed in full then answers that the machine's skill is off, and the chat's
`/` menu offers `hqc:<name>` for `<name>`. Checked on 2.1.328: a skill's `allowed-tools` lets
its tools run without a card while it is active but not past the worker's `deny`, and a
`` !`command` `` in `SKILL.md` goes through the same permission check; only a skill's `hooks`
would run outside them, and such a skill is refused (§20). `--settings` carries the effective rules of the session's environment
(§14: `[permissions]` merged with the environment's; since 0.84 with `allow_subagent_messages`
also `crossSessionInbound`, below), and the adapter's own policy (deny
before asking, `policy_hint`) reads the same merged lists. In the process env: `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` (§7.1): milliseconds, default
1e8 ms, minimum 1000 ms (checked on 2.1.307).

The first line the worker writes to the stdin of every process, new, resumed or forked (since
0.161), before any input: `{"type": "control_request", "request_id": "hqc-init-<uuid>",
"request": {"subtype": "initialize", "perTaskStopAffordance": true}}`, as the VS Code tab sends
its `initialize` first; with the flag an interrupt stops the turn and spares the background
subagents (below, "Interrupting a turn"). Every field of the request but `subtype` is optional,
and the worker sends no other. By the 2.1.312 binary: a user message marks the process
initialized, and an `initialize` after it is taken as another client's and does not set the
flag, so it must come first; the CLI handles stdin one line at a time, so an input written right
after it waits until the `initialize` is handled, and the worker does not wait for the answer.
The CLI answers `control_response` `success` (its commands, agents, models, account, `pid`) or
`error` (`initialize: …` for a malformed field); since 0.162 the adapter takes the slash commands
from a `success` (below, "Slash commands"), which come before the first turn, and only logs an
`error`.

The hqc MCP server (since 0.33, T30): `--mcp-config '{"mcpServers": {"hqc": {"type": "stdio",
"command": "<the worker's own binary>", "args": ["mcp", "--socket", "<$HQC_HOME/mcp.sock>"],
"env": {"HQC_SESSION_TOKEN": "<session_token>"}}}}'`, built per process start with the
session's latest token (§7, §7.2), and `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT = (ask_timeout_s + 60) * 1000` in
the CLI's environment on every start. Checked live on 2.1.308 (`live_mcp`): `system/init`
lists `mcp_servers: [{name: hqc, status: connected, source: dynamic}]` and nothing else — with
`--strict-mcp-config` neither the user's servers nor the claude.ai connectors of the logged-in
account reach the session — and the tool shows as `mcp__hqc__hqc_list_sessions`; the model
loads it with `ToolSearch` first (one model turn), then calls it, so a turn that calls an hqc
tool needs at least two model turns. With `--allowedTools mcp__hqc` the call runs without
`can_use_tool`. The title runs (`title.request`) get no `--mcp-config`.

A tool loaded with `ToolSearch` keeps the schema it had then (since 0.47, T42; checked on
2.1.308 with `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true`, live test `live_tool_schema`, notes in
`docs/notes/t42-questions.md`): the CLI writes the loaded tool's whole definition (description,
`input_schema`) into the transcript as an attachment `deferred_tools_record`, and the
`ToolSearch` result itself is only a `tool_reference`. A `--resume` with a restarted MCP server
that lists a changed schema (here `hqc_send` without and then with `files`) still sends the
recorded definition to the model (the request's shape hash did not change); the model named
the old parameters and the old last sentence. A call with a new argument still goes through:
the model may pass it anyway and the server checks its own schema. So after a worker update a
resumed session does not learn about new tool arguments; a new session does. hqc does not
rewrite Claude Code's transcripts; what an agent must know about returning files is also in the
ask's header (§7.1), which is built fresh for every input.

Session restrictions are never dropped silently **[decision]**: `disallowed_tools` → `--disallowedTools`
(each rule as a separate argument), `system_prompt` → `--append-system-prompt`,
`restricted` → `--restricted` (§8.4). The worker rejects `session.start` (`invalid_frame`)
if `model` does not match `^[A-Za-z0-9._:-]{1,64}$` or starts with `-`, or a
`disallowed_tools` rule is empty, starts with `-` or contains control characters.
Settings of someone else's repository: `-p` has no folder trust dialog, so
`.claude/settings.json` from the workspace (hooks, `defaultMode: bypassPermissions`) would apply
without asking. The adapter passes `--setting-sources user,local` (the project file is not read;
`settings.local.json` is read: `always` writes there) and an explicit `--permission-mode` with
the "ask" mode: in the help of CLI 2.1.308 this is `manual` (`default` is not among the options),
before that `default`; on start the worker reads `claude --help` and picks the one present
(a session in `auto`, §3, §14, gets `auto` instead, and since 0.129 one in `allow_all`
`bypassPermissions`). Checked on 2.1.308 (T12,
fixture `always-git-push`): with `--setting-sources user,local --permission-mode manual`,
`always` is still offered and writes the rule to `settings.local.json`; `manual` shows in
`system/init` as `"permissionMode": "default"`. Since 0.83 the worker owner can lift this for
one environment (§14, `project_settings`): its sessions get `--setting-sources
user,project,local`, so the CLI also reads the project source, the repository's `CLAUDE.md`
and `.claude/settings.json` (checked on 2.1.312 with `claude -p --model haiku`: with
`user,local` the agent does not see the project's `CLAUDE.md`, with `user,project,local` it
does). Turning it on
trusts every repository in that environment's folders with everything its
`.claude/settings.json` sets: hooks that run outside the worker's `deny` and approval requests,
permission rules, `env` that reaches the CLI itself, `defaultMode` as far as the explicit
`--permission-mode` does not override it (§14). A restricted session still gets `--restricted`
and no `--setting-sources`.
The process environment is scrubbed: from the worker's environment only `PATH`, `HOME`, `USER`,
`LOGNAME`, `SHELL`, `LANG`, `LC_*`, `TERM`, `TMPDIR`, `CLAUDE_*`,
`ANTHROPIC_*` pass, then the `env` of the session's environment (§14; it may replace one of
those, e.g. `PATH`), then the worker's own `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` (only in an environment with
`ssh_keys`: the socket of this process's own ssh-agent, §14; since 0.57 the user's
`SSH_AUTH_SOCK` no longer passes), `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` and `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT`;
`HQC_*` never, except `HQC_SECRETS`: a session that may have secrets (since 0.147, §14
`session_secrets`) gets an ssh-agent of its own in any environment, empty when nothing is to be
loaded, with its environment's `ssh_keys` and the keys kept for its workspace, so
`SSH_AUTH_SOCK` too, and `HQC_SECRETS`, the folder of its process's secrets; its hqc MCP server
gets `HQC_SECRET_TOOLS=1`. The command line has `--chrome` for a session given the browser
(since 0.148, §14), with `mcp__claude-in-chrome__file_upload` and
`mcp__claude-in-chrome__upload_image` in `--disallowedTools`, and `--no-chrome` for every other
one, so the CLI's own default (`/chrome`'s "enabled by default") never gives a session the
browser; the browser tools take the session's mode and the approvals as any other tool. A session on a provider (since 0.144, §3 Provider) gets on top of the environment's
`env`: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (its `base_url`), `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` (the `api_key` of
`worker.toml`, which since 0.243 may be a Vaultwarden entry read at every start of the agent
(§14), else a placeholder, so the CLI sends no OAuth token of the subscription there),
`ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_{OPUS,SONNET,HAIKU,FABLE}_MODEL`,
`ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL` and `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` all set to its `model`, so that a
server which swaps models on one GPU is never asked for another, `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONTEXT_TOKENS`
from `context_tokens`, `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1`, and `--model` its `model`;
the worker's own `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` do not pass then, so they
never reach another endpoint. A session without a provider gets the environment exactly as
above: an `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` of the worker's own environment or of an environment's `env` (an
owner's gateway) passes unchanged. The session's title is still made by the worker's own
`claude` with the worker's environment (§8.1 titles), not by the provider. The worker
stores the working directory in canonical form, requires it to exist and rechecks it before
every process start (a symlink could have changed). At most `max_sessions`
(local config, default 8) agent processes at once. Since 0.183 (#41) one more does not fail: the
worker takes its `session.start` (`ack`), writes `system waiting_for_slot` once ("N agents already
run on this worker (max_sessions): this session starts when one of them stops"), holds its inputs
(the hub shows it `queued`, §17.1, and counts no failed start) and starts it, with what it holds,
as soon as another agent of the worker stops (an idle stop, an archive, a deletion, a crash),
in the order the sessions began to wait; nothing is stopped to make room. A kill, a release to VS
Code (§9.3) or a restart takes the session out of the line (a restart that needs a slot again
waits at its end). Before 0.183 the start got `error {agent_start_failed, retryable: true}`,
which failed the input after `max_start_failures`.

Identifiers. Checked on 2.1.307: the `uuid` of `assistant` and `user` messages
(including `tool_result`) in stream-json **equals** the `uuid` of the corresponding records
in jsonl. So the adapter derives `event_id` as a uuid v5 of this `uuid`, as the mirror does
(§3 Event, §9.2). The record of the user's original prompt does not come in stream-json
without the echo: the adapter takes its `uuid` from the `--replay-user-messages` echo
(`isReplay: true`); checked on 2.1.307: the echo's `uuid` equals the `uuid` of the prompt
record in jsonl.

Input attachments (`session.input.artifact_ids`, §5.3, §12). Before passing the input to the
runtime, the worker downloads each artifact via `GET /worker/artifacts/{id}` with its token (no
redirects) to `<workspace>/<cwd>/.hqc/inbox/<event_id>/<name>`. The name comes from the
response header `x-hqc-artifact-name` (percent-encoded UTF-8) and is sanitized by the worker:
the last path component, control characters and `:*?"<>|` → `_`, no leading or trailing dots
and spaces, up to 120 bytes keeping the extension, empty → `file`; names that collide within
one input (case-insensitively) get `-2`, `-3`… before the extension. The directories `.hqc`,
`inbox`, `<event_id>` are created one at a time inside the canonical working directory; none
may be a symlink; the file is written to a temporary file and renamed into
place. If the workspace is a git repository (a `.git` directory, or a `.git` file of a
worktree, in which case the common git directory from `commondir`), the line `.hqc/` is added to
its `info/exclude`; since 0.59 also on every input of a workspace that has a `.hqc/` folder, files
or not, so a repository made after the first file came (the agent's `git init` writes a fresh
`info/exclude`) gets it before the next turn. A block is appended to the input text: an empty line, `Attachments:` and a
`- <path>` line per file, paths relative to the working directory
(`.hqc/inbox/<event_id>/<name>`); an empty text gives only the block. Images (`kind: image`,
`image/png|jpeg|gif|webp`, up to 5 MB) also go into the stream-json user message: `content` is
an array of a text block and blocks `{type: image, source: {type: base64, media_type, data}}`
(Messages API format; **[verify]** on a live CLI, fixture `crates/hqc-worker/fixtures/inbox`).
An artifact the hub does not serve (`401`, `403`, `404`, `410`): the input is rejected with
`error {internal, retryable: false}` (on the hub: `input_rejected`); network and disk errors:
`retryable: true`; whatever was partly downloaded is deleted.

Permissions: with `--permission-prompts host --permission-prompt-tool stdio` a request arrives on stdout as
a `control_request` with `subtype: can_use_tool` (`tool_name`, `input`,
`permission_suggestions`); the adapter replies with a `control_response` with `behavior:
allow|deny`. Options for the client: `once`, `session`, `always`, `deny`
(`always` only if `permission_suggestions` contains `addRules` in `localSettings`), and since 0.213
for an MCP tool `server_session` and `server_always` (`server_always` only for a session with a
workspace that is not restricted; neither on a request only a person may answer, nor, since 0.224,
for a tool name another server's tool could share; §10.1). Since 0.224 the adapter keeps the ids
of the options it offered with the open request and refuses an answer with any other (the request
stays open), as the hub does against the stored request (§10.1).
Mapping: `once` → allow;
`deny` → deny as the "No" of the VS Code tab (since 0.69; extension 2.1.309): `message` "The user
doesn't want to proceed with this tool use. The tool use was rejected (eg. if it was a file edit,
the new_string was NOT written to the file). STOP what you are doing and wait for the user to tell
you how to proceed." with `interrupt: true`, so the CLI ends the turn at once: the `tool_result`
with that text, a `user` text `[Request interrupted by user for tool use]` (mapped to nothing)
and `result` `error_during_execution` (`terminal_reason: aborted_tools`), so the turn ends as
after a stop (since 0.161 `system turn_interrupted`, then `status idle`), and the process takes
the next input (checked live on 2.1.312);
since 0.71 `interrupt` is `false` for a request of a background subagent (one not started in
the foreground), which outlives its turn: the call is denied, the turn running by then goes
on; before 0.69 it was "The user denied this tool call." and the model went on; `always` → allow plus `updatedPermissions`; Claude Code itself writes the
rule to `.claude/settings.local.json` **at the root of the git repository containing the cwd**
(or of the cwd itself if there is no repository; checked on 2.1.308). Adapter rule: only the
`permission_suggestions` items with `type: addRules` and `destination: localSettings` go into
`updatedPermissions`; the other suggestions (`setMode`, `addDirectories`
etc.) are dropped — otherwise the session switches to `acceptEdits` and extends
its directory list (checked on 2.1.307). If there are no such items, `always`
is not offered; `session` → allow and a rule in the adapter
until the process ends; for `Bash` and other tools that run commands, a suggestion without
`ruleContent` ("the whole tool") is not turned into a session rule — only the exact input is
remembered. Since 0.207 the request carries `args_preview` (the call's arguments, as `tool.call`
does, also for a subagent's request) and a `grant` on `session` (`place: session`, `exact: true`,
`rules` — the rules of the suggestions the adapter takes into a session rule, in Claude Code's
rule form: for `Bash` `Bash(<prefix> *)` or `Bash(<command>)`, for another tool `toolName`) and on
`always` (`place: local_settings`, `rules` — the rules it sends in `updatedPermissions`), so the
card says what each grants. Under `--restricted` (§8.4) local settings do not apply, so
`always` is not offered (before 0.224 an answer `always` there was taken as `session`). The hub stores no permissions of Claude Code's own; its only
standing ones are hqc's allow rules of a folder (since 0.52, below). The
`AskUserQuestion` tool arrives through the same `can_use_tool`: the adapter turns it into
a `clarify.request`, assigning its own `id`s to the questions, and returns the answers via
`updatedInput.answers`, whose keys are the question text and whose values are the option's
`label` (the adapter maps `id` to text itself), a typed text instead of a label (the tab's
"Other"), or for `multiSelect` the labels joined with `", "`, as the VS Code tab answers. Since
0.69 the question carries `header` (from `questions[].header`) and `option_descriptions` (from
`options[].description`, paired with the labels: an option without a `label` is dropped with its
description). Since 0.199 also `option_previews` (from `options[].preview`, paired the same way),
each cut to 8 KiB of UTF-8 on a char boundary with `\n… (truncated)` after it. The
`control_request`/`control_response` format was checked on 2.1.307 with `--permission-prompt-tool stdio`;
exact JSON: `docs/notes/claude-control-protocol.md`; fixtures:
`crates/hqc-claude-jsonl/fixtures/*-2.1.307.jsonl`.

A request only a person may answer (since 0.180): a `can_use_tool` with
`requires_user_interaction: true` (the CLI: "no stored grant or automatic approval may answer
it" — a call the classifier of `auto` handed to a person, a tool whose card is its own input, an
MCP server named like a claude.ai connector, an ask the host worded), with `matched_ask_rule` (a
user's `permissions.ask` rule forced the prompt) or with `suppress_always_allow_rule: true` (no
persistent rule may be offered). Neither a `session` rule nor the folder's hqc rules answer it,
the card offers only `once` and `deny`, without `rule_suggestions`, and the `approval.request`
carries `human_only: true`, which the hub's `auto_approve` leaves to the owner (§10.1); the deny
check of `[permissions]` still comes first. `AskUserQuestion`, which comes with
`requires_user_interaction: true` every time (checked live on 2.1.312), stays a
`clarify.request`. Every `approval.request` carries the request's `decision_reason` (why the CLI
asks: a safety check, a hook, a classifier) as `reason`, cut to 1024 bytes, and its
`display_name` (the CLI's name of the tool, `Bash` for Bash on 2.1.307) as `display_name`, cut to
256 bytes. For a call a `permissions.ask` rule caught the CLI sends no `decision_reason`, only
`decision_reason_type: "rule"` and the rule's `decision_reason_rule_source`, also in
`bypassPermissions`, where such a rule still asks (checked live on 2.1.329 for `Read`, a compound
`Bash` command and `Artifact`); since 0.217 the adapter then writes `reason` itself: "An ask rule
for <tool> in <place> requires approval for this call", or, when `matched_ask_rule` comes (also
beside a tool's own ask, `decision_reason_type` `subcommandResults` or `mode`), "The ask rule
<toolName>(<ruleContent>) in <place> requires approval for this call", without
`(<ruleContent>)` for a rule on the whole tool, `<place>` being the CLI's name of the source
with its file — "user settings (~/.claude/settings.json)", "shared project settings
(.claude/settings.json)", "project local settings (.claude/settings.local.json)", "enterprise
managed settings", "MCP server policy", and so on. The rule itself is not sent: none of the four
calls (`Read` under `Read(./x.txt)` and under `Read`, the `Bash` command, `Artifact`) carried
`matched_ask_rule`, and `Artifact` came with `suppress_always_allow_rule: true` (2.1.329), so its
card is `human_only`; `matched_ask_rule` was not seen live (**[verify]**).

A withdrawn request (since 0.180): the CLI sends `{"type": "control_cancel_request", "request_id"}`
when it stops waiting for a request of its own (the wait was aborted: the turn stopped, the call or
the subagent ended). For an open `can_use_tool` or `elicitation` the adapter sends `approval.cancel`
/ `clarify.cancel {withdrawn}` and forgets the request, so an answer that comes later is not written
to the CLI (which drops one anyway) and gets an error result; another `request_id` is ignored.
Before, such a card stayed open until the turn's `result` or, for a background subagent, its
`task_notification`. While a Stop or a denial that stops the turn is being carried out, a request
the turn's end would cancel (the main agent's or a foreground subagent's) is cancelled `stopped`
when the CLI withdraws it; a background subagent's and an MCP server's request are still
`withdrawn`. The turn is no longer being stopped once it ends, also when it ends with no `result`
(a carried input cancelled before it started).

An MCP server asks for input (since 0.180, **[verify]** on a live CLI): `control_request
{subtype: elicitation}` (`mcp_server_name`, `message`, `mode?` `form`/`url`, `url?`,
`requested_schema?`, `property_order?`) → `clarify.request` with `server`, `message` and, for
`mode: url`, `url` and no questions. A form's questions are `requested_schema.properties` in
`property_order` (then any it leaves out), ids `1`, `2`, …: a string with `enum` gives its
values as options, a boolean the options Yes and No, a string, a number or an integer free text;
`title` is the question's `header` and `description` its `text` (the title, else the property's
name, without one); a property the schema's `required` lists gives `required: true`, an integer's
question `input: integer` and a number's `input: number`, by which the card holds back an answer
the server would refuse (§4): a server on the MCP SDK checks the answer against the schema
(`Server.elicitInput`, as bundled in 2.1.312) and throws on a mismatch. Constraints beyond the
type and `required` (`minimum`, `maxLength`, `format`, `pattern`) are not checked. What is only
shown is cut: `server` to 256 bytes, `message` to 4 KB and
then ended with "…", a question's `text` and `header` to 1024 bytes; what goes back to the server or is opened is kept
whole: the property names (the keys of the answer), the `enum` values and `url`. For a property
of another type (an object, an array), a link without `url`, or a request whose `clarify.request`
is over 256 KiB of JSON (the `enum` values are not cut, and the hub drops a worker's connection
on a message over 1 MiB, §20, which the worker would resend from its outbox on every reconnect)
the adapter answers `{action: cancel}` at once and writes `system elicitation_unsupported` (§4).
The answer goes back as the `control_response` `{action: accept, content}` — the answers by
property name, a Yes/No as `true`/`false`, an integer's or a number's text as a number when it
reads as one (else as typed), an empty one left out, no `content` without questions —,
`{action: decline}` for `clarify.response.action: decline`, `{action: cancel}` for the hub's
cancel (empty `answers`, no `action`). The request names no agent, so the turn's end does not
cancel it; its withdrawal does. Before 0.180 the adapter answered every `control_request` but
`can_use_tool` with `error`, which the CLI takes as `cancel`. Unlike the agent's question, one
cancelled by a worker restart or Stop is not answered later by a message (§10.1): a message goes
to the agent, not to the server.

Mapping of stream-json to §4: `stream_event` text delta → `agent.delta`; since 0.208 the main
agent's thinking delta (`content_block_delta` with `delta.type: thinking_delta`) with text in
`delta.thinking` → `agent.delta` with `thinking: true`, an empty one → nothing: the chunks carry
text only with `--thinking-display summarized` (above; the 2.1.307 and 2.1.308 fixtures, recorded
without it, have empty ones), and the finished block still comes as the `assistant` `thinking`
(`agent.thinking`, above), as long as the chunks joined. The chunks come in bursts, a sentence or a
paragraph of the summarized thinking at a time, the last right before the block (2.1.312, sonnet
5.5 on a test install: 45 chunks in three bursts over 3.5 s, 543 characters, and a block of 543);
`assistant` with text → `agent.message`, where the adapter holds the last text until the
next stream item: `tool_use` → `final: false`, `result` → `final: true`;
`tool_use` → `tool.call` (since 0.135 the `args_preview` of an `Agent` or `Task` call has its
`prompt` last: the input's keys come sorted, and a prompt cut at 4 KB took `subagent_type` and
`run_in_background` with it: `subagent_type` in 8158 of the 11437 such calls in the owner's
transcripts; since 0.155 any call's input has its fields from the shortest value to the longest,
values of 3 KB or more counted as equally long, fields of the same length in sorted order (an
Edit of two long strings keeps `new_string` before `old_string`), an `Agent` or `Task` call's
`prompt` still last, so the cut falls in the longest values and a Write's `file_path` or a Bash
call's `description` comes whole; the mirror builds it the same way, §9.1); `tool_result` →

`call_id` (since 0.135) is the `tool_use_id` of the subagent's latest `task_started` (the
`Agent` call that started it), absent while the CLI's list counts it before that line; a
command's is that of its `task_started` too. A repeated `task_started` of the same `task_id`
keeps the first time, and a `tool_use_id` that differs replaces the row's `call_id`; a subagent
that stops counting is forgotten. Since 0.127 the list holds, after the subagents, the main
agent's background shell commands: the entries of the latest `background_tasks_changed` list with
`task_type: local_bash`, without `ambient: true` (tasks the SDK says hosts should leave out of
activity indicators), whose `task_started` has come, and whose `parent_task_id` is none or a
subagent that has ended (above). 2.1.312 registers a Monitor's
task as `local_bash` too, without `ambient`, and nothing in the list tells it from a command:
the adapter remembers the ids of the `Monitor` `tool_use` blocks of every `assistant` line, the
agent's and its subagents', and marks the task whose `task_started` names one as its
`tool_use_id`; since 0.169 its row has `kind: monitor` (before, a Monitor never showed), with
the Monitor's `description`. A background task joins the list before its `task_started` (SDK),
so a command's or a Monitor's row comes at its `task_started`; a Bash call moved to the
background later, whose `task_started` came while it ran in the foreground, gets its row when the
list takes it. A task whose `task_started` this process did not see has no row, nor has one after
its `task_notification`. A subagent's row stands for its own commands; a command that a subagent
which ended left running gets its own row when that subagent's row goes. Other task types
(`mcp_task`, `local_workflow`, …) are no rows. A command's row is its `task_id`, its `description` —
the entry's, which 2.1.312 sets to the Bash call's `description`, or to the command without one, cut
to 4096 bytes as `args_preview` — and `duration_ms`, the worker's own time since the command's first
`task_started` (for a command a subagent left, since the command started, not since it got its row);
no `activity`, `total_tokens` or `tool_uses`. Since 0.141 each row has `kind`:
`agent` for a subagent's, `command` for a command's, since 0.169 `monitor` for a Monitor's.
Commands and Monitors go in the order they became rows; the list is sent again when one comes,
goes or its `description` changes. They never change `session.state.subagents`.
Since 0.169 the list holds, after them, the main agent's own wakeup and cron jobs (2.1.312;
a subagent's calls arm none and add no row), each told by what the CLI says of it. A wakeup
(`kind: wakeup`): the `ScheduleWakeup` call's result, when it did not fail, gives its
`scheduledFor` (epoch ms; 0 for a stop, which clears it); its `task_id` and `call_id` are the
call's `tool_use_id`, its `description` the call's `reason`, its `duration_ms` the time since the
result came, its `due_in_ms` the time to `scheduledFor`. The CLI keeps one wakeup: a later call
replaces the row. It goes when a `command_lifecycle` `started` with `wakeup_source:
loop_wakeup` has the armed `scheduled_for` (one with an older one leaves it) or a call stops
it. A cron job (`kind: cron`): a successful `CronCreate` result `{id, humanSchedule, recurring,
nextFireAt?}` gives the row, `task_id` its `id`, `description` the call's `prompt` (cut to 4096
bytes), `activity` its `humanSchedule`, `call_id` the call's `tool_use_id`, `duration_ms` the
time since the result, `due_in_ms` the time to `nextFireAt`, none without it; a successful
`CronDelete` result `{id}` removes the job. A cron fire arrives as `command_lifecycle`
`started` with `wakeup_source: schedule_wakeup` and names no job: the adapter takes the job with
the smallest due time that is no later than 90 s after now; a line with none is the CLI's notice
of tasks it missed and changes nothing. A one-shot job is then removed; so is a recurring job
created 7 days or more ago (the CLI deletes it after that fire); any other waits for its next
fire, which the adapter works out as the CLI does (`Hmn` with its default settings): the next
match of the expression after the fire in the machine's local time zone, put off by the first 8
hex digits of the id as a fraction of 2^32 times half the interval to the match after it, but
by 30 minutes at most; a job of `*/N * * * *` whose interval is at least 5 minutes but under 5
minutes 15 s (that is, `*/5`) fires 15 s short of that interval after the fire. When the process
resumes the session (`--resume`: a restart of the worker, Restart session, a move, the next input
after an unload) or starts a copy of it (a fork, `--resume <copy> --fork-session`) the CLI
resurrects the session's cron jobs from the transcript and they keep firing (checked live on
2.1.312: a `*/2` job fired twice after a resume); a pending wakeup is not re-armed (its time passed
with no fire). So the worker reads the transcript (for a copy, the part that is copied; only the
lines with a `CronCreate` or `CronDelete` call and the results of the `CronCreate` calls are
parsed) and seeds
the rows by the CLI's rule, as the first list of the process: every `CronCreate` call of the main
thread (`isSidechain` lines are skipped) whose successful result has a string `id`, that is not
`durable`, not named by a `CronDelete` call and has a string `cron` and `prompt`; a recurring job
(all but `recurring: false`) created 7 days or more ago is left out, any other is due at the next
fire counted from the resume; a one-shot job is kept while its `nextFireAt` is ahead of the resume,
and is due then (the CLI computes the same time again from the call's timestamp, equal up to the
call's delay); a `durable` job shows as a row while the process that created it runs and none after
a resume, although the CLI keeps firing it from `.claude/scheduled_tasks.json` (the worker does not
read that file); `duration_ms` counts from the call's transcript timestamp; no
wakeup is seeded. A change of the wakeup or of a job
sends the list again; none of them changes `session.state.subagents`, `background_tasks` or the
state. The worker sends `subagents.live` directly, not through the outbox, as
`agent.delta`, ignores a list read after the agent's process stopped and sends an empty list when it
stops; after every reconnect it sends the last list it sent again, unless that one was empty,
`duration_ms` grown and `due_in_ms` (down to 0) shrunk by the time since it was sent, since a
restarted hub has none and lists sent while disconnected are lost. Since 0.127 it also sends again
an empty list that followed a non-empty
one, on every reconnect until a non-empty list or the process's stop: the hub keeps the last
non-empty list while a background task runs, and an empty one lost with the link would leave rows of
work that has ended. Since 0.122 the adapter counts the session's token rate (`tokens.rate`, §4)
every 2 s. The main agent's response counts while it is written: a redacted thinking delta at its
`estimated_tokens` (the CLI's own estimate), any other `stream_event` delta (text, thinking summary,
tool input) at four characters a token; its `message_delta` (one per response, at its end) adds what
that missed of its `usage.output_tokens`. A subagent of `subagents.live`, and once more after it
ends, gives the responses new in its transcript `<projects folder>/<CLI session
id>/subagents/agent-<task_id>.jsonl` (each counts when its line is written, so a long one counts at
its end; 2.1.312: each content block is a line, the lines of one response share `message.id` and its
`usage`, counted once; lines written before the process started do not count). The rate is their sum
over the last 20 s per second, rounded; it is sent when it changes, directly, not through the
outbox, 0 when the agent's process stops, and again after a reconnect when it is above 0.
Since 0.181 `session.subagent_history` (§5.3) reads the same transcript of the subagent (the CLI
session id from the latest `system/init`; before one, or with no process, there is none), off the
session's loop, and maps it as the mirror maps a transcript (§9.1): the subagent's text, thinking
and tool calls of its `assistant` records and the results of its calls of its `user` records (all
`isSidechain`), with the event ids of §3 and the mirror's caps on previews. Its task, the text of
its first `user` record, gives none, nor does a text given to it later (a SendMessage that
continues it) or injected by the CLI, nor the CLI's request records; a file that is not there
gives none. It is opened as `hqc_attach` opens one (§7): a symlink in its last component, or
anything but a regular file (a FIFO would hang the read), gives none. Of a file over 4 MiB only
the last 4 MiB are read, the line cut at their start left out, and the reply is `truncated`. The
reply keeps the newest of them, at most 200 that take at most 512 KiB as JSON
together; one over that alone is left out, and the ones before it are kept. With `after` among
them, only the ones after it, with `continues` and not `truncated`; with `before` (since 0.182)
the caps apply to the events before it alone; the ids it compares are of §3, from the records'
`uuid`, so one event has the same id in every read.
Since 0.179 the worker reports what the main agent waits on as `session.state.activity` (§5.4),
whenever it changes, a new thinking estimate at most once per 2 s (the CLI sends one with every
piece of a thinking, about ten a second), and none when the agent's process stops. `system`
`api_retry` (2.1.312: `attempt`, `max_retries`, `retry_delay_ms`, `error_status`, null when the
attempt got no response, `error`; sent in the CLI's retry loop before it waits, and no `status
requesting` comes before the retried request) → `retrying` with those numbers; `system` `status`
`compacting` → `compacting`; `system` `thinking_tokens` (`estimated_tokens`, the CLI's estimate of
the thinking block so far, from 0 at each block, `estimated_tokens_delta`; sent before each thinking
delta) → `thinking` with its `estimated_tokens`. It ends at any other `system` `status` that does
not report the permission mode (`requesting`, `null` at a compaction's end; one with
`permissionMode` changes nothing), at the main agent's `stream_event` `message_start` (a response
begins: a retry went through), `content_block_start` or `content_block_stop` (a thinking block ends,
another block begins), at its `assistant` line and at `result`; the deltas of a block and `ping`
leave it, as do a subagent's lines. A later `api_retry`, `compacting` or `thinking_tokens` replaces
it. These lines were read in the CLI's code, not checked live.
`tool_progress` (2.1.312, read in the CLI's code): while a tool call of the main agent runs, the
CLI sends one every 30 s with `heartbeat: true`, `tool_use_id` `<call id>-heartbeat-<n>` and
the call's id as `parent_tool_use_id`, none while the call waits on the user; at each the
worker sends the session's `tokens.rate` again as it is, so that a call silent for longer than
the hub's watchdog keeps its turn (§17.3). A `tool_progress` with `subagent_retry {agent_id,
attempt, max_retries, retry_delay_ms, error_status, error_category}` (a subagent's request to
the model API failed and is retried; `parent_tool_use_id` is the subagent's `Agent` call) puts
`retry` on the row of the subagent whose `task_id` is `agent_id` (`subagents.live`, §4), and the
next `tool_progress` of the same `parent_tool_use_id` without `subagent_retry` (the CLI's word
that the retry went through) takes it off; the list is sent again at both.
Since 0.179 the CLI's notices are feed lines (`system`, §4; fields read in the CLI's code of
2.1.312, not checked live). `system` `informational` (`content`, `level` `info` | `notice` |
`suggestion` | `warning`; its own and its hooks' messages, "Stop hook says: …") of a level other
than `info`, which the terminal shows only in its transcript view, and `system` `notification`
(`key`, `text`, `priority`) → `system runtime_notice` with the text; an empty text gives none.
Since 0.196 the CLI's Stop-hook notices give no line. The `notification` `stop-hook-error`
("Stop hook error occurred · ctrl+o to see", a key of the terminal; the CLI sends it the first
time in a row a Stop hook blocks the end of the turn, and when a Stop hook fails: an exit code
other than 0 and 2, or an error running it; the hook's output is only in the terminal's
transcript view) gives none, as the VS Code tab and the desktop app show none; so a failing Stop
hook leaves no trace in the feed either. `stop-hook-block-cap` gives none (it repeats the
`informational` line of the same cap, which stays). As in the desktop app, the `informational`
"Stop hook failed: " with no reason after it gives none; one with a reason stays.
`system` `model_fallback` and `model_consent_fallback` (`original_model`, `fallback_model`,
`content`) → `system model_fallback` "<original> → <fallback>: <content>", and the turn's `usage`
names the fallback model from then on (until the next `system/init`). `system`
`model_refusal_no_fallback` (`original_model`, `api_refusal_explanation`, `content`, which the
CLI sends empty) → `system model_refusal` with `content`, else "<original> refused to answer" and
the explanation. A model that refused, answered by another: the new answer's `assistant` names
in `supersedes` the wire uuids of the frames it replaces, the refused answer's text, tool calls
and tool results (the CLI's own description: "Evict the named messages on arrival"), and the
turn's `system` `model_refusal_fallback` (`original_model`, `fallback_model`,
`retracted_message_uuids`, `content`) names them all again. The adapter keeps, for the turn
until its `result`, how many content blocks each record of the main agent had, and sends a
`retraction` with the event ids it derived from those records (as for every event of a record)
before the new answer's events; a held text among them is dropped, never sent; ids retracted
once are not named again. Since 0.195 a `user` line's `retracted_message_uuids` (2.1.325: only on
the message that asks the model again after a response whose tool call the CLI could not parse,
naming that response's frames, which the CLI dropped; "Remove them on receipt") gives the same
`retraction` at once: the next answer's `supersedes` names them again, but a turn stopped before
it brings none. `model_refusal_fallback` is then `system model_refusal_fallback`
"<original> → <fallback>: <content>", and the turn's `usage` names the fallback model unless its
`scope` is `local` (a subagent's, a side question's or a background fork's answer came from it;
`session` or none: the session's model is swapped). Since 0.232 a `local` one retracts
nothing either: the uuids it names are not records of the conversation. These lines are not held for the turn's
text: one that comes while a text is held stands above it. `system/init`, which comes before
every turn: its `mcp_servers` whose `status` is neither `connected` nor `disabled` (turned off
by the user) → `system mcp_not_connected` "MCP servers not connected: <name> (<status>), …"
(live on 2.1.312 a server that did not connect in about 27 s is `failed` and is not tried
again in later turns), its `plugin_errors` (`plugin`, `type`, `message`) → `system
plugin_errors` "Plugin errors: <plugin>: <message>; …"; each line is given when its list
differs from the one given last in the process, and not when the list empties.
The CLI repeats on stdout every `control_response` the adapter sent to stdin; the adapter skips
those lines, and (since 0.161) the CLI's answer to its `initialize`, which since 0.162 gives the
slash commands (below). `in_reply_to` = the `event_id` of the turn's input, as above, once its
echo has come (since 0.69; before that, none); an input written into a running turn does not
change it.

Cost (since 0.28, T27; checked live on 2.1.308, fixtures `cost-turns`, `cost-resume`):
`result.total_cost_usd` is the cumulative cost of the whole Claude Code session, not of the turn:
in one process it grows from turn to turn (0.00216749, then 0.00398629), and after `--resume`
it starts from `totalCostUSD` of the transcript's last `cost-state` record (written when a
process ends) — the resumed turn reported 0.0043361 = 0.00398629 + its own cost. `modelUsage`
is cumulative the same way (since 0.170 the adapter keeps its token sums, `inputTokens`,
`outputTokens`, `cacheReadInputTokens`, `cacheCreationInputTokens` over all models, as the baseline
of a compaction's tokens, moved together with the cost's baseline and read from the `cost-state`'s
`modelUsage` after `--resume`, reset with it on `/clear`); the token counts in `result.usage` are
the turn's. The adapter emits `usage.cost_usd` = this `total_cost_usd` minus the previous total of
the same session: that of the previous `usage` with a `cost_usd` of the process (since 0.115; a
total-only one leaves it) or, for the first turn after `--resume`, the last `cost-state` of the
transcript read when the process starts (none — 0). The difference is never negative,
and a total below that baseline does not lower it. `usage.session_cost_usd` is
`total_cost_usd` itself. After `/clear` (below) the CLI counts `total_cost_usd` from 0 again
(live run `w1-clear` on 2.1.312: 0.00232649, then 0 for `/clear`, then 0.00232689; the new
transcript's `cost-state` has 0.00232689, so a `--resume` of it goes on from there), and since
