0.162 the baseline goes back to none at `conversation_reset`: the turn after it cost 0.00232689,
not the 0.0000004 its total grew by over the last one before. The client's header adds the last
`session_cost_usd` before each `system conversation_cleared` (§4). Since 0.229
`usage.session_tokens` is the sum of the four token counts of the result's `modelUsage` over its
models, which the CLI carries over `--resume` and resets on `/clear` with the cost; the header
counts it the same way (§4).

`/clear` (since 0.162; live run `w1-clear`, 2.1.312): the CLI goes on in a new conversation, its
own transcript in the same folder, and keeps the process. It sends `conversation_reset`
(`new_conversation_id`, `trigger: clear`, `user_message_uuid`, the old `session_id`; its own type,
not a `system` subtype) and then `system/init` with the `session_id` of the new conversation,
which names its transcript `<session_id>.jsonl` (not `new_conversation_id`); the echo of
`/clear` and everything after it carry the new id, and the old transcript is not written
again. `conversation_reset` → `system conversation_cleared` "Conversation cleared" (§4); the
first `system/init` after it whose `session_id` differs from the previous one's moves the
session there: the worker reports that id as `session.state.runtime_session_id` (§5.4), the hub
stores it (a later `session.start`, a move or a fork continues the new
conversation, as the CLI would on `--resume`; `w2-resume-old`: a `--resume` of the old id
brings back the conversation before `/clear`) and gives the session's events so far the old id
as their `origin_runtime` (a fork before one of them cuts the old transcript, §6), the worker's
own next start of the agent resumes it, and from that line on the records the process reads and
the inputs it writes go to the registry of own records (§9.2) under the new id, which is live,
while the old one is not; a holder or another writer of the new transcript releases the session
(§9.3); the transcript the title is read from (below) is the new one. The old transcript stays
the process's own until the process ends, so that what the process wrote there last and the
mirror reads only after the switch (the output of `/cost` right before `/clear`) is not taken
for another writer's (§9.2). The CLI writes the new transcript before that `init` (`w1-clear`:
its first records 12 ms after `conversation_reset` and about 70 ms before `init` on stdout):
from `conversation_reset` until that `init`, the `result` of the turn `conversation_reset` came
in or the process's end the worker marks the transcript's folder in the registry, and the mirror
does not read a transcript there it has not read before (§9.2). Before 0.162 the worker stayed
on the old id: the mirror took the new transcript for another writer's (a session "imported
from Claude Code" next to the hqc one, starting with the raw
`<command-name>/clear</command-name>`), the header's session cost fell to the new total, and
after an idle unload, a worker restart or a move the agent went on with the conversation before
`/clear`.

Wakeups (since 0.162; live runs `x6-wake-*`, 2.1.312): the main agent's `ScheduleWakeup` call
(`delaySeconds`, `prompt`, `reason`) arms a wakeup in the process; its `tool_result` line carries
`tool_use_result {scheduledFor: <epoch ms>, clampedDelaySeconds, wasClamped}`, `scheduledFor: 0`
when the call stopped the wakeup. When it fires the CLI starts a turn of its own, whose
`command_lifecycle` `started` has the CLI's own `command_uuid`, `wakeup_source: loop_wakeup` and
`scheduled_for`, the time it was armed for. The adapter keeps the time of the last such result
of the main agent (a failed call changes nothing, a subagent's is not followed) until a
`started` with `loop_wakeup` and that `scheduled_for` (the fire of an older one, armed again
while it waited, leaves it), and tells the worker each change; idle unload waits for it
(§17.3). A wakeup does not outlive its process: in `x6-wake-kill` the process was stopped
before it fired, and the process that resumed the session (`x6-wake-resume`), alive past the
wakeup's time, got no fire.

The task list (since 0.223). Claude Code 2.1.312 gives the models of its list that predate the 5.x
ones (Opus 4.7 and 4.6, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5) the tools `TaskCreate`, `TaskUpdate`, `TaskList` and
`TaskGet` always, and the 5.x models only with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1` in its environment
(checked with 2.1.329: `init.tools` has none of the four without it and all four with it, and then
no `TodoWrite`), which the worker sets with `task_tools = true` (§14); the older `TodoWrite` is
followed too. The CLI keeps the list in its own files, `~/.claude/tasks/<session id>`, not in the
transcript. The adapter keeps the main agent's list from the results of its calls (a subagent's
calls and a failed call, `is_error`, change nothing), and sends a `tasks` event (§4) with the whole
list when it differs from the one sent last. `TodoWrite` `{todos[{content, status, activeForm}]}`
replaces the list; when every task of it is `completed` the list is empty, as the CLI stores it. The
CLI corrects the input of a call before it runs it (2.1.312), and nothing else reaches it, the input
schema being strict: a `TaskCreate` input with neither `subject` nor `description` at the top takes
the fields of an object in `task`, and `title` or `name` stand for `subject`, `content` for
`description`, `active_form` for `activeForm`, `subject` is made from `description` and the other
way; a `TaskUpdate` input takes `id` or `task_id` for `taskId` and `active_form` for `activeForm`
only (one with `title`, `name` or a `task` wrapper is an error and changes nothing). So the adapter
takes the id and the subject from the text of the result block the CLI writes after that:
`TaskCreate` adds a task under the id and subject of `Task #<id> created successfully: <subject>`
(2.1.312, 2.1.325), else under the result's `tool_use_result.task.id` and the call's `subject` (or
`title`, `name`), `pending`, with the call's `activeForm` (or `active_form`; both also from the
`task` wrapper). `TaskUpdate` changes the task of the id of `Updated task #<id> …`, setting the
`status`, `subject` and `activeForm` (or `active_form`) the call has at the top; a task it did not
find gives the error or `Task #<id> not found`, and an id the list does not hold changes nothing;
`status: deleted` removes the task. The block's text is read, not the record's `tool_use_result`,
which is of one of the calls when a record holds several results (parallel calls): only a record
with one result gives its `tool_use_result` to a call. `TaskList` replaces the list with the
result's `tool_use_result.tasks[{id, subject, status}]`, a task whose id it knew keeping its
`active_form`; a result that is not the only one of its record, or has no `tasks` array, changes
nothing. A task with a status other than `pending`, `in_progress` and `completed` is left out; a
subject and an `active_form` are cut at 512 bytes and the list at 200 tasks, so the event stays far
under the WebSocket frame limit. `/clear` (`conversation_reset`) empties the list. A process that
resumes a transcript starts with the list the CLI has: the adapter replays the main agent's (not a
sidechain's) task calls and their results from the transcript (`toolUseResult` for
`tool_use_result`), in order, through the same rules as the live ones, and sends no event for it,
the hub has the latest stored one. Only the lines with a task call, and the results of those calls,
are parsed. A copy made by a fork has the source's records up to the cut in its own transcript, with
their uuids (§6), but the CLI's list of the copy only the tasks made after the fork, numbered from
#1 again: when the copy is resumed (its second start; the hub sends `fork` on every start), only the
records after the cut are replayed, all of them when the cut is not found. A fork starts with an
empty list: the CLI keeps the list per session id, and `--resume <id> --fork-session` of a session
with tasks answers `TaskList` with "No tasks found" (checked with 2.1.329); the hub copies no
`tasks` event into a fork (§6 `POST /api/sessions/{id}/fork`), consistent with it.

Slash commands (since 0.28, T27): `system/init` comes before every turn of a process and lists
`slash_commands` (built-in commands, skills and plugin commands, e.g. `compact`, `context`,
`code-review`, `anthropic-skills:pdf`; skills are also listed in `skills`, subagent types in
`agents`, which are not commands) and `terminal_slash_commands` (those that only work in the
terminal UI: `doctor`, `color`, `focus`, `reload-plugins` on 2.1.308). The adapter reports
`slash_commands` without the terminal-only ones and the CLI's internal `__name` ones to the hub
in `session.state.commands` (§5.4): once per process start, and again only when the list
changes. Since 0.162 the list comes with what the CLI says of each command and before the first
turn: the CLI's answer to `initialize` carries `commands`, `{name, description, argumentHint,
aliases?, builtin?}` (2.1.312, 75 of them on the stand, 30 KB; names as the terminal shows them,
a plugin's skill without its `plugin:` prefix, which is in `aliases`), and `system
commands_changed` (`commands` of the same form) the whole list again after a change during the
session (a skill found as the agent works in a subfolder, `/reload-plugins`); the latest of them
is the list, with the first line of each `description` and the `argumentHint`, each cut to 200
bytes, an empty one absent, without the internal `__name` ones and without the
`terminal_slash_commands` of the latest `system/init` (before the first `init` of a process the
terminal-only ones are listed: the answer does not mark them); the names of `slash_commands` only
while neither came (an older CLI). It goes to the hub as `session.state.command_info` with the
names in `commands` (§5.4); the client shows the description and the argument hint beside each
command in the `/` list (§6).

Not every tool call asks for permission: the CLI allows read-only commands (e.g.
`echo`) itself, without `can_use_tool`, so an `approval.request` does not come for
every `Bash` (checked on 2.1.308 in the live run of T4).

The worker's permission policy (`[permissions]`, §14). The `allow` and `deny` lists go to the CLI
on every process start as `--settings '{"permissions":{"allow":[…],"deny":[…]}}'`,
including with `--restricted` (the CLI applies `--settings` there too). Checked on 2.1.308
(T12, `docs/notes/claude-control-protocol.md`, "Permission policy, 2.1.308"):

- a call under `allow` runs without `can_use_tool`; one outside both lists is asked about as
  usual;
- a call under `deny` does not run and **is not asked about**: there is no `can_use_tool`;
  stream-json brings `system` `permission_denied` (`tool_name`, `tool_use_id`, `message`,
  `decision_reason_type` `rule`/`subcommandResults`), a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and
  an entry in `result.permission_denials`. The adapter turns `permission_denied` into a
  `system` event with code `policy_denied` (§4); the `tool.result` with the error comes as usual;
- a deny from `--settings` beats an allow that `always` wrote to `settings.local.json`, and
  beats the `auto` and `bypassPermissions` modes; the CLI guarantees this;
- a tool denied as a whole (`WebFetch`) disappears from the session's tool list;
- Bash rules: `Bash(x:*)` is a prefix up to a word boundary, `*` inside matches any
  sequence of characters (`Bash(curl * | sh)`), a command with `&&`, `;`, `|` is checked
  subcommand by subcommand.

The adapter reads the same rules itself (a second line of defence): a `can_use_tool` that
matches `deny` it rejects without a card (neither `always` nor the hub's `auto_approve` can
answer it) and writes `system policy_denied`; in the other `approval.request`s it sets
`policy_hint`: `allow` if the call matches an `allow` rule entirely (the CLI asked anyway),
otherwise the field is absent. The adapter understands a tool name, an MCP server
(`mcp__hqc`) and `Bash` rules (prefix, `*`, exact command); it leaves the rest
(`Read(./x/**)`, `WebFetch(domain:…)`) to the CLI. A `Bash` deny rule is matched against the
whole command and against each piece between `;`, `&`, `|`, backticks, `$`, parentheses,
redirections and new lines; since 0.62 the shell's words that may stand before a command in a
piece (`do`, `then`, `else`, `elif`, `if`, `while`, `until`, `!`, `{`, `time`) are skipped first,
so `for h in a; do ssh $h; done` hits `Bash(ssh:*)` as the CLI's own parser does.

hqc's allow rules of the folder (since 0.52, T48; §3 Workspace) never go to `--settings`: the
adapter applies them in `can_use_tool`, after the deny check above and the `session` rules and
before a card, and answers `allow` without an `approval.request`; the list is read at every
request, so a change (`workspace.rules`, §5.3) reaches a running process at once. The matcher is
the worker's own and conservative (`crates/hqc-worker/src/permissions.rs`): a command is split
into simple parts at `;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`, `&` and new lines, honouring quotes; it gives up — no
rule covers the command, the card comes — on command substitution (`$( )`, backticks, `$` inside
double quotes), subshells and `{ }` groups, here-documents, process substitution, comments and a
redirection to anything but `/dev/null`, another descriptor or a path that stays inside the
workspace. Every part must be covered by an hqc rule or an `allow` rule of `[permissions]`, at
least one of them by an hqc rule (a call the CLI asked about although `[permissions]` alone
allows it is still asked, as before). A rule's words are compared with the part's first words;
`git -C <path>` is skipped when `<path>` stays inside the workspace (absolute under it, or
relative without `..` while no earlier part is `cd`, `pushd` or `popd`). Suggestions for the card
(`approval.request.rule_suggestions`, §4): `Bash(git <subcommand>:*)` for git (none when an option
stands where the subcommand should, or `-C` points outside), `Bash(<first word> *)` otherwise
(none for an assignment such as `FOO=1 make` or a word a rule cannot hold), the tool name for
another tool. In `auto` the CLI sends no `can_use_tool`, so hqc's rules play no part there;
in `allow_all` it sends one only for a call an `ask` rule of its settings matches and where it
asks in every mode: its safety checks and tools that need a person (below).
Checked live on 2.1.308 (`claude_live::live_folder_rules`): `Bash(touch *)` answered the request
for `touch a && touch b`, no card.

The `auto` mode (`--permission-mode auto`, checked on 2.1.308): the CLI decides itself and
**never asks**: the classifier let through `rm -rf` outside the workspace, `git push --force`
and `sudo` when the user had asked for it; the decision is visible only in
`tool_result_meta[].permission_decision.reason_type` (`classifier`, `mode`). The only
boundary in this mode is `deny`.

The `allow_all` mode (since 0.129; `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`): the CLI runs every
call without asking and without the classifier, except that the deny rules still stop a call
and the ask rules of its settings still ask about one (checked by the owner on 2.1.312 with a
one-shot `claude -p --permission-mode bypassPermissions`: `dd` was denied, a command under an
`ask` rule was asked about), and it still asks where it asks in every mode (read in the code
of 2.1.312): for a tool that needs a person (`ExitPlanMode`) and on its own safety checks (a
dangerous removal, a check it could not finish, an edit of its own configuration files),
which `bypassPermissions` does not waive. Checked live on 2.1.312 (headless, `--setting-sources local`): a
process started with `--permission-mode bypassPermissions` reports `permissionMode:
bypassPermissions` in `system/init`, and a Bash command the `default` mode denies runs; a
`set_permission_mode` to `bypassPermissions` in a process started without
`--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions` gets `error` "Cannot set permission mode to
bypassPermissions because the session was not launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions",
and with that flag `success`, then `system/status` with `permissionMode: bypassPermissions`,
and the command runs. So
with `allow_all` (§14) the worker passes that flag to every process it starts, except a
`--restricted` one, which the CLI refuses with it ("bypassPermissions not supported in
restricted mode"); without it the worker passes no such flag and never asks the CLI for
`bypassPermissions`. A process started without the flag (before 0.129, or before the worker
owner set `allow_all = true`) keeps its mode on such a switch until its next start, as for any
refusal.

Switching a running process (since 0.42, T38): the adapter writes `{"type": "control_request",
"request_id": "hqc-mode-<uuid>", "request": {"subtype": "set_permission_mode", "mode": "auto" |
"default" | "bypassPermissions"}}` to stdin (`default` for `ask`: the CLI takes it and reports
`manual` as `default` anyway; `bypassPermissions` for `allow_all`, since 0.129). Verified on Claude Code **2.1.308** (fixture `permission-mode-switch`, live test
`live_permission_mode_switch`): the CLI answers `control_response {subtype: success, response:
{mode}}`, sends `{"type": "system", "subtype": "status", "permissionMode": "<mode>"}`, and the
next `system/init` carries the new `permissionMode`; a `touch` in the working folder then ran
without `can_use_tool` in `auto` and was asked about again after the switch back. The CLI applies
the mode to its next permission check, so the worker does not wait for the end of a turn (a
request already open stays open); the `--settings` deny list stays in force (it was given at
start). The adapter reports `permissionMode` of `system/init`, of `system/status` and of the
answer to its request as the session's mode (`auto` is `auto`, `bypassPermissions` is
`allow_all`, any other name `ask`) when it changes; a refusal (`subtype: error`) is logged and changes nothing, and the next start uses the
new flag. No restart is needed on 2.1.308. Since 0.43 (T39) every success answer to the
adapter's own request is reported, also of the mode the session already had: a capped input
(§5.3) waits for that confirmation before it is written to stdin. Verified live on 2.1.308
(`live_cap`): a process started in `auto` confirmed `default` within milliseconds of the
request, and the next turn's `touch` was asked about.

Model (since 0.74). `agent.model` goes to `--model`; `session.model` for a running process is
`{"type": "control_request", "request_id": "hqc-model-<uuid>", "request": {"subtype":
"set_model", "model": "<name>"}}`, whose `success` answer is only logged. Checked live on 2.1.312
with haiku: the CLI answers `success` with the full model name at once, also during a Bash call,
and the next model call of the same turn already uses the new model (the turn's `modelUsage` has
both). Since 0.179 an `error` answer (2.1.312, read in the CLI's code: `error`, `error_code`
and `model`, the model it kept) gives `system model_not_switched` with the error as the reason
and that `model`; the worker keeps the model as the session's, so a `session.model` naming it
switches nothing, and the hub makes it the session's `agent.model` (§4). Since 0.195 the same for
a `system/informational` with `model_restriction` (2.1.325: the CLI refused the model asked for,
at the start or at a later pick, and runs on another; `requested_model`, `effective_model`): `system
model_not_switched` "Model not switched: <requested> is not available. The agent runs on
<effective>" with `model` the effective one, in place of the `runtime_notice` its `content` would
give, and the turn's `usage` names it from then on; so the chat header shows the model that
answers, not the one chosen. When it refuses a pick (`at: switch`) of the latest `set_model`'s
model, the CLI sends this line and then the request's `error` with `error_code`
`restricted_by_org`; that error gives no second line. One `at: switch` of another model, after the
adapter sent a `set_model`, is about an earlier pick, and its `effective_model` may be outdated
("a later switch can outdate it"): it is only logged. For an `error` answer, only a refusal of
the latest `set_model` the adapter sent gives the line: one of an earlier request, after which the
user chose another model, is only logged, since the model it names is not the one asked for last.
So is one whose `model` is the model asked for: the CLI's fixed "set_model failed" can follow a
switch that applied, "so it names the model too" (2.1.312).

Limits (since 0.81). The CLI writes a `rate_limit_event` before each turn's answer (2.1.310):
`rate_limit_info.unifiedWindows.{five_hour, seven_day}` with `utilization` and `resetsAt`; the
adapter sends them as `worker.limits` (§5.4), since 0.179 with `rate_limit_info.status`,
`rateLimitType` and `resetsAt` (read in the CLI's code; live only `allowed` was seen). An event
with neither window is not sent. Per-model weekly windows (`/usage`'s "Current week (Fable)")
are not in it.

Fork (since 0.80). A session with `session.start.fork` and no transcript yet starts with
`--resume <copy> --fork-session --session-id <its uuid> --resume-session-at <record>`: the CLI
writes a new transcript with the source's records up to and including `<record>` (their
`uuid`s kept) and continues there; the source is not touched. Checked live on 2.1.310 with
haiku in stream-json mode: the forked conversation knows only what came before the cut. Since
0.123 `<copy>` is the source transcript cut right after the line of `<record>`, written to
`hqc-fork-<its uuid>.jsonl` (mode 0600) in the worker's temporary folder and removed when the
process exits; a path ending in `.jsonl` makes `--resume` read that file. On `--resume` the CLI
reads a transcript from its newest record back through `parentUuid` to the last
`compact_boundary`, whose `parentUuid` is null, so with the source itself a record before a
later compaction is not found (`No message found with message.uuid of: <record>`, exit 1); in
the copy `<record>` is the newest. Checked live on 2.1.312 with haiku: a session told "APPLE",
then "BANANA", then `/compact`, forked before "BANANA" through the hub; the worker started the
fork from the copy and it answered "APPLE", while `--resume <source>` with the same record
exits with that error. The adapter registers the copied main-chain records as its own (§9.3),
so the mirror neither imports them nor takes them for another writer. Since 0.200 the worker also
copies the transcripts of the subagents the copied part names (`toolUseResult.agentId` of its
`user` and `assistant` records, but not of a compaction summary — `isCompactSummary`,
`isVisibleInTranscriptOnly` —, an id of letters, digits, `_` and `-` only) from the source's
`<project folder>/<source id>/subagents/` into the new session's, `agent-<id>.jsonl` up to its
last line break — whole as it is at the fork, not cut at the fork's message — and
`agent-<id>.meta.json` beside it (mode 0600, the folders 0700): the CLI looks for a subagent's
transcript there and does not bring it on `--fork-session`, so `SendMessage` to such a subagent in
the fork failed with "No transcript found for agent ID" (checked live: with both files put there
before the start it works). A file the source lacks is skipped; any other failure is logged and the
fork goes on. The CLI writes the switch into the transcript as a typed `/model <name>` record; the
adapter counts it as its own input (§9.3), so the mirror imports no prompt from it (since 0.77).

Interrupting a turn (`session.stop`): for the owner's own Stop (`quiet: true`, since 0.231) the
adapter first sends a `cancel_async_message` for every line of hqc's that the CLI has not taken (its
`command_lifecycle` is not `started` yet; the CLI answers each it drops with `command_lifecycle`
`cancelled` before the turn's `result`), then `control_request {subtype: "interrupt"}` to stdin. The
interrupt is plain on purpose: `cancel_queued: true` (checked live on 2.1.312; it answers
`{still_queued: [], cancelled: [uuid…]}`) also dequeues the CLI's own queued lines that carry no
`uuid` (the task notifications of background subagents and tasks, cron and `/loop` triggers;
`cli-2.1.312.pretty.js:110256`), which hqc cannot write back. The CLI ends the turn with a `result`
record with `subtype:
error_during_execution`, the partial reply text comes as a separate `assistant` record, and
the process stays alive (checked on 2.1.308). Since 0.201 the adapter also waits for the CLI's
`control_response` to the `interrupt` (2.1.312 answers it in its input handler, ahead of the
turn's `result`; not checked live): a CLI that has not answered within 2 s while the turn runs
is hung, and the process group gets SIGTERM, SIGKILL 5 s later, as a kill does; the Claude app
waits 1.5 s for that answer. The process is lost with its turn as when it dies (§17.3:
`agent_exited`, `turn_lost`), and the next input resumes the transcript. After an answer: if
there is no `result` within 10 s, the process group gets SIGINT; the CLI exits on it, and
the next input brings the process up via `--resume`.
Since 0.143, if the turn still runs 10 s after the SIGINT (a process stuck in a tool call that
the signal does not end), the group gets SIGTERM, and SIGKILL 5 s later, as a kill does: Stop
ends a stuck session together with the commands it started.
Since 0.231 what the owner's Stop (`session.stop {quiet: true}`) cancelled is not lost: the worker
writes each input it marked into the conversation as a quiet line, a `user` message with
`shouldQuery: false` (otherwise as any input, `origin` human for the owner's), which the CLI records
without calling the model. It answers with `command_lifecycle` `queued` and `started`, a
`system/init`, the line's echo (`isReplay`), a `result` `success` with `num_turns: 0` and
`user_message_uuids` listing the line, and `completed` (checked live on 2.1.312; the next turn's
agent remembers the text). Lines written back to back are taken as the CLI pleases: the first alone,
the next ones together, with one `init`, an echo for each (the first one's own `uuid` and text, then
the last one's `uuid` with the texts joined by a line break) and one `result` listing all of them.
The engine takes each quiet line by the `result` that lists its `uuid`, once, and answers it with
one adapter event naming the inputs; the `init` of a quiet line opens no turn of the CLI's own (no
`status running`), its echo accepts no input, and its `result` (`num_turns: 0`) gives no `usage`, no
`status idle`, no end of turn. The line carries `priority: "later"`: the CLI folds a line of
priority "next" or above into a turn that runs, without looking at `shouldQuery`, and a line with no
`priority` is "next" (2.1.312). A "later" line never joins a running turn, neither one of ours nor
one the CLI started by itself on a task notification it kept in its queue; the CLI takes it when it
is idle, after that turn's `result`. The CLI dequeues "next" before "later", so a normal line
written while a quiet one still waits in its queue would run first, before the agent has seen the
stopped text: the worker hands no normal input while quiet lines are out, and writes it after their
acks. The idle unload and a move wait for the quiet lines to be taken too, since the end of the
process loses their acks. A quiet line the CLI drops (`command_lifecycle` `cancelled`: on 2.1.312
the CLI answers that for a line it failed to process) is written again at once, and one whose
process ends before the CLI took it (not through `session.kill`) goes back to the queue and is
written quiet into the next process. A `session.kill` is not held for them (§17.2).
Since 0.161, with `perTaskStopAffordance` in the process's `initialize` (above), the interrupt stops
only the turn: background subagents and workflows go on, as in the VS Code tab (by the 2.1.312
binary, "an interrupt on an open-input (interactive stream-json) session spares running background
agents/workflows (Stop only aborts the turn)"; it still stops observer agents; checked live on
2.1.312 with a background subagent). Without the flag 2.1.312 killed them, each with
`task_notification` `stopped` (checked live with a subagent that
`CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=claude-vscode` put in the background, then `result` `terminal_reason:
aborted_tools`). One background task is stopped alone with the CLI's `stop_task` (below). The reply
cut off is an `assistant` record with `aborted: true` and gives `agent.message` with `interrupted:
true`; the turn ends with `system turn_interrupted` (above).

A write the CLI could not make (since 0.201): `system/session_writes_lost` `{error_code:
"ENOSPC" | "EDQUOT", lost: ["transcript" | "global_config", ...], transcript_session_ids?}`, in the
schema of 2.1.317 and later (2.1.312 has no such subtype; not checked on 2.1.318). The CLI
sends it only when it exits with status 0, which it does when its stdin is closed and its last
turn did not end in an error (by the 2.1.325 binary; after a Stop it exits with 1 and the frame
does not come), so the worker closes a quiet process's stdin instead of sending SIGTERM (§17.3).
With `transcript` among `lost` the adapter writes `system transcript_not_saved` (§4); with
`global_config` alone the worker's log gets a warning and the chat nothing.

A side question (since 0.232, §17.5) is `control_request {subtype: "side_question", question,
history?[{question, response}]}` with `request_id` `hqc-side-<event_id>` (2.1.312, checked
live). The CLI answers `system/control_request_progress` `started` (no event), then
`control_response` `success` `{response, synthetic}` in 2.4 to 3.5 s: while idle, during a
running turn (the answer was about what the agent was doing; the turn went on untouched) and in
a process started with `--resume` that has run no turn. No `system/init`, `stream_event` or
`result` comes with it and the transcript has no record of it. By the CLI's code (not checked
live): `response` may be `null`, `synthetic: true` marks a notice of the CLI's own, there may be
a `refusal_fallback`, `interrupt` does not cancel it, and an `error` `control_response` says
"Session is shutting down", "Side question cancelled" or "side_question timed out: the host did
not answer in time" (660 s). The adapter turns the answer into `side.answer` (§4).

Stopping one task (since 0.161, the VS Code tab's stop of a background task, which
`perTaskStopAffordance` declares): the adapter marks every row of `subagents.live`
`stoppable` but a wakeup's and a cron job's, which are no tasks of the CLI: the subagents', the
commands' and (since 0.169) the Monitors' (2.1.312 registers a Monitor's task as `local_bash`,
and `stop_task` stops a task as its type does; not checked live), and `session.stop_task` (§5.3)
is `control_request {subtype: "stop_task", task_id: <task_id>}` (2.1.312). The CLI stops that
task and answers
`success` with `{}`, also for a task it does not know or one that has already ended, or an
error with the reason it did not stop it; the subagent then ends as any end of it, with
`task_updated` `killed` and `task_notification` `stopped` **[verify]**: its row goes and its
"Background task" line comes (above); the CLI then queues the task's notification ("was
stopped by user") for the main agent, which starts a turn of its own (§17.1, since 0.121)
**[verify]**. A command stopped so ends the same way, its row going and its "Background task" line
coming, but the CLI starts no turn for it: its note "Task … was stopped by the user or by the app
connected to this session" is passive and reaches the agent with its next turn (checked live on
2.1.312 with `sleep 120` run in the background: its processes were gone at once, `task_notification`
`stopped` came, the main agent started no turn of its own, and the next input's turn carried the
note, which the agent answered from). The adapter only logs the answer.

Moving a call to the background (since 0.125, the VS Code tab's "Run in background", extension
2.1.319). A call of the agent itself the CLI runs in the foreground is one whose `system`
`task_started` has `is_backgrounded: false`, a `tool_use_id`, `task_type` `local_bash` (a Bash
call that runs for more than about 2 s) or `local_agent` (a foreground subagent), no
`skip_transcript: true`, no `owned_by_subagent: true` and no `parent_task_id` (a subagent's own
calls are left out: the CLI marks its Bash calls `owned_by_subagent` and gives its subagents
the `parent_task_id` of their parent); it stays one until a `task_started` of the same
`task_id` without all that, a `task_updated` with `patch.is_backgrounded: true` or
`patch.status` `completed`, `failed` or `killed`, or its `task_notification`. The adapter
sends their `tool_use_id`s, which are the `call_id`s of their `tool.call`s, whenever they
change, and the worker repeats them in `session.state.foreground_calls` (§5.4). `session.background` (§5.3) is `control_request
{subtype: "background_tasks", tool_use_id: <call_id>}` (2.1.312): the CLI moves that local
Bash task or subagent to the background if it has not been moved yet and answers `success`
with `{backgrounded: bool}`, or an error when background tasks are disabled; the call gets its
tool result ("Command was manually backgrounded by user with ID: …" for Bash, `async_launched`
for a subagent) and the agent goes on. The adapter only logs the answer.

Since 0.219 the adapter takes input back and sends it now. `session.withdraw` (§5.3) is
`control_request {subtype: "cancel_async_message", message_uuid: <the line's uuid>}` for an
input written and not taken (2.1.312): the CLI answers `success` with `{cancelled: bool}`, and
with `true` writes `command_lifecycle` `cancelled` for the line before it, which then never
reaches the model. The adapter waits for the answer (`interrupt_answer`, 2 s; an error after
it: the CLI is hung, and the input is then a written one again, which a later `cancelled` of the
CLI's own drops like any other) and treats the line as no one's drop: it is not acked, not carried and not
`dropped` at a `result`; one that was carried, or opened the turn, ends the turn it kept
running with no `result` to come, as a carried input the CLI cancelled does. An input echoed or
`started` is not asked for (`false`). `session.input_now` is the line of `session.input` written
into the running turn with `priority: "now"`: the CLI moves the running Bash, MCP call or
subagent to the background and takes the line into the same turn at once (the echo is
`isReplay`, both uuids in `result.user_message_uuids`); during model text with no open call the
turn ends `terminal_reason: "aborted_streaming"` and the line runs as a turn of its own, as a
carried input does. An input already written to the CLI and held there is cancelled first and
written again as it was, with a new `uuid` and the same `event_id`.

The working directory is `<workspace>/<cwd>`. The process environment comes from the binding
of the workspace path in the worker's local config (§14). Authentication is the subscription
already logged in on the machine (Keychain on a Mac); the hub neither stores nor sees it.

Session title. Claude Code writes a record `{"type": "ai-title", "aiTitle": "<title>",
"sessionId": "<uuid>"}` to the transcript: a title the model made up from the first prompt,
sometimes several times per session (the last one wins; fixture `tool-call-2.1.307`, the records
come right after the first prompt, before the model's reply). After every finished turn the
adapter reads the transcript and, if the last non-empty `aiTitle` differs from the one already
sent, sends the hub `session.state` with a `title` field (§5.4); the hub applies it by the
`title_source` rule (§3 Session). Checked on 2.1.308 (T13, live run `live_ai_title`): with
`--input-format stream-json` the CLI **does not write** `ai-title`, neither by the end of the
turn nor 5 s after it; none of the T0 (2.1.307) and T12 (2.1.308) transcripts recorded in this
mode have it either — it is there only in the run with the prompt as an argument
(`tool-call-2.1.307`). So in iteration 1 adapter sessions in practice keep the default title
until the CLI starts writing `ai-title` in this mode or the user renames them **[verify]** on
later CLI versions. Such sessions get a title from the worker via `title.request` (§3 Session,
since 0.25). On 2.1.312 the CLI writes `ai-title` in this mode during the first turn, before the
turn's answer (live run `w1-clear`), and does not stream it: `system session_title_changed`
(`title`) carries only a title a person gave (`/rename`). Since 0.162 that one is sent at once,
trimmed, an empty one dropped; the transcript's title, its last non-empty `custom-title`
(`{"type": "custom-title", "customTitle": "<title>", "sessionId": "<uuid>"}`, a person's:
`/rename`, the VS Code tab's rename), else its last `ai-title`, is read every 2 s of the first
model turn of a new conversation (a new session or the first turn after `/clear`: the CLI writes
`ai-title` then, and not in a fork, whose own title the hub keeps; a resumed transcript without
one, tens of MB, is not read every 2 s; with the token rate, below) while the process has sent
no title yet, and at the end of every turn, so a title a person gave is not taken back by an
older `ai-title`; either is sent only when it differs from the last one sent. At the `init`
that names the new transcript after `/clear` the worker forgets the title the process sent, so
the conversation after `/clear` is read like a new session's; forgotten at `conversation_reset`,
a read between the two would take the old transcript's title back. A transcript over 4 MiB is
not read every 2 s, only at the end of the turn: the CLI writes no `ai-title` for a first
message under 10 characters (2.1.312) or when making one fails, and the reads would go on for
the whole turn. Before 0.162 the
transcript was read only at the end of a turn, so a new session got its title when its first
turn ended.

Goal (since 0.218). Claude Code's own `/goal <condition>` (2.1.312, also in `-p` stream-json) adds a
Stop hook to the conversation: at each end of a turn a model of the CLI checks the condition and,
while it is not met, the agent goes on in the same turn; once hooks have blocked the end 9 times in
a row (seen live on 2.1.312; `CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP`) the CLI ends the turn anyway, and
the goal is checked again at the end of the next one. `/goal clear` (also `stop`, `off`, `reset`,
`none`, `cancel`) removes it, `/goal` alone says what it is. Stop leaves the goal set; on `--resume`
(an idle unload, a pause, a restart, a fork before the goal ended) the CLI sets it again from the
transcript's last goal record. Seen live: a `/goal clear` typed while a turn runs waits for the end
of that turn, as any slash command (§17.2), so a turn chasing a goal is stopped before it can be
cleared. The goal's progress is never streamed (the SDK's `active_goal` comes only under
`CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE`): the CLI writes it to the transcript as `attachment` records of type
`goal_status` — set `{met: false, sentinel: true, condition}`, each unmet check `{met: false,
condition, reason}`, met `{met: true, condition, reason, iterations, durationMs, tokens}`, cleared
`{met: true, sentinel: true, condition}`, impossible `{met: false, failed: true, …}`. The adapter
reads them every 2 s of the process's life (with the token rate, below) and before each `result`
line, by which the check of the turn's last text is written (seen live: so is every record of the
turn) from the end of the transcript as it was when the process started (from its start for a
transcript that appears later, the one after `/clear` too), skipping records written before the
process started (a fork's copied history), and at a resume also the transcript's last one: each
gives a stored `system goal` (§4) whose `event_id` is that of the record, so one read twice is one
event. A record written after the text the adapter still holds (a check of the turn's last text is
written after it, and the next stream-json line comes later) waits for that text and follows it, so
a check stands under the text it judged. The mirror maps the same records to the same events for a
transcript the worker's own process does not write (a VS Code tab, another machine); for its own
process's records the adapter's events stand. The CLI's reply to a local slash command (`/goal`'s
"Goal set: …", `/cost`, `/context`, "/config opens an interactive panel…"), a `<synthetic>`
`assistant` text with `local_command_source`, which the CLI sets on that reply only (2.1.312), is
`system command_output` with that text (at most 4096 bytes), not a `runtime` `agent.message`: it is
the command's output, not an error.

The worker runs `title.request` (T24) as a one-shot process — not through the session's adapter
and not in its process: `claude -p --model claude-haiku-5-5 --max-turns 1 --no-session-persistence
--strict-mcp-config --setting-sources "" --tools "" --system-prompt "<title prompt>"
--output-format json`, with the first message and the first reply on stdin. Binary and
environment as for the adapter, but without `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT`; the working directory is
an empty worker folder `$HQC_HOME/titles/<slot>` (not a workspace), created before the start and
removed afterwards; slot numbers (0 and 1) are reused. Without `--no-session-persistence` the
transcript would land in the mirror and in the VS Code history; with it the CLI writes neither a
transcript in `<config>/projects` nor a record in `<config>/sessions`, and the launch folder does
not appear in `~/.claude.json` (checked in the live run `live_session_title` on 2.1.308, T24;
the CLI accepts `--setting-sources ""` and `--tools ""`; command line and results:
`docs/notes/claude-control-protocol.md`). From the JSON reply the worker takes `result` (with
`is_error`: an error), strips quotes, line breaks and a trailing period, and cuts it to 60
characters. Start timeout 25 s (the process and its group are killed); at most 2 runs at once
per worker.

Claude Code's built-in tools `ListAgents` and `SendMessage` find other Claude sessions
on the same machine and inject messages into them directly, bypassing the hub: the second
session gets a turn with no input event in its history. By default the worker adds both to
`--disallowedTools`; `allow_native_messaging = true` in `worker.toml` brings them back.
Agents talk to each other through `hqc_send`/`hqc_ask` (§7).

`SendMessage` is also how an agent continues its own subagent: with `--disallowedTools
ListAgents SendMessage`, `system/init` of `claude -p` 2.1.312 lists neither tool (`Task` and
`TaskStop` are there). `allow_subagent_messages = true` in `worker.toml` (since 0.84; default
false, `allow_native_messaging` wins over it) keeps `SendMessage` for that: only `ListAgents`
goes to `--disallowedTools`, and `--settings` carries `"crossSessionInbound": "refuse"`, the
CLI setting (`accept` | `hold` | `refuse`) for messages from other sessions, so no other local
session starts a turn in an hqc session past the hub. The setting is in the binaries of
2.1.304, 2.1.312 and 2.1.318. Checked live on 2.1.312 (`claude -p` with haiku,
`--disallowedTools ListAgents`, `--settings
'{"voiceEnabled":false,"crossSessionInbound":"refuse"}'`): the agent started a subagent and
continued it with `SendMessage` (the subagent answered the second message); of two background
`claude -p --input-format stream-json` sessions, both listed by another session's
`ListAgents`, the one with `refuse` ran no turn and the sender got the delivery notice "that
session is not accepting cross-session messages", the one with `accept` ran a turn and
answered. The other direction stays open, and that is what the worker owner accepts by turning
the option on: checked live on 2.1.312, a sender `claude -p --permission-mode manual
--disallowedTools ListAgents --settings '{…"crossSessionInbound":"refuse"}'` called
`SendMessage` to a background session with `accept`; it was delivered without a permission
request and the receiver ran a turn. So an hqc agent in `ask` can hand work to any local
session that accepts such messages (a VS Code tab in `auto`, say) past the hub, its permission
requests and the chain limits (§7.1); without `ListAgents` it has to know the session's name.
Per the 2.1.312 binary, not checked live **[verify]**: the permission check of `SendMessage`
allows the call in every mode but `auto`; the permission-mode parity hold stops only a receiver
in `bypassPermissions`; the tool can also reach the account's cloud and Remote Control
sessions. A restricted session (§8.4) keeps `SendMessage` disallowed under the option too:
`--restricted` does not remove it (it is not among the tools `--help` of 2.1.312 names for the
flag). Which
`crossSessionInbound` applies, per the 2.1.312 binary **[verify]**: the first one set of
managed policy, `--settings` and user settings; project settings and `settings.local.json` can
only tighten it (`accept` < `hold` < `refuse`).

### 8.2 ACP agents (generic adapter)
The adapter starts **a separate ACP process for each hqc session** (stdio JSON-RPC)
with the workspace environment (§14). The start command comes from the worker's local config
by `acp_agent` name, as an absolute path (in a non-interactive shell `hermes` is not on PATH).
On start the worker calls `initialize` on every configured agent and puts its `load_session`,
`resume`, `image`, `isolation` and version into `hello.capabilities.acp_agents`; a missing
binary is visible before a session is created.

Initialization: the adapter declares `clientCapabilities.fs` and `terminal` **unavailable**:
the worker does not implement reading/writing files or a terminal on the agent's behalf. If
`initialize` requires `authenticate` (the provider is not configured), the adapter writes a
`system` event "the agent is not configured on the worker" and fails the start (§5.2).

Mapping to §4: `session/new {cwd, mcpServers}` → creation; `session/prompt` → a turn,
`ack` of `session.input` right after sending; `session/update` with
`agent_message_chunk` → `agent.delta`/`agent.message`, `agent_thought_chunk` →
`agent.thinking`, `tool_call`/`tool_call_update` → `tool.call`/`tool.result`.
The end of a turn is the reply to `session/prompt` with a `stopReason`: the adapter holds
the last text, sets `final: false` on a `tool_call` and `final: true` on the reply to
`session/prompt`; `stopReason: cancelled` → no final message, `status idle`.
Diffs from `tool_call` are stored as an artifact of `kind: diff` and referenced from
`tool.result.artifact_id`, with the first 4 KB in `result_preview`. `session/request_permission`
→ `approval.request` with the agent's **real** `options[]` (by `optionId`), `canonical`
by `kind` and name; the answer is the chosen `optionId`. `session/cancel` → `session.stop`.
Resume is `session/load` if the agent declared `loadSession`; otherwise `session/new`
and a retelling of the history by the adapter. The adapter **checks the `sessionId` in the reply
to `session/load`/`session/resume` against the requested one** and stops with an error on a
mismatch: the agent may have silently created a new session. `usage` only if the agent reports
tokens; ACP has no `clarify`. The adapter never sends a second `session/prompt` during a
turn: the worker runs the input queue (§17.2), even if the agent can queue prompts itself —
otherwise `in_reply_to` goes out of sync.

Sessions without a workspace are not allowed for ACP agents (§8.4): they have no equivalent of
`--restricted`.

Claude Code via ACP (`@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp`, Node, on top of the Agent
SDK) is **not used**: the native adapter of §8.1 is proven, gives `--restricted`,
`--strict-mcp-config`, `--session-id` and the control protocol directly, without Node
on the worker.

#### 8.2.1 Hermes specifics
Checked in the source on llm-server, canary version
`v0.21.4+canary.20261005T071900Z-434-g4787e4d56f` (commit `4787e4d5`); canary has no
stable number, so the hash is recorded.

- Start: `~/.local/bin/hermes-acp` (or `hermes acp`) with the profile via `HERMES_HOME`.
  The profile is set by a **local binding** in `env_bindings`, not by the hub (§14).
  This is not the messaging gateway (`hermes-gateway.service`); that one is left alone.
- `initialize` declares `load_session`, `image`, `fork`, `list`, `resume`
  (ACP v2 methods enabled via `use_unstable_protocol`).
- The worker **always** sets `HERMES_ACP_SKIP_CONFIGURED_MCP=1` unless the environment
  allows `allow_local_mcp`. The hqc MCP is passed in `session/new` in the
  `mcpServers` field; Hermes registers them per session, reconnects them on
  `session/resume` and does not persist them.
- Permission options are built dynamically: `allow_once` always; `allow_session`
  and `deny_always` unless `once_only`; `allow_always` only with `allow_permanent`;
  file edits come as a separate request with only `allow_once`/`deny`. Mapping
  by `option_id`: `allow_once` → once, `allow_session` → session, `allow_always` →
  always, `deny` / `deny_always` → deny. `allow_session` has `kind: allow_always`,
  so mapping by `kind` is wrong.
- The `approvals.timeout` timeout (300 s, read on every request) →
  `approval.cancel {timeout}`.
- `session/resume` with an unknown id **silently creates a new session** with a warning in the
  log **[verify]** — hence the id check of §8.2 is mandatory.
- Hermes's `usage_update` in ACP is an estimate of context occupancy, not the turn's tokens:
  it is not translated into `usage`.
- Steer: the prompt text `/steer <text>` intervenes in the active turn, `/queue <text>`
  queues it in Hermes. The adapter implements `session.steer` via `/steer`;
  `/queue` is not used (the worker runs the queue).
- The `hermes-acp` toolset has no messaging, cron or `clarify` (checked in `toolsets.py`).
  Hindsight memory and the profile's skills work as usual, so a separate profile is used in
  other people's sessions (§11.1, §14).
- A Hermes session has a single writer: hqc does not drive a session the Telegram gateway is
  driving in parallel; its transcript can only be continued by a new hqc session.
- On the gateway, `api_server` is also enabled (needed by `hermes peer` and the Jobs API);
  the adapter does not use it.
- Each session is a separate Python process; recommended `idle_timeout` is 30 minutes.

### 8.3 Bare model
Runs in the hub: OpenRouter, the Anthropic API or a local model through the worker's
proxy (§8.5). Loop: model ↔ hqc MCP tools (§7); no file system.
The default runtime of the personal assistant session if there is no online worker with
Claude Code when it is created; can be changed later in the session settings.

### 8.4 Session without a workspace
For architecture discussions. Options: the bare model (§8.3) or Claude Code
on worker `worker_id` in a temporary empty folder `<worker-data>/scratch/<session_id>`
(`$HQC_HOME/scratch/<session_id>`, 0700; `session.start` with `workspace_path: null` and
`restricted: true`; without `restricted`: `invalid_frame`) with the `--restricted` flag (removes the tools that run commands and confines
the file tools to the working directory). Runs on the subscription. The user picks the worker
at creation; by default, the last used online worker
with Claude Code. ACP agents are not allowed here.

### 8.5 Local models
The worker announces local OpenAI-compatible endpoints in `hello` (on llm-server this is
`ninfer` on 127.0.0.1:8082, model qwen3.8-27b). The hub proxies bare-model requests
in `model.proxy` frames with streamed chunks. By default local models are available
only to the worker owner's sessions; `share_local_models: true` in the local config
opens them to colleagues' bare models in shared projects.

## 9. Mirror and import of Claude Code sessions

The VS Code extension and the CLI write the same files
`<config>/projects/<encoded-cwd>/<uuid>.jsonl`, where `<config>` is `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or
`~/.claude`. Folder name encoding (as in CLI 2.1.308, checked against the folder names of the
T0 runs and against the CLI function itself): the real path of the working directory is
encoded (`process.cwd()`, symlinks resolved: `/tmp` → `/private/tmp` on macOS); every UTF-16
unit that is not an ASCII letter or digit is replaced with `-`; if the result is longer than
200 characters, it becomes the first 200 characters, `-` and base36 of the absolute value of a
32-bit hash of the string (`h = (h << 5) - h + unit | 0` over UTF-16 units). This is how the
adapter and the mirror find the file for a path. The name is **not decoded** back (`/a/b.c` and
`/a/b-c` collide), so the worker takes the session's working directory from the `cwd` field of
the jsonl records, keeps a "file → cwd" cache on disk (§5.2) and uses the folder name as a key
and, since 0.95, to tell which recorded `cwd` is the transcript's folder. A record's `cwd` is
where the agent was when it was written: it changes inside one transcript when the agent `cd`s
(worktrees, sibling projects, `/private/tmp`), and a chat moved to another project by copying
its transcript into that project's folder (same file name, so the same uuid) and continued there
starts with the old folder's records. So the transcript's folder is the first recorded `cwd`
whose encoding equals the name of the transcript's folder under `projects/`; when no record has
such a `cwd`, the first recorded `cwd`. Subfolders with subagent transcripts and files that are
not `<uuid>.jsonl` are ignored.
Verified on 2.1.307: besides `user`/`assistant` the file has `attachment`,
`file-history-snapshot`, `api-request*`, `last-prompt`, `ai-title`, `cost-state`,
`queue-operation`, `system` and other records; the parser skips them, except `ai-title`, which
it parses separately (the `aiTitle` field; the adapter takes the session title from it, §8.1),
since 0.98 `attachment`, whose `queued_command` is a message typed during a turn (§9.1), and
since 0.162 `custom-title` (the `customTitle` field: the title a person gave the session, with
`/rename` or in the VS Code tab; it wins over `ai-title`, whichever came last, §8.1, §9.2) and
`system` (`uuid`, `subtype`, `content`, `isSidechain`, `isMeta`, `timestamp`; the mirror uses
`local_command` and `compact_boundary`, §9.1).

Format on 2.1.308 (T15, fixtures `vscode-takeover-2.1.308` and `adapter-then-outside-2.1.308`,
`docs/notes/t15-questions.md`):

- `claude -p "<prompt>"` (prompt as an argument, as a person in a terminal would) and
  `--resume <uuid>` in the adapter's stream-json mode append to **the same** file: both parts
  carry the same `cwd` and `sessionId`, `entrypoint: sdk-cli`, `version`, `gitBranch`. Each part
  starts with a pair of `queue-operation` records (`enqueue`/`dequeue`, no `uuid`), then the
  `user` prompt record.
- Every content block is a **separate record** with its own `uuid` (`thinking`, `text`,
  `tool_use` of one model response are three records with a shared `message.id` and an
  `apiBlockIndex` field); the record's `message.content` holds one block. In jsonl every record
  of a response has `message.stop_reason`: `tool_use` before a tool call, `end_turn` on the
  records of the turn's last response; in stream-json this field is `null`.
- `thinking` in jsonl is empty text with a `signature`; in the adapter's stream-json there was no
  such record in either run (an `attachment` `thinking_drop` instead), so it does not count for
  detecting a foreign writer (§9.3).
- `attachment` records (environment, tool list, CLAUDE.md, skills) have a `uuid` and sit in the
  `parentUuid` chain between `user` and `assistant`; the main chain is determined by record
  type, not by `parentUuid`.
- New types without `uuid`: `api-request-shape`, `atis-latch`, `mode`; service records
  `cost-state`, `last-prompt`. `ai-title` was **not written** in either 2.1.308 run, not even
  for a prompt passed as an argument (on 2.1.307 it was), so an imported session's title is
  usually "Session N".
- Prompt records have `promptId`, `promptSource: sdk`, `turnOrigin`, `turnPosition`,
  `permissionMode`; records injected by the CLI have `isMeta: true` (the parser does not show
  them); the summary after `/compact` has `isCompactSummary: true`.

### 9.1 Import
Candidates come from `workspace.list_candidates` (§5.3, `GET /api/workers/{id}/candidates`):
the worker walks `<config>/projects/*/<uuid>.jsonl`, takes each transcript's folder by the rule
of §9 (the "file → cwd" cache on disk, §5.2), groups by `cwd` with the session count and
`last_active` (modification time of the newest file) and returns only folders inside
`allowed_roots`. In the client, the "Import from Claude Code" button on the Workspaces screen
shows the candidates; the selected folders become workspaces of the project through the
ordinary `POST /api/workspaces` with `mirror_enabled: true` (body `CreateWorkspaceImport`). The
hub sends the worker `mirror.set` (§5.3), and does the same for every workspace with the mirror
after each `hello`; when a workspace is deleted, `mirror.set` with `enabled: false`. The worker
accepts only a folder inside `allowed_roots` (§2.1). Since 0.23 the mirror is on for every
workspace by default (hub migration `0011` turned it on for existing ones), so importing
candidates is just a way to add a folder; on the Workspaces screen each folder has a "VS Code
sessions" switch (`PATCH /api/workspaces/{id} {mirror_enabled}`, §6).

**No duplicates when turned on for a non-empty workspace** (since 0.23). The hqc sessions in
the folder are already in the hub, and their prompts are hub `user.message` events with their
own `event_id` (v7), not v5 from the record's `uuid`, so importing their transcripts would
produce duplicates. So `mirror.set` with `enabled: true` carries `sessions?:
[{runtime_session_id, since_ts}]`: the hub's sessions in this workspace with a known transcript
and the time of their last event in the hub (at most 5000, the most recent; empty means the
field is absent; example `hub.mirror.set.sessions.json`). The worker's first pass over such a
transcript (a file the mirror has not read yet, offset 0), up to the end of the file, does not
send events for records with `timestamp` <= `since_ts`; the record tree and the last prompt are
built as usual. Transcripts unknown to the hub are imported in full, as before; the list does
not affect files already read.

Import is the mirror's first pass over a file (offset 0): the worker sends the whole history of
the main chain as §4 events through `mirror.event`, with the original `ts` and with `event_id`
per §3 Event (`Event::id_from_claude_block`). Mapping: `user` with text → `user.message`
(`delivery: delivered`), `tool_result` → `tool.result`; `assistant` with text →
`agent.message`, `final: true` when `stop_reason: end_turn`, `in_reply_to` is the file's last
prompt; `tool_use` → `tool.call` (since 0.135 an `Agent` or `Task` call's `args_preview` with
its `prompt` last, since 0.155 any call's with its fields from the shortest value to the
longest, as the adapter's, §8.1); non-empty `thinking` → `agent.thinking`. Since 0.69:
`assistant` text with `message.model` `<synthetic>` → `agent.message` with `runtime: true`
(§8.1), `final` by its `stop_reason` as any other, since 0.168 with `refusal: true` when that is
`refusal`; since 0.180 an `assistant` text that is
exactly `(no content)` gives none, as from the adapter; since 0.193 none for the synthetic
text "No response requested." without `isApiErrorMessage`: the placeholder the CLI writes on a
resume for a turn that ended without a reply (its process died in it, or it was interrupted),
which it shows nothing for itself; the same text with `isApiErrorMessage` (its fallback for a
rate limit) stays a reply; a `user` record with `origin.kind: task-notification` (2.1.312:
`origin {kind, producer: session-task, runId}`, `promptSource: system`, `turnOrigin:
task_notification`, text
`<task-notification><task-id>…<status>…</status><summary>…</summary>…`) → `system
task_notification` with the `<summary>`, else "Background task", never a `user.message` and not
a prompt (an answer after it points at the last prompt a person typed). Since 0.135 one that came
while a turn ran, an `attachment` record with `attachment.type: queued_command`, `commandMode:
task-notification` and its text as `prompt` (2.1.312: a string), not a sidechain, gives the same
event under the record's `uuid` when its text has `<status>` before `<summary>`, as a task's end has
(before 0.135 it gave none; in the owner's transcripts of 2.1.310–2.1.319 none of 607 such
notifications of a command or a subagent is written again as a `user` record); a Monitor's event and
the CLI's other notices that come so (an artifact watch's end) have no `<status>` there and give no
event, as before (of 5481 such records in the owner's transcripts 4999 have it, 479 Monitor events
and 3 notices do not); and both carry `<tool-use-id>`, `<status>` and `<task-id>` of the text before
`<summary>` as `call_id`, `status` and `task_id`, each absent when the tag is. A command's and a
subagent's notification has `<task-id>`, mostly `<tool-use-id>` and `<status>` there (2.1.272,
2.1.312); a Monitor's event has only `<task-id>`, and its `<event>`, after `<summary>`, holds the
watched command's output, which may hold any tag. Since 0.98: a message the person typed during a
turn — an `attachment` record with `attachment.type: queued_command`, `commandMode: prompt`,
`origin.kind` `human` or no `origin` (before 2.1.210, and on some later ones that carry
`delivery_id`), not `isMeta` (another session's message) and not a sidechain; its `prompt` is a list
of blocks or (2.1.296+) a string — → a `user.message` (`delivery: delivered`) per non-empty text
block, at the attachment's own `timestamp` (when it was typed); it is not a prompt either (an answer
after it points at the turn's prompt). An answered `AskUserQuestion` — a `tool_result` whose record
has `toolUseResult {questions, answers}`, `answers` keyed by the question's text — gives after its
`tool.result` a `clarify.request` with the questions as the adapter parses them (§8.1) and a
`clarify.response` with the answers by question id, so the client shows the closed card with the
chosen options; the CLI joins a multi-select answer with ", ", which the mirror splits back by the
question's option labels, the longest label first, and any rest is one answer typed as "Other".
A declined question (`is_error`, no `questions` in the record) stays a `tool.result`. Since
0.162 the CLI's own lines of a `user` record are no message a person typed: the text
"[Request interrupted by user]" or "[Request interrupted by user for tool use]" → `system
turn_interrupted` "Interrupted" (§4); a slash command, which the CLI writes as
`<command-name>/x</command-name> <command-message>…</command-message>
<command-args>a</command-args>` (a skill's, up to 2.1.309 at least, with `<command-message>`
first), → `user.message` "/x a" (without arguments "/x"), as it was typed; what a command
printed, a text that starts with `<local-command-stdout>` or `<local-command-stderr>`, and a
`system` record with `subtype: local_command` (not a sidechain, not `isMeta`) whose `content`
holds the same tags → `system command_output` with what the two tags hold, one after the other,
at most 4096 bytes like other previews (§4), and no event when both are empty. So the feed never
shows a bubble with the CLI's raw tags. A compaction — a `system` record with `subtype:
compact_boundary` and the summary the CLI writes after it, a `user` record with
`isCompactSummary` — → one `system context_compacted` with the summary's text (the text blocks
joined by `\n`; "Context compacted" when it has none), as the adapter gives it (§8.1) but
without `trigger`, `pre_tokens` and `post_tokens` (§4): the event takes its id from the boundary's
`uuid` (the last boundary read in that file before the summary, kept in the worker's memory; the
summary is not always the boundary's child in the record tree, it may hang on an attachment), or
from the summary's own `uuid` when no boundary was read since the worker started; the boundary alone
gives no event. Records that yield no events (other `attachment`s, snapshots, `api-request*`,
`queue-operation`, empty `thinking`, images) are skipped.

For an unknown `runtime_session_id` of this worker the hub creates a session in the
workspace's project: `cwd` is the record's path relative to the workspace, the title is the
frame's `title` field — since 0.162 the file's last `custom-title`, otherwise its last
`ai-title` — if present, otherwise "Session N" (§3 Session),
`system session_created` "Session imported from Claude Code". The initial `locked_by` follows
the frame's `recent` flag: the worker sets it if the file was modified less than 30 s before
it was read (the worker's clock, not the hub's); then `vscode`, otherwise `none`. An author the
worker does not know is filled in by the hub: the workspace owner for `user.message` (and
since 0.98 `clarify.response`), the session's agent for the rest. No push is sent for mirror
events (an import is hundreds of old replies). Since 0.86 a mirrored record whose `ts` is before its session's `created_at` on the
hub (the record's time is the worker's clock, `created_at` the hub's) is read for the session's
owner (§3 ReadCursor), and so is the `session_created` of an
imported session: an imported session comes in read, with the history the owner has seen in VS
Code; a record written after the import counts as unread by the rule of §6.

**Import limits** (§20, since 0.23 T22; behaviour at the daily limit since 0.24). New sessions
from the mirror: at most 200 per 24 h per worker (since 0.85 `HQC_MIRROR_SESSIONS_PER_DAY`;
`0` imports no new transcript, known ones go on) and 2000 in total per workspace;
`runtime_session_id` is a uuid, `cwd` is up to 4096 bytes. The first wave after the update to
0.23 (migration `0011` turned the mirror on for every workspace) may bring more transcripts than
fit in a day: the hub does not accept a record of a new transcript over the daily limit:
`error mirror_quota`, `retryable: true`. On such a reply the worker removes the record from the
outbox (the §5.2 attempt counter does not grow) and rewinds the transcript to the start: the file
is not read until an **hour** has passed since the last rejection, then it goes again in full
with the same `event_id`s. So the wave spreads over several days (200 sessions per 24 h by default) without
losing anything; what is deferred lives in the worker's memory, and after a worker restart such
a transcript is read at once (and deferred again if the limit is used up). Over 2000 per
workspace and with an invalid `runtime_session_id`/`cwd` the record is dropped (`ack` without
`seq`, warn), as in §20.

### 9.2 Mirror
Since 0.23 the mirror is on for every workspace by default **[decision]** (T21): otherwise a
session started in hqc and continued in VS Code is not released, and forks are not visible
(questions of T15 and T20). For a workspace with `mirror_enabled` the worker watches every file
`<config>/projects/*/<uuid>.jsonl` whose `cwd` is inside the workspace path (compared by path
components). Polling every **2 s**, not file system notifications **[decision]**: a pass is a
`read_dir` of the projects folder and a `stat` of every file, and only the bytes after the
offset are read from disk; notifications would not always be enough (FSEvents coalesces events
and reports directories, inotify needs a watch per folder and does not see what was created
before the watch was set), offsets and rescans are needed anyway, and 2 s is much less than the
30 s that matter for takeover. The offset advances only over processed complete lines; an
incomplete line waits for the next pass; a file that got shorter is read again (`event_id`
absorbs duplicates). Offsets, the file's last prompt and `ai-title` (since 0.162 also its last
`custom-title`, a column the worker adds to a state file written before) are stored next to the
`cwd` cache (`$HQC_HOME/mirror/mirror.sqlite3`); `mirror.event` goes through the outbox, like
`event`. The `title` of a `mirror.event` is the `custom-title` when the file has one, otherwise
the `ai-title` (since 0.162). A transcript the worker moves for a moved session (§8.1, since
0.75) gets its row at the new path before it is moved: `cwd` the new folder, the offset at the
file's end, the old row's last prompt, `ai-title` and (since 0.162) `custom-title`. The mirror
reads the row before the records, so it neither imports the file
again nor counts it to the old folder by the `cwd` of its old records. When the file does not
get there (its folder or the link fails), the row is removed again.

**The session follows its transcript** (since 0.95). A row whose `cwd` is not its file's folder
by the rule of §9 (a copy read before the new window wrote to it; a copy's row written before
0.95) is not settled: on every pass, before the workspace is picked (so a copy out of a folder
that is not mirrored is found too), the worker searches the file for a `cwd` that is, the whole
file the first time in its process and afterwards only the bytes appended since the last search
(the size searched is kept in memory); a `cwd` found becomes the row's, and the records of that
pass go out with it. The hub keeps one session per transcript and finds it by worker and
`runtime_session_id`, not by workspace; when a record the session does not have yet comes from
another workspace of the session's owner than the session's, the session moves there once the
record is stored: into that workspace's project, `cwd` the transcript's folder (the frame's
`cwd`) relative to the workspace, as an import there would get it, the connection's start state
back to "not started" and `system session_moved` (§4) in its feed, as after a move (§6). A
session hqc runs (`locked_by: hqc`) does not move: a copied transcript is written from outside
(VS Code, by hand); nor does one any move refuses (§7): archived, a service session, a runtime
other than Claude Code, a subagent running. The record is stored either way. A record the
session already has does not move it:
a copy read from its start brings all of the old file's records again. Nor does one older than
the session's newest event that is not `system` (most `system` events are the hub's own, with
its clock): right after a copy the old window still writes a few records into the old file, and
both files may be read again from the start, so the session ends where the newest record was
written. The hub keeps the newest time it read per session for the connection: it only grows,
so an older record needs no query (a copy out of a folder that is not mirrored has no `since`
and comes whole). Right after a copy both files get records for a while, and the session may
switch a few times, with a line each time. Into a workspace whose `environment` (§3 Workspace,
as the worker's `hello` set it: the record comes on the connection's own loop, so the hub asks
the worker nothing) is not that of the session's folder now, or for a session without one, the
session moves only once the owner allows it: an agent in one environment could write a copy of
its own transcript into another's folder, and the owner's next input would start it there with
that environment's keys, settings and rules. The first such record asks (§10.1): a
PendingRequest `follow` (§3) whose `request_id` is derived from the session, the workspace it is
in now and the target, and the hub's `approval.request` in the session's feed naming the folder
the agent starts in (the workspace joined with the record's `cwd`). A folder with a control
character or a bidirectional control, which the card may not show (as for `hqc_move`, §7), gets
no card, and the record moves nothing; the hub logs a warning. One card per session: while
it is open, records from there and from anywhere else ask nothing. The answer is used once, for
that move from here to there: allowed, the hub moves the session off the answer's request (read
anew, the conditions above checked again: one already in that workspace moves nothing and gets
no line; one refused then stays, and `system session_not_moved` (§4) says why); denied, nothing
moves. Either way a later record for the same move asks nothing and moves nothing; a move back
from there is another move and asks again.

The worker recognises its own records by `uuid`: the Claude Code adapter puts into a shared
in-memory registry (by `runtime_session_id`) the uuid of every `user`/`assistant` message of the
main chain from stream-json, including the `--replay-user-messages` echo of its own prompts, and
marks whether the session's process is alive. Since 0.26 (T25) the adapter also puts there the
text of every input written to the process's stdin; a prompt record (a main-chain `user` with
text) whose `uuid` stream-json did not name is its own if its typed text matches an input not
yet matched (the input is consumed; the last 32 are kept). The typed text is the first text
block, and for a slash command, which the CLI writes as
`<command-name>/compact</command-name>…<command-args>…</command-args>` (since 0.162 also with
`<command-message>` first, §9.1), the command with its arguments. This makes own records of
the `/compact` command record (it is not in stream-json, 2.1.308) and of the prompt if its echo
comes with a different `uuid` (see §9.3). Since 0.105 a
prompt record whose typed text is several unmatched inputs in a row joined by `\n` is own too,
and consumes them: the CLI writes inputs it takes from its queue together, such as a message
typed while a fresh process starts, as one prompt record with a new `uuid` (2.1.312); before, the
mirror took that record for another writer's and the chat showed it as a third message. Since 0.69 a
background task's notification record (§9.1; since 0.135 also its `attachment` form) is own
while the session's hqc process is alive: the adapter reported its stream-json `system
task_notification` line, which has another `uuid` (2.1.312), so the record is neither emitted nor
held nor taken for another writer. Since 0.98 a message typed during a turn (§9.1) is matched by its
typed text (its first text block) like a prompt, and while the session's hqc process is alive it is
own even when unmatched: stream-json does not carry the attachment, and only hqc writes to that
process's stdin. Its `timestamp` counts for the first pass's `since_ts` like any record's. Since
0.162 the same holds, while the session's hqc process is alive, for a `system` `local_command`
record (§9.1), which stream-json does not carry, and for a compaction's summary: only hqc writes
that process's stdin, and the adapter reported the compaction. These four kinds of record are
own also in a transcript the process wrote before its `/clear` (§8.1), until the process ends:
the hub has moved the session to the new transcript, and such a record of the old one, read
after the switch, would make it import the old one as a session of someone else's. Only the
records within the old transcript's length at the switch are: the CLI no longer writes it, and
what is added later is another writer's (`--resume` of the old id, `w2-resume-old`). Since 0.162 a
transcript the mirror has not read yet waits while a process of this worker in its folder has
cleared its conversation (`/clear`, §8.1) and not named the new transcript: the CLI writes that
one first, and in the gap the mirror took it for a session of someone else's and imported it
(one `/clear` in about 25, `w1-clear`). The mark ends with the `system/init` that names it, from
when the transcript is live, with the `result` of the turn of `/clear`, or with the process. The
mirror **never emits** own records (the adapter
has sent them, including the prompt, as a hub `user.message` with its own `event_id`). The rule
for foreign records:

- the hqc process of this session is alive (`locked_by: hqc`): the mirror **does not emit** and
  does not move the offset past the first foreign record while it stays foreign for less than
  **5 s** (stream-json may lag behind the file). After that: on a worker with the holder
  registry (§9.3) the record is emitted like any other, with `held_by` (the hub does not lock
  the session because of it); only a holder releases the session; without the registry this is
  a foreign writer (§9.3);
- there is no process (`locked_by: vscode` or `none`): the record is emitted at once through
  `mirror.event`; with `recent` the hub moves the session to `locked_by: vscode` (if it was
  `hqc`, this is a release, §9.3).
- Since the adapter and the mirror derive `event_id` from the same record `uuid`, the seam
  when `locked_by` switches either way is absorbed by the unique index.
  For a record with several content blocks the §3 Event rule is mandatory for the
  mirror too: block `i > 0` is v5 from `"<uuid>/<i>"`. The CLI has so far written one block per
  record (all fixtures and live runs, including 2.1.308), but otherwise the seam would produce
  duplicates.

A session with `locked_by: vscode` is read-only in the hub: `state: locked_vscode`, the input
field is closed. The client has two banners: with `held_by`, "The session is open in VS Code …
close it there" without a button (takeover would get `409 vscode_open` anyway); without
`held_by` (recent records, no holder or no registry data), "In VS Code" and a "Take over"
button.

### 9.3 Takeover **[decision]**
The T15 rule "30 s of silence in the file" does not tell a closed session from an open idle
one. In practice (2026-10-23) hqc took over a session open in VS Code after 30 s of silence and
appended turns through `--resume`; then the user wrote in VS Code, and the extension attached
its turn to its own last record in memory, not to the tail of the file: the record had two
children, VS Code saw only its own branch, and 37 hqc records never made it into its context.
Since 0.22 (T20) takeover is decided by the transcript's **holder**, and forks, if they still
happen, are visible in the feed.

**Holder.** Claude Code (2.1.308) keeps a registry of live sessions
`<config>/sessions/<pid>.json` (`<config>` as in §9): `pid` (a number; it has also been seen as
a string), `sessionId`, `cwd`, `entrypoint` (`claude-vscode` for the VS Code extension,
`sdk-cli` for `claude -p` and the adapter's processes, there are others), `kind`, `status`
(`idle` | `busy`), `updatedAt` (ms), `version` and other fields. Next to them lie
`<pid>.<hash>.key` files; the worker does not read them. A process that crashed without cleaning
up leaves its file behind, so a record is live only if process `pid` exists (`kill -0`). The
worker reads the directory once per mirror pass (2 s; holders for all transcripts, not only
those under the mirror), excludes its own processes (agent pids and their process groups: the
adapter starts the CLI as a group leader) as well as the `sdk-cli` record of a transcript its
own process is currently driving (in case of a wrapper with a different pid), and skips unknown
fields and broken files. The remaining records are holders; of several for one transcript, the
`busy` one is taken, then the most recent. The worker reports whether the registry exists in
`hello` (`capabilities.claude_code.sessions_registry: true` if the directory exists, §5.4).

- The worker reports a change of holder (appeared, disappeared, changed `status`) to the hub
  with a holder report: `session.state` with a nil `session_id`, the transcript's
  `runtime_session_id` and `held_by: {entrypoint, status} | null` (§5.4), at most once per 2 s
  per transcript, through the outbox, in the same order as `mirror.event` (a direct frame would
  overtake events in the outbox carrying the old `held_by`; this is how the first live run of
  T20 failed). Every `mirror.event` carries the holder the worker saw when reading. On `hello`
