  (§5.3 `session.start.skills`), as the plugin `hqc` (`--plugin-dir`, §8.1), the hub's copy
  hiding a same-named skill of the machine. Turning it on trusts the hub with instructions and
  scripts the agent runs, within the worker's `deny` and the session's mode; a skill with
  `hooks` is never taken (§20). Worker-local like `hub_mcp`, not in `hello`; **Claude Code
  only**; default false;
- `launch`: `process` (the only value in the first version; `os-user` and `container`
  are reserved).

`launch` is not accepted in `worker.toml` yet. `default` cannot be
defined in the file; the name of an environment is letters, digits, `_`,
`-` and `.`; an unknown field is a config error (as in `[permissions]`). An environment no
`[[env_bindings]]` names (since 0.62) is not an error, but no folder runs in it: the worker
logs a warning at start and `hqc-worker env` marks it, since it is most often a table under the
wrong name (`[environments.x.permissions]` after `[environments.y]`).

The folders the worker created for workspaces (since 0.58, T45) are in
`$HQC_HOME/created_workspaces.json` (canonical paths, a clone that runs marked as creating;
since 0.60 a worktree with the canonical path of its origin;
written to a temporary file and renamed, 0600), next to `known_workspaces.json`: the only
folders `workspace.delete` removes; at start the worker removes the folder of every entry still
marked as creating (and prunes a worktree's origin). `git` for a workspace (§5.3) runs with the same process environment as an
agent of that folder's environment (`Environment::process_env`), where its keys come in (T44);
`git worktree add` with the environment of the new folder, not the origin's. A worktree shares
the origin's `.git` (config, hooks, filters), so whatever runs in one folder's sessions can
plant what git runs in the other's environment: two folders bound to different environments are
not separated by making one a worktree of the other.

The `default` environment: no keys, no tokens, `deny` from `[permissions]` (by default it
includes ssh/scp too), local MCP off. Keys of one project (for example `infra`) are moved out of
`~/.ssh` into the worker's store (files in `$HQC_HOME/keys/`, 0700 and 0600, decided on
2026-10-31: Keychain is locked in ssh sessions on a Mac) and are available only to sessions on paths
with that environment. The store holds one private key per file, named as in `ssh_keys`;
`hqc-worker env add-key <name> <file>` creates it with these modes and copies the key in with
0600, and never replaces a key of the same name. The worker does not start (and `hqc-worker env`
does not print) when the store, a file in it or `$HQC_HOME/agents/` is open to group or others,
is a link or belongs to another user (the message names the `chmod`), or when a name in
`ssh_keys` is not in the store. The worker reads key material only in `add-key`; logs, frames
and `hqc-worker env` carry key names, never keys.

Secrets from the chat (since 0.147, iteration 6, `docs/ITERATION-6.md`). `session_secrets = true`
at the top of `worker.toml` (off by default; the hub cannot turn it on) lets the owner give a
running agent a secret or an ssh key from the chat (`secret.put`, §5.3, §6) and the agent ask for
one (`hqc_secret`) or make a key (`hqc_ssh_keygen`, §7), in a session of the worker's owner that
is not restricted (§8.4) and runs Claude Code. The value goes to the agent's process, not to the
model: a secret is the file `$HQC_SECRETS/<name>` (0600) in `$HQC_HOME/secrets/<id>/` (0700),
made when the process starts and removed when it ends (stop, idle stop, restart, crash; a worker
that died leaves folders behind, and its next start removes them), so after a restart the agent
asks again; the agent is told the path. A key is decrypted by the worker itself (a passphrase
never goes on a command line) and loaded with `ssh-add` from a 0600 file in that folder that is
removed at once; every such process has an ssh-agent of its own, empty if nothing is to be
loaded. A key kept for a workspace ("Remember for this workspace", and every `hqc_ssh_keygen`
key) is in `$HQC_HOME/workspace-keys/<the first 32 hex of the sha256 of the workspace's canonical
path>/<name>` (0700 and 0600, without a passphrase, the path in `.path` beside them), apart
from the store of `ssh_keys`: through the hub one adds only a new key to one's own workspace,
and never binds a key of that store to a folder by its name. Every agent process of a session in
that workspace loads them beside its environment's `ssh_keys`; a clone of a new workspace
(§5.3) does not. `hqc-worker env` shows `session_secrets` and the kept keys by workspace (name
and fingerprint), `hqc-worker env which <path>` those of the folder. What the agent then does
with a secret it has is its business: the boundary is that the owner gives it, seeing which
session asks and why, and a prompt-injected agent that has a secret can leak it. The hub keeps
the card it writes (`approval.request` with `secret`, §4) its own: it drops `secret` from an
`approval.request` a worker sends.

A secret from Vaultwarden (since 0.216). `vault = true` at the top of `worker.toml` (off by
default, and only with `session_secrets`) lets an `hqc_secret` card name a Vaultwarden
(Bitwarden) entry instead of a typed value, as T3 Code's card takes a 1Password reference: the
worker reads it with `rbw` 1.15 or newer (from `PATH`; an older one lacks `list --fields type`
and `get --field private_key`, and is refused as such) on its own machine and the value goes
into the agent's process as a typed one does, so it passes neither the client nor the hub. The
entry is the one whose name or id equals what the card says, exactly: `rbw get` alone would also
take an entry whose name merely contains it, or one with a matching site address, so the worker
first finds the entry's id in `rbw list --fields id,name,type` (none, or several of that name,
is refused) and reads by the id — the password (a note's text for a note), the private key of an
entry of Bitwarden's type "SSH key" (`--field private_key`), and such an entry only for `kind:
ssh_key` (into the agent's ssh-agent): as a plain `secret` it would be a file the agent reads, so
anything else — a plain secret, with a field or without, a provider's key — is refused, naming the
entry, before anything is read. With a field (`vault_field`, since 0.243) the
worker reads the whole entry (`rbw get --raw`, one JSON object) and picks the field itself, by
its exact, case-sensitive name: `notes`; else a key of the entry's own data whose value is text
(`username`, `password`, `totp` — the key as stored —, a card's `number` or `code`, an identity's
names, an ssh key's `public_key`, `fingerprint`, `private_key`); else the one custom field of
that name. `rbw get --field` is not used for it: it matches a custom field by a substring of its
name and could print another field than the one shown. `rbw unlocked`, the list and the read
take at most 25 s together (since 0.243; 15 s before). What the worker can read is what the account `rbw` is signed in
with there can, and while `rbw` is unlocked there the commands of every agent on that machine,
which run as the same user, can read it too without a card: the card decides what the worker
gives, not what an agent there can reach. Since 0.243 a locked `rbw` is not refused: `rbw
unlocked` only tells whether it was locked, and `rbw list` then unlocks it, `rbw-agent` asking for
the master password through the `pinentry` configured on that machine; with a Touch ID pinentry
and a short `lock_timeout` in `rbw`'s config a read that finds the vault locked again asks for a
confirmation there, as `op` does through the 1Password app. The 25 s are the time to answer. Reads on a worker run one at a time, so concurrent ones wait
for one prompt (the 25 s covers the wait) instead of opening one each. If it is not unlocked
(the prompt is cancelled, there is no `pinentry` that can ask, as on a machine without a screen)
or not answered in time, the owner is told and the card stays open: unlock `rbw` on that
machine, or type the value. A prompt nobody answered stays open there, as `rbw-agent` runs its
`pinentry` without a time limit and the worker giving up does not close it: answer it, then
give again. The errors of the read name the reason and the action for `rbw`; the card's "or
type the value" is added by the worker for a card only, and not to a refusal typing would not get
past (an SSH key entry asked for as a plain secret, a value over 64 KiB). An unlock done for one
read opens the vault to every process of that user, and `rbw-agent` (1.15) starts its
`lock_timeout` (3600 s by default) again at every use by any of them, so an agent's own `rbw get`
there keeps it open for as long as it reads, without a prompt; a short `lock_timeout` locks it
only once nothing uses it. The `pinentry` window does not say who asks (an agent's own `rbw get`
raises the same one).
`hello.capabilities.vault` tells the hub (§5.4);
`hqc-worker env` shows `vault`.

The task list tools (since 0.223). `task_tools = true` at the top of `worker.toml` (off by default;
the hub cannot turn it on) starts every agent process of the worker with
`CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`, which gives the 5.x models of Claude Code 2.1.312 and later the
task tools (`TaskCreate`, `TaskUpdate`, `TaskList`, `TaskGet`, §8.1, and then no `TodoWrite`) that
fill the task list row above the input (§6); the older models of the CLI's list (Opus 4.7 and 4.6,
Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5) have them without it. The worker's own value wins over one of the
environment's `env`; without `task_tools` the variable is removed from the child's environment.
`hqc-worker env` shows `task_tools`.

The note of background work that runs long (since 0.244). `long_run_note` at the top of
`worker.toml`, in seconds like `idle_timeout`, is how often the agent is told that a background
command or subagent of its own still runs (§8.1): 3300 (55 minutes) unless written, `0` for no
notes at all. With the 1-hour prompt cache it is below the hour the cache lives after the
agent's last request, so that the turn of the note reads the cache; a value of an hour or more
makes that turn miss it, and is not refused; with the 5-minute cache or on a provider that turn
misses it at any value. `hqc-worker env` shows `long_run_note`.

A provider's key from Vaultwarden (since 0.243). The `api_key` of a `[providers.<name>]` is
either a string or a table `{ vault = "<entry name or id>", field = "<optional field>" }`, the
entry and the field as `vault` and `vault_field` of `secret.put` name them (§5.3; unknown keys
in the table, a bad or empty entry or field are a config error). The owner wrote the reference
in his own `worker.toml`, so `vault = true` (which gates only the card) is not needed. Whenever
the worker starts or resumes the agent of a session on that provider it reads the key with
this machine's `rbw`, as for the card — a locked `rbw` asked to unlock through its `pinentry`,
25 s in all — and puts it into the `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` of that process, and into a copy of
the start's spec only: never into the session's own spec, a log line or an error, and not
through the hub. Each start reads again, so a key changed in Vaultwarden is the next start's; the reads of one worker run one at a time;
a running agent keeps the key it started with until its next start (a restart of the session,
an idle stop and the next message). When `rbw` cannot give the key the agent does not start:
the session's start, or the input that woke it, is answered `agent_start_failed` with "the key
of the provider <name> could not be read from Vaultwarden: <reason>", not retryable: the hub
fails the pending input at once instead of retrying three times, which would stack a prompt a
locked `rbw` left open each time; the owner unlocks `rbw` (or answers the open prompt) on that
machine and sends again. He sees it where any failed start is shown (§8.1). `hqc-worker env` lists such a provider as "api_key from
Vaultwarden entry <entry>[, field <field>]".

The browser (since 0.148). `browser = true` at the top of `worker.toml` (off by default; the hub
cannot turn it on) lets the owner give a session's agent their Chrome on this machine (`PATCH
/api/sessions/{id} {browser}`, §6): Claude Code runs with `--chrome` and reaches the browser
through Anthropic's Claude in Chrome extension and its native messaging host, which Claude Code
installs at its first such start; the CLI must be signed in with `/login` (with an API key or a
`setup-token` token it keeps the integration off). The agent works in a tab group of its own in
the user's profile, signed in as the user, and sees the tabs the user drags into that group; it
reads, navigates, clicks and types there under the session's mode, while uploading files of the
machine (`file_upload`, `upload_image`) is never offered. Only a session of the worker's owner
that is not restricted; a refused one starts without it (`browser_refused`). Every other
session runs with `--no-chrome`. The extension's own per-site permissions apply too. What the
agent does in the user's accounts is the owner's to watch: a page it reads (a listing's
description) can carry instructions, and nothing but the session's mode stops a click there.
`hqc-worker env` shows `browser`. Checked on 2026-11-15 with Claude Code 2.1.322: under `-p` and
`--strict-mcp-config` the CLI connects `claude-in-chrome` (`source: dynamic`) and lists its
tools; **[verify]** through hqc's own stream-json run.

Limitation: without a container or a separate OS user the agent sees the files
and the process environment of the user, including other workspaces and session tokens on the
same machine. The boundary is the absence of keys; prohibitions in settings are the first line,
not a boundary. So without a separate OS user the agent can still read `~/.ssh` and use the keys
there directly: a project's keys must be moved out of it into the store, and only then does a
folder without them lose ssh to that host. Likewise a session can reach another session's
ssh-agent socket while that process runs (same OS user, §2.1). Windows in the first version:
only `env` and `permissions`, no `ssh_keys`.

## 15. Search

Postgres full-text search over what a session said and did, and session titles. Results are
filtered by grants. One index, two consumers: the search page in the client and
`hqc_search_history` (which has no filters but the project).

Since 0.36 (T33; `crates/hqc-hub/src/search.rs`, its measurements in
`docs/notes/t33-questions.md`), reworked in 0.97 (migration `0037`) so that
it finds commands, their output and word forms and puts the best match first:
- **What is indexed.** `payload.text` of `user.message`, `agent.message` (final or not),
  `peer.message` and `system`; since 0.97 also a `tool.call` (the tool's name and its
  `args_preview`), a `tool.result` (`result_preview`) and a `clarify.response` (the strings of
  its `answers`); in previews the JSON escapes `\n`, `\r`, `\t` are read as spaces, so a word
  after a line break stays a word, and everywhere `/` and `.` are, so a path, a file name, an
  address or a URL is a sequence of words (`search` finds `crates/hqc-hub/src/search.rs`). Not
  thinking, requests or attachments. One column of `events`, `search_words`, the `tsvector` of
  that text in the `hqc` configuration, weighted A for messages and answers, B for calls, D for
  output, which Postgres keeps on every insert (a stored generated column until 0.156, a
  trigger since, which leaves out a fork's copy — below) and the migration's table rewrite
  backfilled for old rows; a GIN index on it and one on session titles (an expression
  index, as titles change).
- **Configuration `hqc`.** A copy of `russian` whose Latin words go to an English and the rest
  to a Russian Snowball stemmer, both without stop words, so every word stays searchable and
  "переезд" finds "переезда", "deploy" finds "deployed".
- **Whose.** Until grants (iteration 11): the user's (the calling session's owner's) sessions,
  archived ones included and marked `archived: true`, the workers' service sessions left out and
  (since 0.172) of a room's agents' sessions their inputs from the room, which the room has
  (§7.1.1); since 0.175, for an agent of a room (`hqc_search_history`, §7) also the room and
  every other agent's session of it left out (§7.1.1), the owner's `GET /api/search` unchanged.
- **Matching.** The hub parses the query itself into a `to_tsquery('hqc', …)`: every word must
  be there, `"a phrase"` in sequence, `or` either side, `-word` without it, `word*` a prefix
  of the word as typed or of its stem; a prefix of Latin letters also finds the whole stems,
  of 4 letters at least, shorter than it and beginning it, that the stemmer gives it with
  common English endings (`s`, `ed`, `ing`, `ion`, `ment`, `er` and the like, not `y`, `ies`,
  `ly`), as the stem of a longer word may be shorter than the prefix (`connecti*` finds
  "connection", whose stem is `connect`), while `worker*` does not find "work"; `/` and `.`
  in a word are spaces, as in the index, so `docs/SPEC.md` is a phrase; each word and phrase
  is quoted, so punctuation cannot become an operator. A `-` excludes only before a quoted
  phrase or four letters or more (`-test`, `-staging`; a shorter word is excluded in quotes,
  `-"ok"`); before anything else it is part of the word, so a command pasted with its flags
  finds its call: `-rf`, `-lah`, `--force` are the words `rf`, `lah`, `force`, as the index
  reads them. Fuzzy (at least 3 characters) widens each plain word of 3 or more characters,
  leading dashes not counted, with up to 6 similar words (`pg_trgm` `similarity` 0.4 to its
  stem) from `search_vocab`, the words of the index (letters only, 3–40 characters) that the
  migration collects and a trigger on `events` adds to; it finds typos (`pg_trgm` is a trusted
  extension, created by migration `0016`). Titles are matched with the same query; a title hit
  has no `seq`.
- **A fork's copy** (since 0.156, migration `0048`). `search_words` is a plain column a
  trigger fills as an event is written or its `type` or `payload` change, except for the
  events a fork copies (`origin_id` set, §6): they go in without words, so neither the index
  nor `search_vocab` takes them then, and the hub writes their words as soon as the copy is in,
  without the fork's answer waiting for them, 500 events per statement, into the index only —
  `search_vocab` has them from the source. Until it has, the copy is not found; a hub stopped meanwhile leaves the rest of that
  copy unindexed, its source still found.
- **Order and pages.** Best match first: `ts_rank(search_words, q, 1)` (the query without its
  `-word`s), then newest; a title is ranked as text of weight A; since 0.111 `order=newest`
  puts the newest first instead. The cursor is the number of hits already shown, so a page
  after new events may repeat or skip a hit.
- **Filters and counts** (since 0.111, for the client's search page; `GET /api/search`, §6). A
  query may keep to one session, one kind of hit (`message`, `command`, `output`, `answer`, by
  the event's type; a title hit is of none) and the hits since a time, and hold at most so many
  hits of each session, its first ones in the order. Each hit carries the number of hits its
  session has under the same filters; the first page of a query over all sessions carries the
  hits and sessions of the whole query, all and by kind, whatever kind it asked for; a page
  carries the words of its hits that the query found besides the words typed (other forms of a
  word, the similar words of a fuzzy query), those of the most hits first.
- **Snippet.** About 160 characters on one line around the first query word (or fuzzy
  alternative, or since 0.111 such another form) found in the text (ignoring case), else its
  beginning; `…` marks a cut. The text of a call is the tool and its arguments, of an answer its
  strings joined with "; ".
- **Cost.** Each statement of a search (reading the query, then finding the hits, since 0.111
  counting them and finding the other forms) runs with
  `statement_timeout` 5 s; over it the search is refused. Over our hub's 916k events (720k
  indexed): a rare or ordinary word or phrase 14–80 ms, a word in 11–36k events 0.2–0.6 s,
  "the" (229k events) about 2 s; fuzzy 40–560 ms, with a word in most events 2–3 s (SPEC
  0.97, a copy on a shared build host). The migration took 4–5 minutes there, holding
  `events` locked. Since 0.39 (T36, §20): per owner 30 searches a minute, 10 of them fuzzy
  (`GET /api/search` and `hqc_search_history` together; `429 search_limit` /
  `limit_exceeded`), and at most 4 searches run at once on the hub (`503 busy` /
  `unavailable`), so one owner's agent cannot keep the database busy with fuzzy queries.
- **Client** (since 0.114). The search is a page, `#/search`, in the place of the session column
  and the chat on a desktop (the project bar stays) and the whole screen on a phone, opened by
  the magnifier in the head of the session column (on a phone, of the first screen and of a
  project's screen); the session list has no search field of its own, archive mode keeps its
  filter by title and path (§6). Its head: "‹ <project>" back to the address it was opened from
  (Esc too, unless a menu or the slid-out session column takes it), the field, "N results in M
  sessions". Filters: the kind — All, Messages, Commands, Tool output, Answers, each with its
  count —, the project (all of them or one on the bar), the time (any, the past day, week or
  month, sent as `since`), "Also typos" (fuzzy, from 3 characters), and Best match or Newest.
  From 2 characters, 300 ms after typing (a changed filter at once), the page asks for 50 hits,
  at most 4 of each session, and shows a card per session in the order of its first hit: the
  project's tile, the title (opening the session), "archived", the project, "N results" and how
  long ago the session was active, then its hits — the kind (Message, Command, Tool output,
  Answer, Title), the snippet with the query's words and the other forms marked, the time — and
  "N more in this session ›", which loads that session's hits a page at a time (`session=`);
  "Also finds: …" lists the other forms, "More results" loads the next page. The page keeps its
  query and filters in its address
  (`#/search?q=…&kind=…&project=…&time=…&order=newest&fuzzy=1`, replaced, not pushed), so
  Back from an opened hit brings the same search back; the Compact look puts all the filters on
  one row. A hit opens `#/s/<session>?seq=<seq>`:
  the chat loads its newest page and then the older pages down to the hit (§6) and, once the
  event is there, renders the feed from the block that holds it if it did not and scrolls the block that holds it (the last block starting at or before `seq`) to the middle
  and marks it.

## 16. Notifications and hub cron

Web Push on events: `approval.request`, `clarify.request`, `worker.approval.request`
(to the worker owner; since 0.17 this is an `approval.request` event in the worker's service
session, §10.2: `title` is the worker's name, `tag` is `<system_session_id>:<request_id>`; no
push for `worker_log` lines); the final `agent.message`, `peer.message` and `system` about
undelivered input (except mirror events: those get no push at all, §9.1) — to the session owner and to users with a grant who have written
in this session, if they have no active WS subscription to it. On iOS Web Push works
only from an installed PWA, a limitation of the first version. A Telegram bridge is
optional, via `hermes send`. Since 0.172 (§7.1.1) the final `agent.message` of a room's agent
pushes nothing; the agent's post in the room, a `peer.message` there, pushes with the room's
`session_id`, so the click opens the room, the room's title and the body "<agent's title>:
<text>".

Push body (JSON, `hqc_proto::api::PushMessage`, example `examples/wire/api.push.json`):
`{session_id, type, title?, body?, tag?, payload?}`, where `type` is the event type and
`payload` is the §4 event itself as stored. The hub sets `title` (the session title), `body`
(a short text), `tag` (`<session_id>:<request_id>` for requests, otherwise
`<session_id>:<type>`: a notification with the same tag replaces the previous one) and omits
`payload` if the message does not fit into a push (about 4 KB). The client's service worker,
without `title`/`body`, builds them from `type` and `payload`, shows `approval.request` and
`clarify.request` with `requireInteraction`, and on click opens `#/s/<session_id>`, or
`#/s/<open_session_id>` when that is set.

A request of a session that other sessions of its owner wait on through open `hqc_ask`s
(since 0.41, T37; §7.1, §10.1): still one notification per request, with the request's own
`session_id` and `tag` (so a later notification of the same request replaces it), plus
`open_session_id` — the top of the chain (the session the user started the work in, where the
card is shown too). No push while the user watches the request's session or any session
waiting on it. Only the session owner gets `open_session_id`; a worker owner who is not the
session owner gets the push as before.

Hub cron: `ScheduledMessage` — at `at` or by `cron` in the user's `timezone`,
send `message` to `session_id`, or create a session from the project template
in `workspace_id` and send it there. Missed runs (the hub was down): with `catch_up`
it runs once, otherwise they are skipped. No task scheduler for agents;
anything more complex is Hermes cron.

Since 0.38 (T35, `crates/hqc-hub/src/schedules.rs`):
- A run is a `user.message` of the owner (`author: {kind: user, id: <owner>}`) with
  `schedule_id` in the payload, stored `pending` and delivered like the user's own input (§5.2):
  it queues behind a running turn and waits for an offline worker. Its `event_id` is derived
  from the schedule and the run's time, so a run is stored at most once.
- `cron` is 5 fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week; `L`, `W`, `#` and the
  `@daily`-style names are accepted, seconds and years are not), evaluated in `timezone` with
  the crate `croner` and the IANA database of `chrono-tz`. DST as in Vixie cron: a fixed time
  in the skipped hour runs right after the gap (02:30 on a spring-forward night runs at 03:00), a
  fixed time in the repeated hour runs once, the first time; a daily 09:00 stays 09:00 local
  time across the change.
- `next_run` is kept in the table, so the loop survives a restart. Every 10 s the hub sends what
  is due. A run found more than 2 minutes late was missed (the hub was down): with `catch_up`
  it is sent once, late, otherwise skipped; either way the next run is the first one after now
  (several missed runs of a `cron` give one message at most). An `at` runs or is skipped once
  and is then finished (`next_run` null), kept for the list until deleted.
- A paused (`enabled: false`) or deleted schedule never fires; the hub locks the row while it
  sends, so a pause or a delete during a run waits for it. Resuming a `cron` skips the runs
  missed while paused. Deleting the session deletes its schedules. A session that is archived or
  driven from VS Code takes no input (§6, §9.3): its runs are skipped (`next_run` moves on, a
  warn in the hub's log), not queued. Since 0.160 so are the runs of a `cron` while the session is
  paused (§17.3), which would pile up for the resume; a run of an `at` is stored and waits for
  it.
- Since 0.39 (T36): a schedule made by an agent (`hqc_schedule`) keeps the chain of its call,
  and its runs carry it (§7.1); since 0.43 (T39) with the chain's permission cap, fixed when
  the schedule is made: a run of a schedule made by a session in `ask` runs in `ask` (§5.3).
  Since 0.44 (T40) the cap of each run is the lower of that cap and the creator's
  (`created_by`, §3) mode at run time, taken as in §7.1: a run of a schedule whose creator has moved
  from `auto` to `ask` since runs in `ask`, and so does one whose creator was deleted, or was
  not stored (a schedule from before 0.44). The hub sends at most 60 runs per owner and hour; a run over
  that is skipped like a run of a target that takes no input (a warn, `next_run` moves on). The
  count of schedules that may still run and the insert are made under a per-owner lock.
- Since 0.169 the hub sends the session's subscribers `schedules.live` (§4, §6): the enabled
  schedules of the session with a `next_run`, ordered by it, `due_in_ms` counted from the hub's
  clock; on subscribe (when not empty) and whenever a schedule of the session is created (the
  tool and the API), paused, resumed, deleted or run, so a finished `at` and a paused schedule
  are not in it. It is made from the table each time and kept nowhere.
- The hub's clock is injectable for tests (`AppState::clock`).

## 17. States and lifecycle

### 17.1 Session state
`state` is computed by the hub when serving, from `archived`, `locked_by`, the worker's status,
open requests, `process_state` and delivery. Priority top to bottom, the first true one wins;
`queue_len`, the number of inputs in `pending`, is served separately:

| state | when |
|---|---|
| `archived` | archived |
| `locked_vscode` | `locked_by: vscode` |
| `worker_offline` | the worker is unreachable |
| `waiting` | there is an open `approval`/`clarify` |
| `error` | there is an input with `delivery: failed` and no later input was delivered after it (since 0.117), or the last turn ended with a process error |
| `running` | a turn is in progress |
| `paused` | `paused_at` is set (since 0.160, §17.3) |
| `queued` | `queue_len > 0`, no turn (the agent is starting) |
| `idle` | otherwise |

The `status.state` event uses the same set.

The client shows the turn from `state` (from `summary`/`session.summary` and the session object),
with no separate events: `running` — a pulsing "Running" pill in the header and, since 0.189, the
main agent's row, the first of the live block above the input (§6), not a line at the bottom of
the feed: "Main agent: Working" ("Command: <command>" while the last `tool.call` that is a shell
command has no `tool.result`, T26, otherwise "Main agent: Running <tool and its argument>", with
the run time at the row's right, the time since the call's
`ts`, as the block's other rows show it, `42s`, `1m 24s`; since 0.132 once that call has run
for 2 s, counted from its `ts` or from a later answer to a request after it (a permission or a
question it, or a subagent it runs, waited for; since 0.187 also an answer of this client whose
event has not come yet, from when the hub took it), since 0.161 only a call after the last end of a
turn, §6; since 0.177 the tool as the feed names it, `move (probe-bench)`, its paths relative to
the session's folder; since 0.125, when that call is one
of the session's `foreground_calls`, §6, the row ends with a small icon button, "Run in
background" (its tooltip and name), which sends `POST .../background` with its `call_id`, a
failure shown as a notice; the button
goes once the worker reports the call moved or ended; since 0.179, with no such call, the
session's `activity`, §6, stands in place of "Working": "Retrying 3/10 (529), next in
8 s" — "no response" in place of a status the attempt did not get, the delay rounded up to
whole seconds and left out when it is 0 —, "Compacting the conversation…", "Thinking · 12.34k
tokens" — since 0.227 a count that runs up to each new estimate, as in the VS Code tab: from the
number shown, linearly, over the time since the estimate before it (0.3–3 s), redrawn every
100 ms, the first estimate and a smaller one (a new thinking block) shown at once —; a waiting
`hqc_ask` is "Waiting for a reply from <session>"), `queued` — "Main agent:
Input queued"; since 0.233, when the session has an `activity`, that activity in its place, the
row drawn as a running one (Claude Code echoes an input, which opens its turn, only after the
auto-compaction it runs before it, so the input waits while the agent compacts), `paused` —
"Paused" in the header and the session's row,
`waiting` — "Main agent: Waiting for approval" if the open request is not in the feed (otherwise
its card is that row). In a room each agent at work has its row, led by its name in place of
"Main agent: ". The row is not in the feed, so the feed's window gets shorter when the block appears at
the start of a turn: the chat stays at the bottom, as it does for any change of that window's
size.
A `status` event is not drawn as a feed line, except `error` with `detail`.

The hub tracks "a turn is in progress" itself: a turn is opened by the worker's `ack` of
`session.input` (the worker passes input to the runtime one per turn, except an input that joins
a running turn, §17.2: its `ack` has `joined: true` and opens none, since 0.70), since 0.121
also by `status running` from the worker while the session's `process_state` is `running` (a
turn the runtime starts by itself, with no input: Claude Code after a background task's end,
§8.1), and closed by
`agent.message` with `final: true`, `status` with `idle` or `error` (the latter means "the turn
ended with an error"), the process stopping or the watchdog (§17.3, also "the turn ended with
an error").
"The turn ended with an error" keeps `error` until the next input: a new `user.message`
clears the flag, and since 0.121 so does a turn the runtime starts by itself (`status
running`). `worker_offline`: the session has a worker and it is not connected now.

### 17.2 Input during a turn **[decision]**
Input from the input queue (§7.1) that arrives during a turn waits for the final answer
and starts the next turn; one turn per item, in `seq` order. Since 0.70 a Claude Code turn
takes a person's input as the VS Code tab does: while a turn runs, the worker writes the first
waiting input that may join into it. A person's input may join when it has no `peer` and no
`schedule_id` (a run of a schedule, §16), its `text` does not start with `/` after leading
whitespace (a slash command; since 0.71) and it is not capped to `ask` (§5.3; since 0.129 to
`auto` either: no cap below `allow_all`). Since 0.174 a `send` of another session may join too:
a `peer` of mode `send` (not `ask`) with no `schedule_id`, whose cap (`permission_cap`, §7.1)
is not below the session's own mode and which the runtime's mode, as it confirmed it, is not
above (a switch it refused or has not confirmed yet leaves the turn above the cap, as for a
capped turn, §5.3), so that it does not hold the turn's mode down; it goes in with its peer
header like any input of another session (§7.1). It goes past the waiting inputs in front of it
that are no person's and cannot join (an `hqc_ask`, a run of a schedule, a send that does not
fit its cap), which keep their places and run as turns of their own after this one; a person's
input that cannot join (a slash command, a capped one) stops the search, so a person's own
inputs keep their order. Of several that may join the worker writes the first one, then the
next. The turn takes nothing only when its own input is an `hqc_ask`, or another `peer` input
that is not a `send`: its final answer goes to its sender and an input written into it would
shape that answer or, carried with the ask into a turn the CLI runs by itself, take it. A turn
started by a `send` or capped to `ask` or `auto` takes what may join (a capped turn runs in the
lower mode, which only makes it safer). The agent must also have no open `approval` or
`clarify`. A person's input that carries buffered sends of other sessions (`peer_prefix`, §7.1)
may join: the cap of §7.1 caps it whenever one of them comes from a session in `ask` or (since
0.129) `auto`, and the worker never writes a capped person's input into a running turn. The hub
honours `joined` only for a `user.message` without `schedule_id`, a room's input to its agent
(since 0.172), which the worker gets without `peer` (§7.1.1), and (since 0.174) a `peer.message`
of mode `send` without `schedule_id`; a `joined` on any other input is the worker's mistake, logged, not kept, and the
input's turn opens (since 0.71). Since 0.112 the hub keeps an honoured one on the message,
`payload.joined: true` (§4) and, since 0.221, `payload.joined_after`, where the agent took it
(§4, §6), and sends them with the `delivery` frame (§6); the client marks the first line of a person's message with an icon before the time, "Joined the turn" its tooltip (since 0.178; the words in the line before; a send's bubble has no such note).
What may not join waits for the end of the turn as before (scheduled runs and slash commands
always do), and a person's inputs keep their `seq` order among themselves. Since 0.75 nothing
is written into the turn either while a move of the session waits (§5.3): the input is for the
agent in the new folder.
The CLI takes the input at its next step, after the result of the
tool call running then, and the worker answers `ack {event_id, joined: true}` on its echo; the
turn's final `agent.message` stays `in_reply_to` the turn's own input. When the turn ends
before that (the input came during the final answer, or before an interrupt), the CLI runs it
as the next turn by itself (§8.1): the first such input becomes that turn, its echo gives a
plain `ack`; the others stay written into it and are acked with `joined: true` when the CLI
takes them (that turn's `in_reply_to` is then the last of them the CLI took; such inputs are a
person's or a send, which nothing answers by `in_reply_to`). A send that becomes the next turn
this way keeps its cap on that turn (since 0.174): an owner's raise of the session's mode
during it stays at the cap, as for a send that waited in the queue. The runtime is then moved to
the mode of that turn at once (the lower of the cap and the session's mode; to the session's own
mode when the new turn is not capped but the one before it was), since it already runs it, with
no wait for the confirmation: usually that raises the mode and the change may lag a moment;
after the owner raised the mode during the turn before, it lowers the runtime to the send's cap.
The same holds for an input sent during a turn the CLI began by itself after a background task
(since 0.161 it leaves that turn's last text held for its `result`, §8.1); since 0.71
`session.stop` interrupts such
a turn too (the adapter knows it from the CLI's `system/init` with no input of hqc's). With no turn
of hqc's running, the worker gives such an input as a turn of its own; when the CLI takes it into
the turn it began (the echo comes before that turn's `result`), since 0.251 the worker acks it
`joined: true` when the hub honours `joined` on it (no `schedule_id`; no `peer`, or a `send`; a
slash command or a capped input too: the worker gave it as a turn of its own, in its cap's mode,
and the CLI took it into its turn), so the hub keeps its `joined_after` and the feed stands it
where the agent took it; an `hqc_ask` or a run of a schedule taken so gets a plain `ack`. The
CLI's `result` still ends that turn, and an input the CLI runs after it gets a plain `ack`. Before
0.251 both got a plain `ack`, and the message stood at its own `seq`, above the steps the agent
made before it took it. An input
the CLI cancels after a `session.stop` (a carried input on a second Stop) fails, not retryable,
instead of going back to the queue: the person cancelled it. Since 0.231 the owner's own Stop of a
turn that runs (`session.stop {quiet: true}`: the stop button, a room's Stop; a pause's stop is none
of these) is "stop the turn, send everything that waited, stop again": when it comes the worker
marks the inputs it holds (its queue; a capped input waiting for its mode), and when the stopped
turn ends it marks the inputs the runtime dropped from that turn (cancelled or not taken: they were
written before the Stop). It writes the marked ones into the agent's history without a turn (§8.1),
in `event_id` order, the hub's creation order. The agent knows them next time and does not act on
them now. Each is acked `quiet` when the runtime has taken it, and acked `quiet` again when the hub
resends it. A slash command among them fails, not retryable ("cancelled by Stop"): it runs or it
does not, it is no text for the history (what decides is the text the runtime gets: a message of
another session whose text starts with a path carries a header first and is no command).
Since 0.241 so does an input whose cap is below the session's own mode (T39, §7.1: a message of
another session or a run of an agent's schedule sent with a lower ceiling), and since 0.248 every
input with a cap below `allow_all`, also one at the session's own mode: it was never handled under
its cap, and the next turn would find it in the history unhandled in the session's mode then, which
the owner may raise to `allow_all` meanwhile. The worker fails it, not retryable ("dropped at Stop:
it may run only in a permission mode below Allow all": the feed shows it not delivered with that
reason, and an `hqc_ask` it carried fails at once, §7.1), and writes in its place, after the quiet
inputs, a quiet note of its own that names what was dropped and never its text: "[hqc] A message
from the session <address> was dropped at the owner's Stop because of a permission conflict: it may
run only in a permission mode below Allow all. Its text is not shown." ("A scheduled message" for a
run of a schedule, "A message" otherwise). The note is no input of the hub: the feed does not show
it, nothing is acked for it, and a `session.kill` or a worker restart before the runtime took it
loses it. Limitation: an input capped only by the buffered `send` messages it carries in front (T40,
§7.1), the owner's own message among them, is dropped the same way, and the buffered messages come
with the next input. Until the
stopped turn ends nothing new goes into it, and what comes after the Stop is never marked: it waits,
and goes as an ordinary input once the quiet lines are taken (the CLI runs a "next" line before a
"later" one, and the agent must see the stopped text first). So a message typed after the Stop runs,
and so does a slash command typed after it (Clear goal is a Stop, then `/goal clear`). The idle
unload and a move wait for the acks. A Stop with no turn running (idle, no process, the agent waits
for a slot or a move) and a stop with no `quiet` (a pause's, which keeps the waiting messages for
the resume) mark nothing and write nothing. The hub keeps `payload.quiet: true` on such a message
and sends it with the `delivery` frame (§6); the feed stands it behind its `joined_after`, where
Claude Code recorded it, and never shows it as waiting (§6). An input the hub has not handed to the
worker yet is not touched. Before 0.231 an input the CLI cancelled after a Stop failed, not
retryable, and the others waited and ran. Send now (§6) is no way past that hold: while the stopped
turn ends, an input that came after the Stop is `error not_now`. The runtime's `cancelled` for the
turn's own first line, which a Stop's cancel can reach before the CLI started it (a cold start),
makes that input come back as dropped at once, so it is written quiet like the others (not in a turn
the runtime started by itself, where that line is not what keeps the turn open). Take back of an
input the Stop marked withdraws it as ever: one still in the worker's queue leaves it, and one the
CLI already cancelled is withdrawn at once, without asking the CLI again, and is never written
quiet. One already written as a quiet line is on its way into the history and is `409
already_taken`. Limitation: a `session.kill` or a worker restart at any time between the Stop and
the quiet acks (during the stopped turn, and while quiet lines wait behind a turn the CLI started by
itself) drops the marked inputs at the worker; the hub, which holds them `pending`, sends them to
the next process as plain inputs, which run as before 0.231. The "interrupt and send" button does
`session.stop` and then the input. For runtimes with `steer` (Hermes) a "steer" button is
available: `session.steer` without interrupting. Two users with `write` share the same queue.
Each turn runs in its own input's mode (since 0.43, T39): a person's input queued behind a
capped turn runs in the session's mode (§5.3), unless (since 0.44, T40) it carries a buffered
send from a session in a lower mode (§7.1).

Since 0.219 the owner may take a message of theirs back, or send it in at once, while it waits
for the agent: it shows `queued` or `awaiting delivery` and, beside its Copy button,
Take back and (only while the session's turn runs) Send now. A message waits in the hub (the
worker is away, the session paused), in the worker's queue, or written into the CLI's queue and
not yet taken. Take back (`POST .../inputs/{event_id}/withdraw`, §6) removes it from wherever it
waits, or has the CLI drop the line (§8.1), and then no one ever sees it: it is `delivery:
withdrawn`, never acked, never failed, never copied into a fork, and the client puts its text
after what is typed in the input (a blank line between them) and its files back among the input's
files, read from the device when it holds them (§6), else from the hub, and not kept on the
device; a refusal, because the agent took the message first, is `409 already_taken` and says so,
and the bubble stays. A message that was handed to a worker is asked
about at its connection whatever the session's start state (a paused session's worker holds
nothing: `true`); with no worker connected it is `409 worker_offline`; while the question is open
the message is `withdrawing`, handed to nobody and refused a second take-back (`409 withdrawing`);
a message taken back already is `409 withdrawn`, and the client that asked puts the text back as on
success; a worker's answer after the hub's `504` is dropped, and a take-back whose answer the
client lost hides the message without putting its text back (§6, limitations). Only a message the
owner typed (`payload.human`, §4) has them, and Send now not a slash command.
Send now (`.../now`) writes a message the worker only queues into the turn with priority now (§8.1),
or has a line the CLI holds cancelled and written again that way; the CLI moves the call the agent
is in to the background, which is the point; while the agent writes its answer, the answer stops and
the message runs next. It goes past the inputs waiting in front of it, as the owner chose; the turn
takes it under the rules of the input that joins (no `hqc_ask` turn, no move waiting, no open
request, no slash command, no cap): a turn that waits for an answer to a card of the agent's takes
nothing, so that is `409 not_now` (the client says "The agent cannot take this message into its turn
now"); one the agent took meanwhile is `sent_now: false` (the client says "Not sent now: the agent
took it already, or it goes next") and nothing else. A turn's own input is not sent now; it is not taken back once the CLI
started it. A message the hub handed to a worker in an earlier connection is neither taken back nor
sent now until that worker is connected (§6).

### 17.3 Processes
- An idle agent is left alone by default. With the worker's `idle_timeout` > 0 the
  process exits, and the next input brings it back via resume. Since 0.70 an agent is not idle
  while its subagents run (`session.state.subagents` > 0, §5.4) or while Claude Code lists
  background tasks of the session (`background_tasks_changed`, §8.1; since 0.166 not those
  marked `ambient`). An idle exit stops such a watcher with the process: while the agent is
  unloaded, comments on a page it published start no turn of it. Since 0.70 the worker's
  reconnect to the hub and a change of the holder of any transcript (§9.3: Claude Code in VS
  Code or a terminal on the same machine) do not count as the agent's activity; a holder of
  the session's own transcript stops the agent anyway. Since 0.162 an agent that armed a wakeup
  for itself (Claude Code: `ScheduleWakeup`, §8.1) is not idle before the wakeup is due: the
  timeout counts from the later of its last activity and that time, so a wakeup that never
  starts keeps the agent at most `idle_timeout` past it; the wakeup lives in the process and
  dies with it, which before 0.162 an idle unload did before it fired. Since 0.192 a turn the
  runtime starts by itself (Claude Code: e.g. after a background task's end or on a wakeup,
  §8.1) is not idle until its `result`, as a turn of hqc's is not: before, the timeout counted
  from its last output, so such a turn that waited longer than `idle_timeout` for an approval or
  an answer, or ran a command that long, was killed and lost. Since 0.200 a cron job of the
  agent (`CronCreate`) holds the unload off as a wakeup does: the timeout counts from the
  latest of the last activity, the wakeup's time and the next fire of each cron job the worker
  last listed (`due_in_ms` of its `kind: cron` row, §4; a job whose next fire is not known holds
  nothing), so an unload no longer kills a job that has yet to fire. While such a job waits, the process
  holds its slot of `max_sessions`: a new session waits for a slot (`waiting_for_slot`), as it
  does beside any running agent. Since 0.232 an agent is not idle while
  a side question is unanswered (§17.5).
- Since 0.201 the worker ends a process with nothing running by closing the CLI's stdin: a CLI
  with nothing to do exits on it, with status 0, and then reports what it could not write
  (`system/session_writes_lost`, `system transcript_not_saved`, §4); SIGTERM was sent before and
  the CLI never exited so. One that is still there 5 s later gets SIGTERM, SIGKILL 5 s after that.
  This is the idle unload; `session.kill` (restart, pause after a turn, archive, deleting a
  session or a project) when no turn runs (the CLI's own included) and neither a subagent nor a
  background task is listed; and a move with no background task listed, which this way lets the
  transcript be written out before it is moved. Every other end is SIGTERM to the process group,
  SIGKILL after 5 s, as before: `session.kill` with work going on, a move with background tasks,
  a change of the permission cap, the hand-over to VS Code (§9.3: it stops at once) and the
  worker's shutdown (10 s for all its agents); a turn running when the close is asked ends so too.
- Restart (since 0.130, `POST /api/sessions/{id}/restart`, §6): the hub sends `session.kill` and
  right after it `session.start` with `mode: resume`: the process ends and starts again at once,
  resuming its transcript, so its MCP servers and settings are read anew. A turn that runs is
  lost as when the process dies (open `approval`/`clarify` get `stopped`, `system turn_lost`);
  inputs the old process did not take go to the new one after the start's `ack`.
- Pause (since 0.160, `POST /api/sessions/{id}/pause`, §6; Claude Code has no pause of its own):
  the hub sets the session's `paused_at`. With no turn running it ends the agent's process at
  once as a restart does (`session.kill`) and starts nothing; with a turn running it stops the
  turn at once as Stop does (since 0.191; before, it let the turn run to its end) and ends the
  process when the turn has ended, on the worker's `status` `idle` or `error`, or the watchdog's
  turn loss. A kill the worker never got (its link was dead, it was away, the hub restarted) goes
  after its next `hello` while the process was last reported alive; so does (since 0.191) the
  stop of a turn that still runs. When the hub ends the process itself, it sets `paused_at`
  again: the time the agent stopped. A process that ends another way (a restart for a change of
  provider or browser, a worker restart, a crash) leaves the time of the pause. The agent's
  background subagents and commands, and what it set to wake it up, end with the process. While
  `paused_at` is set the hub neither starts the agent nor delivers input to it, whatever asks for
  it (a worker's `hello`, a process that stopped, a schedule, a peer message, a move): inputs
  typed meanwhile wait in `pending`, and the session is `paused` once no turn runs (§17.1). A
  turn that still runs gets the answers to its requests that its worker has not acknowledged,
  which after a reconnect only a start's `ack` would send otherwise. A run of a `cron` schedule
  is skipped (§16), a run of an `at` one is stored and waits; `hqc_ask` to the session is refused
  at once with `unavailable` (§7.1; one queued before the pause waits out its timeout),
  `hqc_send` is queued. Resume (`POST .../resume`) clears `paused_at`, and the hub stores, as a
  pending `user.message` of the user who resumed with `resume: true` (§4), the note `[hqc] You
  were paused at <HH:MM> UTC on <YYYY-MM-DD> and are resumed now: <elapsed> passed.`
  (`<elapsed>`: the two largest units, rounded down, a zero second one left out: `45 s`,
  `12 min`, `1 h 20 min`, `3 d 2 h`). Since 0.191, after a pause that stopped a running turn
  (`pause_cut_turn`), the note goes on: `If the pause cut a step of your work (it shows as a tool
  use the user rejected or interrupted), that was the pause, not the user: go on with the task
  from where it stopped.` Claude Code shows the agent the step an interrupt cut as one the user
  rejected, and without it a resumed agent took the pause for a refusal and stopped; after a
  pause of an idle agent a rejected step is the user's own, and the note does not say it. The
  note goes to the agent ahead of the inputs held during the pause. When the process was ended,
  the hub starts the agent with `mode: resume`, the same history; resumed before the turn the
  pause stopped has ended (since 0.191; before, such a turn ran on and got no note), the process
  still runs and the note goes to it without a start.
- Worker offline: input accumulates in the hub (`pending`), the session is `worker_offline`,
  delivery on connect in `seq` order. Open `approval`s on an offline worker
  stay open until it returns or until `expires_at`.
- The hub detects a worker restart by a new `boot_id` in `hello` (§5.2): all agents are
  `stopped`; open `approval`/`clarify` get `approval.cancel`/`clarify.cancel
  {worker_restart}`; an unfinished turn is lost, the hub writes `system turn_lost`, and a
  `status running` the worker's outbox sends again after that `hello` opens no turn (§17.1);
  `pending` inputs are resent after `hello` (via `session.start` with `mode: resume`).
  A reconnect with the same `boot_id` is not a restart, nothing is cancelled.
  Since 0.256 (#220) the agent is told what the restart took: before it forgets the counts, the
  hub takes each live session of the worker (no room, no paused or service session) whose turn
  was open, whose `subagents` or `background_tasks` were above 0, or that had a kept
  `subagents.live` list (its wakeups and cron jobs die with the process too), and stores for it a
  pending `user.message` of the session's owner with `restart: true` (§4): "[hqc] The worker
  running you restarted at HH:MM UTC, and your process with it.", then, for a cut turn, that a
  step shown as rejected or interrupted was the restart and to check what is done before
  repeating a step that changes something, and the lost work by kind and description (each a
  JSON string, as in the leftovers notes, §8.1) or by count, with "check what got done and start
  again what is still needed". The starts after `hello` deliver it like any pending input, so the
  agent goes on at once instead of at the next message. A session that got such a note in the
  last 10 minutes gets none, so a worker that dies again at once does not restart an agent into
  it over and over.
- A worker that gets `SIGUSR1` (since 0.256) stops as on `SIGTERM`, but only once no session's
  agent works: no turn (its own or one hqc started), no input waiting for it, no background
  subagent or command, no side question, no mode switch under way; armed wakeups and cron jobs do
  not count. It waits at most 30 minutes, then stops anyway. The service manager (`KeepAlive`,
  `Restart=always`) starts it again: an update then loses nothing an agent was doing.
- An agent process that exits within 500 ms of launch is a failed
  start: the adapter's `start`/`resume` returns an error (the worker replies
  `agent_start_failed`, retryable, §5.2), not "process exited"; otherwise a worker with a
  non-empty queue would restart it in a loop. A process that dies later with an error or
  in the middle of a turn gives `system agent_exited`; the worker brings it back via `resume`
  if there is input in the queue.
- Hub restart: workers reconnect and resend their outbox; `PendingRequest`s
  are restored from the database, undelivered `mcp.result`s are resent.
- Turn watchdog **[decision]**. If a session is `running` (§17.1) and its worker has sent no
  event for it, `agent.delta`, (since 0.113) `subagents.live` and (since 0.122) `tokens.rate`
  included, for longer than `HQC_TURN_WATCHDOG_S` (default 900 s, `0` turns it off), the hub
  considers the turn lost: it cancels open
  `approval`/`clarify` with `timeout`, closes the turn without a final message
  (the input stays `delivered`), writes `system turn_lost` with the text "no events for N s",
  and the session shows `error` until the next input. The countdown runs from the worker's last
  event or from the moment the session became `running` again: waiting for the user's
  answer (`waiting`), waiting for the reply to its own `hqc_ask` (an open ask of the session,
  since 0.35) and the worker being offline (`worker_offline`) do not count. The hub keeps
  event times in memory; after a hub restart every open turn gets the full
  period. The hub sends nothing to the worker: the process and its input queue are left alone.
  Since 0.179 the worker sends `tokens.rate` again at each heartbeat Claude Code sends every
  30 s while a tool call of the main agent runs (§8.1), so a call that runs silent for longer
  than the limit keeps its turn.

### 17.4 Archiving and deletion
- Archiving: the hub sets `archived_at` (since 0.53; unarchiving clears it), sends `session.kill`, open requests get
  `approval.cancel`/`clarify.cancel {archived}`, `pending` inputs are marked `failed`,
  the send buffer is cleared. Unarchiving returns `idle`, or `paused` for a session paused before
  it was archived; the process comes back via resume on the first input, or for a paused one on
  Resume (§17.3). Since 0.61 (T47): archiving the last unarchived session of an
  `ephemeral` workspace marks the workspace for deletion, and unarchiving one clears the mark (`marked_for_deletion`, §3 Workspace); nothing is sent to the worker for it.
- Session deletion: events, `ReadCursor`, `PendingRequest`, the session's artifacts
  (unless another session references them) are deleted; jsonl files on the worker
  are **left alone**; late events from the worker's outbox get `ack` and are dropped
  (§5.2).
- Cleanup on the worker (since 0.23, T21). When a session (or its project) is archived or deleted,
  the hub sends the worker, after `session.kill`, the frame
  `session.cleanup {session_id, workspace_path | null, cwd, event_ids[]}`
  → `ack` (example `hub.session.cleanup*.json`; added purely additively, `session.kill` did not
  change): `event_ids` are the session's inputs with attachments (since 0.46 also its
  `peer.message`s with files, buffered ones included, and the `request_id`s of its asks whose
  reply had files, §7.1). The worker deletes
  `<workspace>/<cwd>/.hqc/inbox/<event_id>` of these inputs, and for a session without a workspace
  (`null`, §8.4), its folder `<scratch_root>/<session_id>`. The worker does not trust the hub's
  paths (§2.1): the workspace is inside `allowed_roots`, `cwd` is relative without `..` and is
  resolved inside the workspace, `.hqc` and `inbox` are real directories, not symlinks; only
  direct children of `.hqc/inbox` named with an event uuid and only `<scratch_root>/<uuid>` are
  deleted, a symlink there is deleted as a link. The worker deletes nothing outside `.hqc/inbox`
  and `scratch_root`. If the worker is offline the frame is not resent; the cleanup at start
  covers this: inbox folders (children of `.hqc/inbox` named with a uuid) older than 14 days by
  modification time in workspaces known to the worker —
  `known_workspaces.json` and the working directories it wrote attachments to
  (`$HQC_HOME/inbox_dirs.json`), only inside a known workspace and `allowed_roots`.
- Worker deletion (`DELETE /api/workers/{id}?purge=1`, §6; only a revoked one with no
  non-archived sessions): its service session is deleted like a session above, its workspace
  records as in §13.2 (archived sessions lose `workspace_id` and `worker_id`, the history stays),
  then the worker's record. Files on the machine are left alone.

### 17.5 Side questions

A side question (since 0.232; the backlog's "a side question to a running session": T3 Code and
Orca ask it in a copy beside the session) is answered by the session's own agent without a turn
and without a trace in its context: the runtime reads the conversation, answers, and the agent
is not asked, does not see the question or the answer, and does not work on it.

- The owner types `/btw <question>` or `/side <question>` in the chat's composer; the client
  sends it to `POST /api/sessions/{id}/side_question` (§6) instead of the input. A text with
  files, `/btw` alone or any other command name goes as a message as before.
- The hub stores `side.question` (§4) and sends the worker `session.side_question` (§5.3),
  after `session.start` (with `no_wait`, §5.3) when the agent is not started on the connection:
  with all `max_sessions` slots busy the session is not put in line, the feed has no
  `waiting_for_slot` line, the question is answered with the error "All the agent slots of this
  worker are in use" and no agent starts later with nobody to answer; the settings of that start
  are kept for the agent's next start, as those of any start. Refused, with nothing stored: a
  room, an archived or paused session, one VS Code holds, a session of a runtime other than
  Claude Code, a worker that is offline. `history` of the frame is the earlier side questions of
  the session whose answer (the first stored, by `seq`) is a `text`, not an error one, after the
  owner's last `user.message`, the last 10, oldest first.
- The worker starts the agent's process when none runs, as for an input (resuming; no input is
  written), asks the runtime (§8.1) and stores the answer as `side.answer {question, text}`.
  The runtime's notice of its own (`synthetic: true`) and its errors go as `error`, a `null`
  answer as the error "No answer", a question that could not be asked as the reason. A process
  that ends with a question unanswered (a kill, a crash, a pause) answers it with the error
  "The agent's process ended before the answer". The idle timeout (§17.3) does not unload the
  agent while a side question is unanswered. A
  hub stores an `error` the worker answers `session.side_question` with as the question's
  `side.answer {error}`. The hub keeps the questions sent through a connection that have no
  answer yet, and when that connection closes, however it closes (the socket drops, or a new
  `hello` of the worker replaces it), it stores "The worker went offline before the answer" for
  each of them; an answer the worker sends later from its outbox is dropped (§4), and nothing
  resends the question.
- The runtime's API cost for the question is added to the process's running total, so the next
  turn of the same process shows it in its cost (`usage.cost_usd`) and in `session_tokens`
  (0.229); a process that ends before a turn does not show it. The question has no line of its
  own. Claude Code asks it on the conversation's prompt cache, which the read renews; the
  header's cache time (§6) counts from the last turn's `usage` and does not see that.
- The feed shows the question and its answer as one muted block "Side question", the answer as
  Markdown, "Answering…" until it comes, the error text when there is none; it is neither a
  message of the owner nor of the agent. A fork (§6) does not copy side events, and the hub's
  reckoning of a turn's order (§6, `agent_work`) does not count them as the agent's work.
  The events list of the client returns them as stored; `hqc_read` (§7) leaves them out, also
  in the calling session's own feed, as the agent sees neither the question nor its answer; the
  search index (§15) takes none.
- Order (§6): a question asked while the agent's text or thinking is being written has
  `during_text` and stands under that text, in the order it came, as an input does: with a
  message M, a question Q and the final answer A stored after them, the feed shows A, M, Q. A
  fork before such a message looks for the answer above it past side events.

## 18. Stack

- Hub: Rust, axum, tokio, sqlx, Postgres. Artifacts: disk or S3.
- Worker: Rust, one static binary on macOS/Linux/Windows, systemd/launchd/
  Windows service, optional tray icon. MCP server on `rmcp` (subcommand
  `hqc-worker mcp`). ACP client: the `agent-client-protocol` crate (the protocol's official
  Rust SDK), **[verify]** that it is current. Secure store for the worker token: Keychain
  on macOS (ssh keys of environments are 0600 files, §14); on Linux and Windows in the first version the worker token is a 0600 file (§5.1),
  libsecret and DPAPI later.
- Client: TypeScript, responsive web, PWA; Tauri on the same code later.
- Shared crates: `hqc-proto` (event and frame schema, versioned),
  `hqc-claude-jsonl` (transcript parser), adapters as separate crates.

## 19. Iterations

1. Hub with Postgres and Access JWT verification, worker with enrollment and outbox, delivery
   both ways with ack and the `failed` policy, Claude Code adapter with `can_use_tool`,
   web chat, permission buttons, Web Push. Simplifications: a single workspace set by
   the worker config, a single (personal) project — both lifted in 0.16 (T14), no hqc MCP.
   Criterion: start a session from the web, continue it from a phone, approve a permission.
2. ~~Projects and workspaces~~ (done in 0.16, T14: projects, several `dir` workspaces in a
   project, `fs.stat`/`fs.list_dirs`, sessions in the chosen workspace; the iteration 1
   simplification "a single workspace from the worker config" lifted), ~~the worker's service
   session~~ (0.17, T17), ~~artifacts, `.hqc/inbox`~~ (0.18, T16, without `hqc_attach`),
   ~~VS Code import and mirror, takeover both ways~~ (0.19, T15; consolidation — T18; takeover
   by the registry of live sessions and forks — 0.22, T20). Criterion: take over from a phone
   a session started in VS Code (live test `live_takeover`; checked by hand through the UI on a phone on 2026-10-25).
   Closed on 2026-10-25.
3. hqc MCP: attach, send, ask, spawn, list, search, schedule; `mcp.call` frames;
   MCP server per §7.2. Tools work on the owner's own sessions only (grants are iteration 11).
   Tasks: `docs/ITERATION-3.md`. Criterion checked by hand on the production hub on 2026-10-31.
   Closed on 2026-10-31.
4. Workspaces: ~~clone~~ (0.58, T45), ~~worktree~~ (0.60, T46), ~~ephemeral~~ (0.61, T47). Environments and bindings on the worker. Moved
   ahead of the agents on 2026-10-31; the session template (§13.3) went to `docs/BACKLOG.md`.
   Tasks: `docs/ITERATION-4.md`. Criterion checked by hand on the production hub on 2026-11-03.
   Closed on 2026-11-03.
5. Model providers (since 0.144): an Anthropic-compatible endpoint with one model, picked per
   session in the model menu; the hub keeps the owner's providers, a worker runs only those its
   `worker.toml` allows with the same `base_url`, keys stay on the worker; Claude Code stays the
   harness. Tasks: `docs/ITERATION-5.md`.
6. Secrets in a session (since 0.147): the owner gives a running agent a password or an ssh key
   from the chat, and the agent asks for one (`hqc_secret`) or makes a key for its workspace
   (`hqc_ssh_keygen`); the value reaches the agent's process, not the model, the transcript or
   the hub's storage; a key may be kept for the workspace; only a worker with `session_secrets`
   takes them (§14); and the owner's Chrome for one session (since 0.148, `browser`). Tasks:
   `docs/ITERATION-6.md`.
7. Remote MCP servers from the hub (since 0.235, #59): the owner adds a server reached by URL
   once, for all projects or chosen ones; a session's agent gets it under its own name
   (`mcp__<name>__<tool>`) through a stdio relay of the worker, and the hub makes the calls
   with the token or OAuth sign-in it keeps, so no worker, agent or transcript sees it; only an
   environment with `hub_mcp = true` takes them (§14). MCP servers that run on the machine come
   after it. Tasks: `docs/ITERATION-7.md`.
8. Skills from the hub (since 0.245, #62): the owner uploads a skill (a folder or a `.zip`)
   once, for all projects or chosen ones; the worker fetches it by its hash, puts it into a
   plugin folder of its own and starts the agent with `--plugin-dir`, so the agent has it as
   `hqc:<name>` (and `/<name>`) on every worker; the hub's copy wins over a same-named skill of
   the machine; a skill with `hooks` is refused by the hub and the worker; only an environment
   with `hub_skills = true` takes them (§14). Tasks: `docs/ITERATION-8.md`.
9. MCP servers on the machine (planned, the rest of #59): `[environments.<name>.mcp_servers]`
   of `worker.toml` declares the `stdio` and local `http` servers an environment's agents get,
   each by name next to `hqc` and the hub's relays, with `--strict-mcp-config` kept, so no
   server of `~/.claude.json` and no `claude.ai` connector comes with them; secrets are read
   from Vaultwarden at every start through a launcher of the worker, never on a command line;
   the launcher pins a hash of each server's tools (unless the server says `pin = false`), and a
   changed list fails the server until the owner approves it on the machine; `hello` names them for Settings. The hub cannot add or start one (§2.1). Tasks:
   `docs/ITERATION-9.md`.
10. Generic ACP adapter (the first agent is Hermes, including steer) and `acp_agents` on the
   worker; the bare model; the personal assistant session (moved from 3: its default runtime is
   the bare model, §8.3), until then `hqc_send` needs `session`.
11. Sharing: Grant, the "share" dialog, the "who pays" and foreign session rules. ~~Hub cron~~
   (0.38, T35, with `hqc_schedule`).
12. Tauri, native notifications, several agents in one session.

## 20. Hosting and security

- The hub listens only on the tunnel interface (in OIDC mode, only the reverse proxy reaches
  it); `/api/*` is behind Cloudflare Access with JWT verification (in OIDC mode, behind the
  proxy's sign-in, the hub verifying the provider's ID token, §6); `/worker/*` is outside
  Access, worker tokens only, rate limit on enroll;
  `artifacts.<hub-domain>` is public, signed links with a TTL only; the publication domain
  (`HQC_PUBLISH_BASE`, since 0.209) is public too, published files only (§12).
- The hub's dev mode (`HQC_DEV=1`, no Access) is allowed only on a loopback
  `HQC_HUB_LISTEN` address and without `HQC_ACCESS_*` or `HQC_OIDC_*`; otherwise the hub does
  not start (§6).
- Worker tokens: random 256 bits, only the hash in the database; revocation from the UI.
- `provider.probe` (since 0.236), what is accepted: the hub can make a worker `GET` an http(s)
  URL it names, in the worker's own network, which the hub could not reach. What comes back is
  only model ids and context windows parsed from a models list, so a compromised hub learns at
  most whether an address answers like a model server; nothing is sent there but the key the
  worker keeps for that same `base_url`.
- Remote MCP servers (since 0.235), what is accepted: the relay authenticates to the worker with
  the session token, which is on the CLI's command line as for the hqc server (§7.2), so an agent
  allowed to run commands can start a relay of its session's servers itself and call their tools
  without the CLI's permission card for each; the servers it reaches are only those of its
  project, with the owner's credentials. Give a server to the projects whose agents may act on it.
  The hub itself, not only the worker, refuses a restricted session, another runtime, and a
  session on a worker that is not its owner's: a foreign worker holds the session's token.
- Remote MCP servers (since 0.235): their header values are sealed under `HQC_MCP_KEY` and never
  leave the hub but to the server itself; no worker, agent, transcript or log line sees them. A
  server's URL is https, and the hub refuses to connect to a private, loopback, link-local or
  CGNAT address (also behind a name) unless `HQC_MCP_ALLOW_PRIVATE=1`, so an owner's server entry
  cannot reach the hub's own network by surprise; the name is resolved once per request and the
  connection goes to that address, and redirects are not followed. A relay request needs the
  session token of a session the sending worker runs; a server answers only sessions of the
  projects its owner gave it to.
- Skills from the hub (since 0.245): a skill is instructions and scripts the agent follows and
  runs, so a hub (or whoever uploads to it as the owner) that gives one to a project steers that
  project's agents on every worker with `hub_skills`, within the worker's `deny`, its
  `--disallowedTools` and the session's mode, as input can. Its `allowed-tools` lift the card
  for those tools while it is active, which a hub could do anyway by answering the card (§2.1).
  Its `hooks` would run shell commands outside all of that, so the hub refuses a skill with a
  `hooks` key in any of its `SKILL.md` files, and the worker, which does not trust the hub for
  it, refuses it again. The check finds the frontmatter as the CLI does (2.1.328: one BOM
  stripped, `^---\s*\n` with JavaScript's `\s`, up to the first `---` anywhere), refuses a first
  line with anything but spaces after `---`, and takes the frontmatter only when no character in
  it breaks a line or spaces but `\n`, `\r\n`, a space and a tab (a lone CR, U+0085, U+2028,
  U+FEFF and the like are refused: YAML and JavaScript take some of them for line breaks or
  spaces, and a security review made a hook run past a looser check with a lone CR and with
  `---` followed by U+FEFF), no line of it starts with a tab, each of its top-level lines is a plain `key:` (no quotes, `{`, `?`,
  `!` tag, `%` directive, `...` or `<<` merge) and none is `hooks`; and no line of the file at its
  first column is a `hooks:` key. The worker writes the plugin's manifest itself and the skill's
  files only under `skills/<name>/` of its own folder, so a skill cannot add a plugin's hooks,
  MCP servers, agents or commands; it unpacks only relative paths without `..`, no links, with
  the limits of §6, and checks the archive's sha256, also of an archive it kept, on every start.
  A set's folder name holds the version of the checks, so a stricter check never reuses a folder
  an older one built. What is accepted: the folders are the worker user's, so an agent of
  another session on the same worker can change a set its owner's sessions use (add a plugin's
  hooks to it), as it can change `~/.claude/settings.json`, which the CLI reads too (§14, the
  boundary between sessions of one worker is soft).
- `Origin` **[decision]**: a WebSocket upgrade of `/api/ws` without `Origin`, or with an `Origin`
  that does not match the request's `Host`, gets `403`; non-GET `/api/*` requests with a foreign
  `Origin` get `403` (without `Origin` they pass: that is how non-browser clients come). A match
  is scheme `https`, or `http` for a loopback host (dev), with host and port equal to `Host`.
  Protects against cross-site WebSocket hijacking and CSRF with an Access cookie with
  `SameSite=None`; Access additionally has SameSite Lax (RUNBOOK §1.6).
- Headers on all of the hub's responses: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self';
  connect-src 'self' wss: https:; img-src 'self' data:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
  object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`,
  `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`. The client build has
  no inline scripts (a client test checks this). HSTS is set by Cloudflare (in OIDC mode, by
  the reverse proxy, RUNBOOK §1.9).
- Limits (in the hub process's memory; the address is `CF-Connecting-IP`, otherwise the
  connection's address; with `HQC_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` (since 0.68, required in OIDC mode, §6), for a reverse proxy that puts
  the TCP peer's address in a header of its own, such as Traefik's `X-Real-Ip`, it is that header,
  otherwise the connection's address, and neither `CF-Connecting-IP` nor `CF-IPCountry` (§5.1)
  is read, since there the client could set them): `POST /worker/enroll` — 10 per minute and 10 live unconfirmed codes per
  address, 1000 in total; `POST /worker/enroll/poll` — 60 per minute per address; `/worker/ws` —
  20 invalid tokens per minute per address (beyond that `429` without a database query), a token
  of the wrong shape does not reach the database, at most 16 token checks at once (`503`); client
  and worker WebSocket messages up to 1 MiB, the send queue to a worker is bounded (overflow drops
  the connection, the state is resent from the database after `hello`). On top of that, a
  Cloudflare WAF Rate Limiting rule on `/worker/*` (RUNBOOK §1.6).
- Limits against a compromised worker or its token (since 0.23, T22; threat model
  §2.1). The numbers are the hub's `Limits` (`config.rs`); there are no environment variables for
  them. Where a rule differs from the text of the section given in parentheses, this table wins:
